and is an exact imitation of' the regular thing, except .oat the bees fashion their cells of walls only 1-125th of an inch wide, while human artificers have not yet become so deft. The cells are filled with glucose, which is the swis syrup of common corn, and looks and tastes like honey, The cells, once filled, are closed by smearing a hot iron plate over the wax tops, and the product is sold as the "best clover honey." It is in great demand and outsells the regu- lar honey.—Hereford Times. THE NIGHTCAP.—Dr. Richardson has supplied a few figures which will tend to shake belief in the fashionable " nightcap"—that is, the glass of grog which precedes bed. A man in a standing position will have a pulse at 74, 70 whilst he is sitting, and 64 when in a recumbent attitude. This is the effect of position on the pulse. At night nature gives the heart rest. The heart is doing ten strokes less per minute. Multiply that by an ordinary night's sleep of eight hours, and it is nearly 5,000 strokes of rest. As the heart throws out six ounces of blood at every stroke, it makes a difference of 30,000 ounces of propelling during the night --The nightcap" of grog accelerates the action of the heart, and therefore works it more. Instead of getting , test you put on something like 15,900 extra strokes, and the ' result is that you are not only not so much rested as you might be, but nature has been unduly taxed by extra exer- tion and it is the pace that wears. This sounds very rea- sonable. Dr. Richardson is an authority who cannot be well ignored. BORING FOR SALT I'TEAR MIDDLESBROUGH.—The salt boring operations are proceeding at Port Clarence, opposite Middlesbrough. At the mouth of the taint+ there is a col- lection of "cores," composed of red sandstone, mostly in a " shaly " condition. These had been brought up from be. ow, and each of them contained a mark signifying the depth where it was found. The bed of salt, which was touched in boring on Saturday, is almost like a basin in shape. The top layer is formed of chloride of sodium. thloride of potassium is also met with, which on the Con- tinent is worked with good commercial results. In the case iat the crystalline that is met with in boring, it seems to be 'questionable whether the method of boring will admit of its bSing made valuable. The deposit at Port Clarence is from 11000 to 19 100 feet deep, as compared with 600 feet at Nancy, a and in another instance on the Continent it was only 40 yards from the surface. At Port Clarence they had met with a layer of gypsum some 10 feet deep. They Met 45 feet of clay; then at 95 feet from the surface they came to sandstone rock, and at 120 feet they first brought up a "core." They found gypsum at 1,-003 feet, whereas in former borings in adjoining land they had found it 95 feet leaver down. The succeeding gradations would be first salt, then good salt, and then rock salt. -

-------- --- THE ROSY SPRING. Stoma, I come, with the birds and the flowers, And deck with rich foliage the trees, woods, and bowers; To spread over nature a garment of green, The verdure springs bright where my footprints have been, I loose with mx,hreatjo h , fr,ozen up streams. And spread fight eat Olir With bright sunny beams. itiit The blithsome young ' ^bians that Sport on the lea, The gay singing warblers are companions for me. I bring the light'showers to water the earth, And enliven the scenes which winter made dearth; I prepare the gay beauties for summer so fair. Then to other lands over the seas I repair, The bright vernal scenes and the birds on the wing Rtjoieevit my coming, for I am called Spring. at. Relent. . J. G. Piciftwanirt. ------ FANTASTICAL BICYCLE. Fanciful structure on course espeditional. Thou strikest the gaze like a form apparitional. With strangely bewildering slide. Thy shadowy outline is phantasmagorical Thou deentist (to littera phrase metaphorical) A sort of personified glide. What wondrous inventor with mind methodistieal Conceived. thy idea, aerial, mystical. Yet se-matisematielly true? The bradirjwhich concocted thy airy machinerylmagise&thrsptral effect on the scenery— Was ghostly and dreamy as you. Philosophers tell us inventions mechanical Are made by observing the structure organicai Which all throughout nature abound. But were she subjected to strictest of scrutiny By geniuses Archimedean or Newton-Y Thy prototype would not belotind. Thou lams nature—thou wild. irresponsible. Filmy objective to all that's demonstrable— Fantastic, ridiculous word I Thy gyrates mesmerical puzzle hutnanity, Thou outcome of science, inspired by insanity, Thou wavy, embodied absurd.

_ HELEN THE FAIR. How sweet in the evening. When free from all care, To roam in the twilight With Helen the fair. Her fairy form's slender. Light golden her hair • She trips o'er th•l sod nimbly: Sweet Helen the fair. The glance of her bins eyes There's few can compare Irja She's the choicest of jewels Is Helen the fair. .1 In Devon's thire, blooming, ..r.jr Where sweet violets grow. - • , Sbe.is seen from the hills • • In-the valley telow.

Jrug's Clough. THE NIGHTINGALE. When nigh t.'s dark curtains close around, And hushed is e'en the faintest sound. When flowers their lovely petals close, , And nature sinks to sweet repose. Each bird has ceased its so,gs to sing. And hides its head beneath its wing. ' The pale moon sheds a silvery light, And zephyr's blow on the balmy night.-14 At midnight's hour when all is still, The queen of songsters witchingly fill The senses of man with a glad delight As she sings her songs to the still, still night. New soft and low like a spirit voice, Then full and clear, and mellow and sweet,— The ears of the raptured listener greet. Etherial music the soul would entice, belleVeTn another world it lives. So charmingly sweet are the songs she gives. St. Helens. - J. G. PICZERSGILL.

1100 D FOR Faux HORSES.—The fall allOwance of oats for a farm horse may be set down at fourteen pounds per day, which, in my opinion, is a very full allowance; in- teed, except in cold, wet weather, when working hard under p lverse conditions, fourteen pounds Is more than I should give, preferring rather to make up with hay. Maize is daily becoming more extensively used, and will eventually be- come as indispensable an article of horse food as was formerly oats, over which it has undoubtedly superiority in some directions, whilst in others the oppesite is the case. One of the largest firms of carriers in London gives but eight pounds of corn per day, it consisting of equal portions of oats and maize, with a few beans and such like additional flavourings as time and opportunity may suggest. The horses of these carriers are always fat and healthy-looking, appearing to all intents and purposes to do as well as the adverse conditions of their existence in a cramped city will I allow. The shortcoming, if ally, is a mere matter of opinion as far as regards corn, is made up by hay and straw chaffed to the usual fineness, each horse receiving a certain quantity, but not by any means measured in the style of "as much as it will eat."- On the contrary, every lot is weighed out carefully. , NORTHERN FARMERS AND ,SorrTHERN FARMS.—The landlords of the Southern and Midland Counties would do well to have upon some of their numerous tenaptless farms a few of the Northern farmers Who are keenlynooking out for good investments. Between South Lancashire and Scot- land there are hundreds of farmers making a living, and paying good rents to Lord Derby fend other great land- owners, upon land which would starve the majority of far." mers in the South. They are able to work like Trojans ; have a good sound agricultural knowledge; many of them a' little capital, some more than a little, and are content with an expenditure upon their own needs and those of their' families which would seem comparative beggary to many Southern farmers. These are the men to farm at a profit where others would fail, when the margin between butler and return is narrowed as it is at present. Instanees are now, being given of this movement extending to the Midlands, five farmers from one parish in Scotland having just migrated to English farms. Special note is made of Mr. Lawson, a Forfarshire man, who has been granted a nineteen years' lease of one of Lord Lytton's farms in Hertfordshire, upon terms encouraging to the tenant, and promising to be remunerative to the landlord.—Land. BITFTER MAKING.—THE TRMFERATORE OF THE CREAM. —Much depends upon the temperature of the cream when the churning is commenced. Cream when put into the churn should never be warmer than 53deg. to 55deg. F. It rises' duriiig the churning from 4deg. to 10deg. above its original temperature. The importance of attending to the temperature and to the quickness of churning when the best quality of butter is required is shown by the following series of results, obtained in the churning of cream at different temperatures and with different degreeri Of rapidity. These experiments were made in Edinburgh, hy Mr. Baliantyne between June and August. ' The quantity of crewel he timed at each 'churning waa eight gallons—weighing eight pounds to the gallon : Temperature. Butter. Cream. Butter: Time. Per Gal. ' F. deg:4'. deg.. Hrs. lbs. oz. 66 ...... 60 52, these two could not be stir- -52 65 50 ing. • 531 .. 574 To obtain butter from cream, therefore, both finest in quality and largest in quantity, these experiments prescribes the following temperatures of the cream, and time in churn- ing :--52deg. to 56deg., two hours ;'sSitieg. to 574c1eg.; hours. It as probable that the nature of the erearnr obtained at different seasons Or in different localities may render a long time necessary in the churning on some occasions or in some places than in others. PROSFEcTS ax NORTH LANCASHIRE.--Writing, on April ‘1.2, R., in Agricultural Gazette, says :—We have the first rain that' has fallen since March 25, since when severe uight frosts and cold east winds have prevailed, and only last week Bassenthwalle Lake was frozen over. The fields And hill 'sides are bare and brown, and look AS though vegetation had been stricken with death. Our carts of swedes may now be 'counted on the fingers of one hand; but we have yet agitbd reserve of masgeli. Hay and 'straW are getting scarce, and even in the middle of the warm sunny days there was nothing in the shape of food worth turning out the mllch stock for. Despite all efforts, ewes were short of milk, the lambs set up their backs, and, their coats looked as though ,they had been combed the wrong' way, a ante sign-that they are not making healthy progress. In the Duke of Devon- shire's flock at balker, I am told that 170 ewes have pro- duced doubles, and 70 singles, and this without the loss of a single ewe. I hear of isolated cases of sheep dying of fluke; but in the neighbourhood of Furness the land is mostly too dry for the disease to spread, and we are particular in giving Chanee of pasture. The greatest evil, I believe, that you' San do to sheep is to keep them too long on the same ground. The dry weather has been useful in allowing -us to bring up arrears of arable work. We have finished both oat and barley sowing, and have made fair progress in preparing for turnips, mange', potatoes, Sze. The latter now sell at about £3 per ton; butter, Is. 7d. to is. Bd. per lb. Both oat and barley land harrowed up very kindly, and as some gentle showers fell at intervals yesterday, continued throughout the night, and for some hours this morning, iollowectfiy, warm sunshine this afternoon, and a much heightened tem- perature-, we anticipate "seeing grass grow.", , APTAarcsna, Fianatraga.—Seldom have so many points of advanced farming been comprehended in a" single speech as we find in one recently delivered by Mr: W. Mathew, at a meeting of the Lsavorth Farmers' Club. A paper had been read on "Neat &ear.," and Mr. 'llaathew, in joiningin the discussion, observed, in the first place, that a greatjcieal d nonsense ha.d,been talked ,pf, and appeared in the papers, about giving up corn growing; and laying land,,down to grass. This would not enable them to keep more stock 9n the land, as larger numbers might be reared and fed under the four-course system of arable management than by lay- ing down a field entirely to grass. Mr. Mathew then went on to speak of dairy husbandry, and said that in the old times his mother used to make a good profit when butter only sold for 10d. a pound, but she only gave her dairymaids £4 a year, and now they were scarcely procurable at four times that amount. Besides which the old servants were much more efficient, the only fault to be found with them being that they got up so very early in the mokning that ' they consumed too much fire and candle, the modern ones never being guilty of this now. Mr. Mathew advocated strongly the employment of cottoncake in feeding dairy cows. It was first used at his place when procurable at only £4 per ton as an experiment, and although lineeed cake had been eipployed in the feeding previously, an improvement in the creardt hid been diaceverable in 24 herirs. lie had fed his dairy cows with the substance ever since, but now that it was almost double the cost, and the duty had been taken , off malt, perhaps the latter product mightbe advantageously' I substituted. He also alluded to the great hen:efits derivable I by feeding dairy -cows, in houses during hot weather, ob- serving that a cow,ln the 'open 'field' on a hot day 'maid stand for hours under some shady tree, tormented by Ales. After giving fnll adhesion to the 'opinion that the Ctirnber- land farmers, by turning all the produce of the farm into butter, cheese, or meat, had laid hold of the most, remunera- tive 'ystein of rnantigement, this advanced practical man went on toI score vet another point in recotinmenling grazing farmers to rear ti;eir own stock. This he' illustrated by the reflection that in bringing up a beast to be worth £l6 or 417 there was a good deal of manure made, which was lost to the buyer, who might just as well have brought up the beast from a calf, and thus got the manure. Beef could also be fed more economically by the grazier rearing his own stock, for even good judges were often deceived in what they bought in finding cattle not practically worth as much by a a head as their cost, although they might have ap- peared chap et„the'time of purchase.—Farmers' Chronicle.

At the annual meeting of the Durham .County Franchise Association on Saturday, was resolved that, in the event of the Government passing ti bill ..ssimilating the county and borough franchise, the miners should take steps to send a candidate of their own Go the House of Commons. It was understood that Mr. W. Crawford, the general secretary of t,he Miners' Association, will be selscted. The progressof Brighton has been astonishingly rapid. A hundred years ago it contained 7QO houses, inhabited by some 3,000 persons many of whom were engaged•inlishing. The property in the village was then assessed at £2,3C0 a year. .To‘day - Brighton contains 16,000 houses, 100,000 souls, and is assessed at considerably in excess of half a

, million. The Rev. T. Pelham Dale, late of St. ,Vedast's, has been inducted into the living of Sausthorpe, Lincolnshire, by the Bishop of Lincoln (Dr. Wordsworth). Archdeacon 'Kaye, in whose archdeaconry Sausthorpe is situatdd, on heiring of the intended induction at onde tendered his resignation. The living given to Mr. Dale is of the annual value of £220, mil the population is about 126. The Rev. C:Trollope Brian is the patron. ' Mr. H. Kains-Jackson, reporting on our crop prospects, says the farm lands of the country must now be worth ten millions sterling more than they were two years ago. As regards the growing crop they are all very backward, and the wheat plant is not regular in colour, but it is generally well rooted and is tillering satisfactorily. The tender -Of the engine, Which was going first, almost miraculously escaped being thrown off the rails, and the steam, being applied the train fortunately got over the obstructions. • Several arrests have been made. , . A WIFE BEATEN ON HER WEDDING DAY.—At Bury, on Monday, a well-dresseciyoung woman applied to the magis- trates for a warrant for the apprehension of her husband. She said she was married to James Buckley, a pattern maker, at Radcliffe, on the 10th March. On her wedding clay her husband beat her twice-, he had since frequently ill-used her, and on Friday last he knocked her down. She had been acquainted with her husband three years before their marriage. She had now left him.—The magistrates granted a summons. Several " professional " London burglars and two persons "occupying respectable positions" in Abingdon have been convicted at Reading Assizes, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, and sent to penal servitude. One of the'Abingdun "respect- ables," aman named Heath, who-had invited the London professionals down to his house, and with their aid. coin- mitted several robberies, was sent to penal servitude for 14 years; four others were sentenced to shorter terms. , Bernsr UNION.—The annual session of the Baptist Union of Great Britain .and Ireland was opened on Monday, in Bloomsbury Chapelo London, under the presidency of the Rev. Di. Tristrail, the retiring president. The new presi- dent, the Rev. Henry Dawson, was inducted, and delivered hie address upon "Our Union in Connection With the First Principles of Divine Truth." The financial stateinent was afterwards submitted and adopted. The Rev. J. Jenkym Brown, Birmingham, was appointed the president for the year; and a resolution was adopted embodying a petition to Parliament against the opium traffic.—ln the evening the BiLle Translatioa Society held its annual Meeting in Blooms- bury Chapel. . . , Mr. Bradlaugh appeared before • the Lords Justices on 1 Wednesday, and requested to be allowed to argue a fresh point in the action brought against him.by Mr. Clarke. The point was—lie was sued for a penalty of £5OO for sitting and voting in the House of Commons without first taking the oath prescribed by statute. To the action' he pleaded that he had made an affirmation, and the plaintiff replied that he was not'a person entitled to make an affirmation; as be had no religious belief. The question of "religious belief" was not argued, and he wished to argue it, unless the plyntiff would agree to strike out those words, when he I Would. be content. Lord Justice Bramwell-said Abet substantially. the question had not been argued before them, and they would 'accede to the /triplication; and fix Monfav next ftir the hearing. . On Tnes&aj miirrarig i man named' George Cruse was passing through the railway arch in Walworth-road what he discovered afire- on the premisei of Me'. Alted;'-atitioner and bookseller, 98, Walworth-road, London, *Litt once gave the alarm, and five engines from the surrounding Eititlinns were promptly on the spot. A search 'was made in the building but no one was found, and it was concluded thht no one Slept on the premises.' In abed two hours the'. fire, which had burnt the house And shop clean through, was got under, and Captain Shaw and most of the 'firemen left. Shortly after this'efireatart named Dobbin went,to the back part of the honset.,4o4 thought he saw a man at the window of, i smelt ante-inotrt 'OVer 'the seullerY *Bich 'had eseaPed the fire. He made his way to the room, and found that the proprietor (Mr. Allen), his wife, and children Were in this room and were all dead except Mr. Allen, who was taken to, Guy',o Hospital. The bodies of Mrs. Allen and the tpree children weiii itineved toNiiiington Mortuary.' . At a London Police Court, on Tuesday, some extra- 1 ordinary statements- Were Made relative to the alleged ill- treatment of a lady who died lately, after having been three years confined in a county lunatic asylum. The revelAtione are simply incredible. It is stated that the deceased lady had been literally starved to death, there being hardly any flesh on the body, and the bones coming through the skin. There werekleo bruises on the body, appearing to show that the deceased had been subjected to violence of 'a serious character. The case will be brought under the notice of the Lunacy Commissioners, and a full investigation . will, no doubt, show that the deceased patient's relativea have been labouring under some grave misapprehension of the real ;Acta of the, case. -The horrors enacted within the walls of lunatiC asylums are happily a thing of the past, and the public would be greatly Shocked-to believe anythiag to the contrary. At the present day there are few things left un- done in our asylums to alleviate the unfortunate condition of those suffering from the most tersible of human infirmities. PROSECUTION OF Ali ANTINACCINATOE- SCENE IN A COURT—At Leicester Amos Booth, secretary of the National Anti-Compalsory Vaccination League, was summoned for non-compliance with the Vaccination Acts. In his defence Mr. Booth proceeded to show reasonable excuse according to the act, and to read a letter from Lord Clifton. He was stopped by the bench, and Mr. Booth declared that he was stopped because he was not a red tape Sollciter'. Be ras also stopped reading extracts from the reports of thelocal medical- officer of health, but be declined to discontinue his . his speech. Defendant called upon subpcena Dr. Denton, -vaccination officer for 'St. Margaret's, who admitted that about three years ago vaccination was suspended in his dis- trict because children had died from erysipelas after being vaccinated. Dr. Beggs was called, but failed to answer, and a certificate of death from vaccination, given by him, was produced. There were continuous interruptiOns by the bench during the defendant's speech, which lasted over an hour. The bench fined him ' 10s. and £2 10. costs, or seven days' imprisonment,. As defendant was leaving the court be was stopped by-tWo policemen, who tiled to detain him, but the chief constable reprovedthern, and subsequently Mr. Booth harangued the crowd in front of the Town-hall, inviting the people to the sale of Pis goods under distraint to see who would buy Stolen property. • Compulsory Church rates survive, it appears, in the parish of St. Saviour, Southwark, where, it may be remembered, a " contest" is going on for the appointment of chaplain. Two magistrates for Surrey were engaged on Saturday in adjudi- csting upon summonses against persons who could not or would not pay. The rate is levied under a local Act dating from the time of the pi ou s, Charles rr. and ratified in the time of George 111., and it is expended in providing for the stipend of the minister and the repair of the fabric of the church. A working man out of work, a "poorly clad woman" who appeared for her husband, the representative of a gas company, and several merchants and tradesmen were amongst the people objecting to the rate. One of the magistrates, a Mr. Brookskank, when asked by a defendant "if it was rational that he should spend £2OO in appealing," remarked, with singular appropriateneis and dignity. "that a greet many people would do so in order to attain t e dignity. of martyrdom?' One of the defendants objected o pay for the wasting of surplices, and was informed thl t that was a question the Court could not entertain. Orders for payment were made in every case.

1. The object of the bill is for the purpose of further amending the 'laws relating to the occupation and owner-

- _ ship of land-in- lraand, and-for 'otfierPurposes relating part relates to the ordinary- co'nditions of the ' to. The first' te cies, and givtakpoweroto the tenant for the time being I of ery tenancy to which the bill applies to sell his tenancy, but to one person only. He must-first give notice to his tan lord that he is going' to Belli and the landlord may then eta' to purchase the tenant'a interest, the amount .to be settled by the Court, in case the Partlea cannot agree. The Co 'rt referred to is the Comity Court where the land is situ-. atb If landlord will not Purchase, tenant may sell to some oth r person; but landlord may refuse 'to accept the pou- ch er as tenant if ,he bias man,of, insufficient means, or of back character, or if he has already- failed as a farmer, or for an,, other reasonable cause whidh the Gourtaithy deem suffi- cie t. The salts 'mast also be Made subjeckto provieions Con- ti tai ed in the bill with respect to the sale of a tenancy which is übject to statutory conditions, and which are hereafter setf out ithr aragraph 4. -Where tenancy, is subject to pat to conditions, and sale is made in consequence of proceed. logs by landlord for recotering possession by reason of the -br ach by the tenant of any condition except payment of re t, the Court may grant landlord out of. sale compensation for any injury sustained by tenant's default. Where any improvements are made by landlord, during tenancy, 'for which no increased rent has been 'charged to tenant, the landlord shall be ,entitled to compensation out of sale of tenant's interest. If tenant sells his tenancy, the purchaser from him shall pay to landlord out of purchase-money any arrears of rent or other moneys.due from tenant to landlord. Tenant is not to be entitled both to sell his tenancy and to receive compensation for being disturbed therein and for improvements he may have made. Tenant holding under Ulster tenant-right custom, or to a usage of a similar character, may sell his interest either under the custom or the clauses in the bill, but not partly Ander both (Section l,). (Note.—By the Ulster tenant-right custom, which has mined in that part of Ireland for a long period, the tenant of a holding or farm may sell his tenant-right and interest. and give up possession to the purchaser.) , 2. The tenant may by will leave his tenancy to one per- son, but if tenant • dies without a will, or he leaves his tenancy to more than one person, the landlord may require the tenancy to be sold by the representatives of the, deceased, within twelve months after death (section 2). 3. Where landlord demands increased rent from present or future tenant beyond amount paid at beginning of tenancy, then for 15 years after rent increased (called in the bill a statutory term) such tenancy is to be subject to sta- tutory conditions (see paragraph 4). , It tenant will not pay increased rent be may sell, his tenant*, and, in addition to price he obtains for it, he shall be entitled to claim from landlord ten tithes the amount the Court may decide to be ,the excess of the increased rent demanded by the landlord over a fair rent, or, if the tenancy were subject' to Uleter tenant right custom or similar thereto, such an ammint as the Court might decide the selling value to have been de- preciated, whichever of the said sums might be the greater. Where tenant will not pay increased rent, and is compelled. to quit, but does not sell his tenancy, he is to be entitled ti compensation as if landlerd,.had turned him out. Instead of either agreeing or declining to pay increased rent, tenant may apply to Court to have a fair rent fixed. ' (Section 3.) 4., Tenant shall not during stOtocory term (fifteen Yeare) ' be compelled to pay higher re.i:. than he paid at commence-, ment, and shall not be compelled to quit except for breach of' one of the following Conditions (called in bill statutory, conditions) :—He must pay rent when due; he nthist not commit waste by dilapidation of buildings or'deterioration of the soil after notice from landlord to desist from such in- jurious acts; he must permit the landlOrd (on receiving reasonable compensation for any injury to farm) a mine and take the minerals—quarry stone &c.--ctit turf &Aim-. ber, make roads or drains, view condition of premises, and to hunt, shoot, and fish over the propertY.t • The tenant also must not sub-divide or sub-let his holding, nor do any act whereby it might be taken possession: of by his judgment creditor or by his assignee if he became 'bankrupt. If, dur- 1 ing statutory term (15 years), the landlord can satisfy the Court' that it will be for the benefit of the estate, or Otelie labourers on the estate, in respect of cottages, gardene, Or 1 allotments, that he (the landlord) should resume possession,' the Court may require the tenant to give up his tenancy to the landlord, upon receiving full compensation. (Secticin 4.) 5. The fifth section of the bill relates to cotilpensation to tenants for disturbance by landlords, and it repeals section 3' of the Irish Landlord and Tenant Act,lB7o, which fakes the compensation to be paid to the tenant for disturbance at not more than £250. In lien of that Section, this bill provides that the tenant shall be entitled for compensation for dis- turbance in his tenancy as follows :—Where his yearly rent is under £3O, a sum not' exceeding seven year's rent; under £5O, not exceeding -five years' rent; under £lOO, not ex- ceeding four years' ; and where. the rent is £lOO or upwards, nth exceeding three years' rent. Section 6 also provides that a tenant shall be entitled to compensation for :improve- ments made by him, notwithatanding he may have surren- derecL,his old tenancy daring which improvements were . 1 Suede, and a new lease has been granted. 6. The second part of the bill relates to the power of the Court to interfere between landlord and tenant as to rent to be paid. It provides that the present tenant, or the land- lord and tenant jointly, may apply to the Court from time io time to fix what is a fair rent to be paid. A fair rent is defined to be such as the Court thinks (taking the dream- etances of each case into consideration) a solvent tenant Would undertake to pay one year with another—if rent fixed , (which is to be-ailltia' ihillidielal- rent) is equal tO be less' titan rent paid before, it' is to horantenee fibni 'nen rent day. If rent fixed is more than Was paid before, it is to be paid from rent day next 'after landlord gives notice that he will claim increased rent, which he may do any' time within 15 Years. If landlord does not claim increased tent, then if tenant sells his tenancy, the Court may grant landlord Mich a sum as considered reasonable for his not having advanced the rent. Where judicial rent fixed, then or 15 years' tenancy cannot be terminated by landlord 'au' plying-to resume the holding. If an application be made by tenant to Court to have rent fixed, the Court may eefuse, if satisfied that the' landloni has made the improve- 'ruents. On the holding.' On an application to fix rent for Iholding not subject to Ulster tenant-right, the landlord and ttenant may agree to fix, or, in case of dispute, court may fix a specified value for the holding—then, if ,at any time tenant wishes to sell, landlord may resume possession on payment to tenant of amount fixed and the value of thp improvements afterwards made by tenant. A further statu- tory term of 15 years shall not commence until a former one has expired, nor shall any alteration of judicial rent be made at less intervals than 15 years (Section 7.) 7. If Court, on hearing application, be of opinion that conduct of either party is unreasonable, or that one party has refused any reasonable proposal of the other, it may im- pose upon him the costs of the proceedings or make such other order in the matter as the Court thinks consistent with justice. (Section 8.) 8. Part 3 of the bill giies power to landlord and tenant to exclude it in certain cases. It provides that the parties may agree to a lease (called a judicial lease) for 31 years or upwards, and if lease sanctioned by Court, the tenancy shall not be subject to the clauses in the bill. (Section 9.),--- 9. The landlord and tenant may also agree that a tenancY shall be a fixed one, subject to a rent to be agreed upon, and in that case the tenant cannot be compelled to quit, except' on breach of some one of the statutory conditions set out in ! the 4th paragraph. (Sections 10 and 11:, 10. The fourth part of the bill contains sevteral simple- ' mental,. provisions to the above. It provides that where landlord demands -a higher rent from a new tenant who has purchased old tenant's interest than the preceding tenant paid, the new tenant may sell his tenancy at once, and land- lord shall be liable for depreciation 'in value in consequence of his increasing the rent. (Section 12.) 11. Where proceedings taken by landlord to compel tenant to quit, the tenant may sell his tenancy and apply to Court to fix future rent. (Section 13.) Landlord, in order to compel tenant to quit for non-payment of rent, must proceed in legal course by judgment; and for any, other breach by tenant the landlord cannot proceed against him except by ejectment founded on nntice to quit. (Sec-. tion 13.) , 12. A tenancy for a year certain shall be deemed to be one from year to year, and the tenant under a tenancy less than a yearly tenancy shall have some rights as yearly tenant, except where land is let for some temporary purpose. (Section 16.) 13. Any tenant whose holding is valued at not less than 450„a year may by writing contract himself out of the provisions of the bill, but any other tenant cannot. (Sec- tionl7.) 14. A landlord, being a limited owner, may, with sanction of Court, exercise powers given by bill as if he were absolute owner, and any moneys arising therefrom are to be dealt with according to law applicable with respect to purchase money or compensation coming to parties having limited interest. - (Section'l3.) 15. The fifth part of the bill relates to the important snb- jects of the purchase or acquisition of land by tenants—the reclamation of. waste lands and emigration—it provides a Court to be called the Land Commissioniand gives power to Court to advance to tenant who has agreed to purchase his holding three-fottrths of the purchase-money,. and where tenant has -agreed to purchase on the terms of paying his landlord, a certain sum called a fine and afterwards a yearly rent called a fee farm rent, the Court may advance to tenant one-half of fine he has agreed to give landlord, but the fee farm rent must not be more than three-fourths of what the Court thinks is a fair rent for the property, where an tate is subject-to any mortgage or other incumbranee the Land Commission may ideathify the tenant who purchases against such incambrance. (Section 24.) • • „ • 2a.r II& provisions surto reclamation of land are moat importadt--*they provide that the Treasury may authorise the Board of Works to advance to companies such sums of , money as the Treasury think expedient for reclamation or improvement of waste or uncultivated lands—for drainage of land or agricultural improminent works. The amount' advanced is not to be more than that company have ad- vaneed or expended out•of their own.moneys, 'except where a satisfactory guarantee is given, and theh the advance may be two-thirds of such guarantee. The advances are to be made at such interest and repayable within such periods as the Boatdrof Works advance money under the Public Works Loan Act of 1879. (Section 25.) 21. Emigration is provided for as follows :—The Land Commission may, with concurrence of the Treasury, enter into agreements with any person er &sly 4,f pereons having : authority to contraet,on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, or of any province thereof, m on behalf of any British colony, or any State or district therein, or on behalf of any public body or company, to advance such sums of money as Land Commission' may think desirable to promote emigration from Ireland. Such loans are to be repayable at such times and at such interest as advances made for reclamation of land, and which are mentioned in the last paragraph. (Section 26) 22.. An advance made by the Land, Commission ,to pur- chase hi respect of one purchase shall not exceed £3,000, unle.as there are special circumstances when, with the con- sent of the Treasury, the advance may extend to £5,000. , one of whom must be or have been a Judge of the Shpreme • Court of Justice in Ireland, each of them shall receive a salary not exceeding £2,000 a year. Assistant Land Com- missioners may be appointed when necessary. (Sections 34, 36, and 39.) 25. Any person not satisfied with the decision of the County Court with respect to the determination of any matter may appeal to the Land Commission, and such Commission may confirm modify, or reverse , the decision of the County Court (Section 41.) , 27. Where the landlord purchases the tenant's interest in .exercise of his right of pre-emption, and not on, the appli- cation or by the wish of the tenant, or as a bidder in the ' .open market, then if the landlord within 15 years from the passing of the Act mike the same-holding to anothettenant, the same shall be subject from the time when it has been relet to all the pro.visions of the bill; and a tenant holding under Ulster tenant-fight mibtom shall be entitled to the . benefit of such custom, notwithstanding the determination of tenancy by breach Of one of the statutory conditions men,. - fioned in the bill. (Section 45.) 28. The bill, with the exception of st) much thereof as amends the Act of 1870 in respect of compensation for im- provements, and with the exception of that part which re- lates to tenants purchasing their holdings, the reclamation I of 'lend and emigration shall notapply to any holding whichl is not either agricultural or pastoral;or partly of each, or any holding near to a town which bears an incregaed value as accommodation land over and above the ordinary letting value of land occupied as a farm, and is in the occupation of a person living 'in the town: or its suburbs, or any holding used wholly or mainly for pasture, and having an annual value of not less. thin £5O; or any holding used chiefly for pasture if tenant does not reside thereon, or on some hold- ing adjoining which is in his' oc6ipation or where the tenant holds by reason of his being a hired. labourer or servant or any letting or agistment or for temporary convenience or pasturage, nor is it to apply to any cottage allotment not exceeding a quarter of an acre. E.... 63.386 West Virginia 618,443 ... 314,479 ... 303,984 ... 98,165 Wisconsin 1,315,480 ... 682,106 ... 635,374 ... 93,42 Wyoming 20,788,... 14,151 ... 6,637 ... 46,90 AN ORIGINAL REMEDY FOR MOUNTAIN SICIENNss.-Mr. Whymper, in his recent lecture on Chimborazo and Cotapaxi to the Society Of Arts, described that dreaded enemy of the Alpine climber, " mountain sickness," and stated that he was not aware that anybody who had fought with the enemy "has ever suggested the bare possibility of coining out vic- torious from such an encounter." In ;the course of an as, cent of Mont Blanc made many years ago I achieved such a victory in a very odd manner, and the incident may be worth recording, as it suggests a physiological problem and a possible means of performing journeys which this sickness renders quite impracticable to men of ordinary constitution. It was late in the season and we had great difficulty in crossing the " Bergschrund," or last crevass where the ice is parted from the pyramid of rock forming the summit. At last we found a'practicable place, and on crossing it David Coutet, our chief guide, and then a very old man, performed a rolling somersault iodine snow by way of jubilation. I followed his example, i improved upon it by standing for a while on my head and kicking my heels in the air, in fur- ther exultation. Up to this moment I had been very faint and sick, though not actually vomiting, but after this ex- ploit I recovered and suffered the sickness no longer. Was this a mere coincidence, or was the recovery connected with the inversion by any link of natural causation? To answer this question we must consider the nature of the sickness. It is doubtless produced by-the rarity of the air, but how? We know that when breathing such attenuated air the blood is insufficiently supplied with oxygen, and we may justly infer that the brain is thereby deprived of the nourishment Nig stimulus demanded for its normal vigorous action. This riWuntain sickness is evidently not merely a disturbance of the stoupch,. but an affection of the brain producing a general lowering of vitality. The languid funereal crawl of brawny vigorous men is quite ludicrous. Talking, even thinking, demands a fatiguing effort. The sense of faint- ing and sickness is similar to that which is produced by loss of blood, or the contemplation of some ghastly horror. The , ordinary treatment of fainting is to lay the patient down, in order that as much blood „Is possible may reach the brain, or , even to keep the head below the general level of the body. Thus, without any theory, or any intention of relieving the sickness, I applied the ordinary remedy for ordinary faint. ing, but in an exaggerated form. I therefore conclude that the bodily inversion was the Vera causa of the altered sens Pa" - tions, and recommend Mr. Whvm er, when he "does Mount Everest, to try this as well as chlorate of potash. A Httle preliminary practice on a soft pillow will enable him to turn up at a moment's notice, and as often as desirable, on the soft snow, which is especially favourable for the exploit._ Further practice on the " Catherine wheel" mode qProgreision familiar to street Arabs will qualify lAncti apply, this remedy without breaking the jopti- nev.by tne usual gaspipg halts, that render all upward loci- gressiowat great altitudes so very slow and tedious 4-- Gentleman's Magazine. ..• HOUSE OF CODEKONS.--Motrnay. • ' -Upon, the House of Commons reassembling after the Easter vacation there was a Ike attendance of members and of strangers. ,

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. ' The St. Helens and 'District Trams Bill was read a third time. . The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Bill was read second time. NATIONAIii MEMORIAL TO LORD BEACONSFIELD.—TANd RICHARD GROS/ENOR intimated that on that day fortnight Mr: filadstonemill'proposer that theS House resolve itself into committee to prepare a !mishit 'address to Her Majesty, praying her to' issue,her commands that a monument _ke' ere-cted, in the Collegiate Chapel of St. Peter, Westminster, to the memory of the Earl of Beaconsfield. SOLICITORS GUILTY OF CORRUPT PRACTICES.— An in- teresting question was put by Mr. Rylands relative to the numerous solicitors scheduled by the election commissioners as guilty of corrupt practices and bribery. Tim Attorney- General stated that it was not intended to take any steps against the gentlemen in question who had received certifi- cates of indemnity. Though these latter did not come techni- cally within the Act, the Incorporated Law A ~sociation con- sidered that they came within its spirit, and therefore refused to' take action. Tan Tstannefasx:--It was stated by Mr. GRANT-DUFF that tio petition had been received at the Colonial Office from the inhabllants of the Transvaal on the subject of the Queen's suzerainty. Ths Focrr AND MOUTH Diszaan.-,--Mr. Mundella announced that foot-and-mouth-disease had broken out at Carlisle, and and that the whole of the city had been declared an infected area. Islzw Mzunzas—Mr. Ross and Mr. Tollemache took their seats respectively for St. Ives and West Cheshire. THE Fansocx COMMERCIAL TREATY. Replying to 'a question, Sir CHARLES DILER stated. • that Mr: Kennedy was in Paris making preliminary quiries affecting the French commercial treaty, but no formal negotiations had yet: begun. He had promised to keep the country well informed of what was going to be done, and he should do so. , • - Ts Lawn BlLL.—Thet- ATronsunr-Ginermat for Inn-. Lltrolormally moved the Second reading- Of the Land Bill. —The attack on the measure was opened by Mr.Glissott, the latiatterney-General for Ireland, who pleaded the cause of the landlords at considerable length, and endeavoured-to- show that the Government proposals not only went beyond the 'Aetiof 1870, but tnirpassed in some respects the sugges- tions of the Horne Rule party as led by the late MT. Isaac Butt. The landlords, said Mr. Gibson, were to be subjected to a furnace of legislation and litigation. He believed the bill was understood by very few, and he had the most rionte sympathy for the Irish law officers, who would be called OD to explain its provisions. As to the working of the measure, it was contended that, while it deprived the landlord of the power of raising rent, it handed the incoming tenant entirely over to the mercy of the outgoing tenant or the nearer who had lent him money. Mr. Gibson complained that, no tinction was drawn between good and bad landlords.) and between improving and disimproving tenants. Loud den. sive Cheering was provoked by Mr. Gibson's statement' that the landlords were centres of charity benevolence, civilisation, and enlightenment, and that undk the proposed bill they would be reduced to the position of mere rent chargers. At the close of the next speech, by Mr. RICHARDSON, no member of the Government happening to rise on the instant to reply to Mr. Gibson, there were demands for a-division:— Mr. WARTON moved the adjournment of the debate to give the Government time to make up their mind, and Mr. GortsT, spoke of the Irish law officers as sitting with "wooden faces making neither assent nor dissent."—Tire PREMIER, in a keenly satirical speech, rebuked the member for Chatham for the mode in which he had addressed the House, at Ore same time announcing that the Government would exercise their own discretion as to the precise time when they would answer the questions raised by Mr. Gibson. After some further discussion, in the course of which Sir William Har- court denounced the obstructive tactics of the Optionition, the motion for adjournment was withdrawn, and after some further waate of time a discussion ensued on a motion of Mr. Villiers Stuart, urging the claims of the Irish farm labotirers to be considered in the bill.—Speaking in reply to this motion, Mr. Fonwrzn said it was very cheering to see .that no proposal to reject the bill had come from the Con- servativ'e side of the House.

Mn. Biaammettrwa AND Tan OATH.—Mr. Bradlaugh, es- corted by Mr. Labeuchere and Mr. Burr, advanced to the table to be sworn. As the clerk at the table handed him the book, Sir S. Northcote rose to object.—Mr. Bradlaugh still remaining at the table, the SPEAKER rose, and, reading from a written paper, said if the honourable baronet, the member for North Devon, proposed to make a motion on the matter before the House, he felt it right first to say that the mem- ber for Northampton having come to the table to take the oath required by law, and in the accustomed form, and having declared that he was prepared to comply with the provisions of the statute in order to take his seat, the pro- ceeding was regular and formal, and, under ordinary cir- cumstances, would proceed without interruption. Having regard to the reports of the two select committees, and to a resolution of the House, he felt, however, bound to give the House an opportunity of expressing its judgment on the matter. The honourable member for Northampton would I therefore withdraw.—Mr. BRADLAtiGH : In complying, sir, with your direction,l most respectfully ask you--(Cries of. " Oh,"" Order.")—The SPEAKER said the honourable mem- ber for Northampton was entitled to be heard, and, he was not, in his judgment, out of order.—Mr. BR.ADLAUGIt : lii complying, sir, with your direction to withdraw, I ask through you,before the House comes to any judgment on my claims .to fulfil the duty imposed on me, that it will accord me the privilege of being heard. (Hear,. hear.)—Mr. Bradlaugh having withdrawn from the bar, Sir S. NORTHCOTE said he was desirous of submitting a .motion for the judgment of the Home. 'The issue to be decided was one of a simple 'character. He had waited to see whether the honourable member proposed to take the oath or to affirm. He had proposul to take the oath, and this being so. he (Sir S. Northcote) would remind the House that on the 22nd June last the House resolved that, having regard to the reports, of two committees, Mr. Bradlaugh be not permitted to take the oath. That resolution stood in the journals of the House unrescinded. The part which forbade his affirming had been rescinded, and Mr. Bradlaugh bad affirmed and sat in the House. Since then proceedings were taken in a court of law, and Mr. Bradlaugh was held not to, be entitled to affirm. Mr. Bradlaugh, therefore, did not now come before the House as a stranger, And the House, which regarded the solemn obligation of an oath, felt that it was • not their duty to sit by and permit what they regarded as a profanation of that obligation. The honourable member for Northampton luld never withdrawn the statement on which the House had made its orders, and he (Sir S. Northcote), therefore, moved that, having regareltelbe resolutien of the House and the reports of two committees, Mr. Bradlaugh be not permitted to go through the form of repeating the words of an oath.—Mr. H. DAVEY rose to move as an amendment that, in the case of a member dulytelected presenting himself at the table to comply with the pre- scribed formality of taking the parliamentary oath of quali- fication, the House would not, on the ground of information extraneous to the transaction, offer any impediment to the fulfilment of his duty. The resolution before the House was one that he thought would constitute a bad precedent,' and one fraught with danger in the future. Singe the action of the House, referred to by Sir S. Northcote, Mr. Bradlaugh had been re-elected for Northampton, and he (Mr. Davey) 'contended that, at the .present moment, the House was not justified in considering matters that were estraneous to the question immediately before it, nor in entering into the re- ligious opinions of Mr. Bradlaugh.—Mr. LABOUCHERE se- conded the • amendment, remarking that he thought the 1-louse would show its wisdom in adopting that proposition. He was surprised that the right honourable gentleman (Sir S. Northcote) having stepped forward with the weight of his position to interpose between an honourable member and the oath; but the object was apparent: it was to stir up the smouldering element of religious bigotry, and to delude the country into ana 'belief that the Conservatives were the champions of.. Christianity and the Liberals its opponents. Christianity had nothing to do with the present question. The House has ceased to be exclusively a Christian assembly when it admitted the Jews. Mr. Bradlaugh, holding the views he did and representing a particular constituency, was bound to press on his right to .come to the table and take the oath; and the alternative I would be the passing not of the amendment, but the keep- ing of Mr. Bradlaugh continually in prison. The House might succeed in keeping Mr. Bradlaugh out for a time, but in the end, as was the case in the instance of John Wilkes, it would not succeed against the opinion of the country.— MIN E. CLARKE said the question was one of the dignity of the House and the sense of what was line to itself ;rand the " amendment was one founeed on fantastic special pleading,' inasmuch as it asked the House not to ect on extraneous in- formation. The House had already acted on the avowal of the honourable member for Northampton, and yet the same House which had passed the resolution of last year was asked to say that it would in passing the resolution before it act on extraneous information.—Mr. BamaitT : If any one in the House ten minutes ago had a doubt as to the exact question brought before the House they can have no doubt atwfuetechrtatvhee 18 lspeechisteefnetdhetohonourable member (Mr. E. Clarke) because disability. i ly one of religiou's "Irreligious," and cheer& "irreligious disability." nyohuit iosbj(ceClcertaieerds thatob ef` riNetoit,son:loitt,s;e: honourable member y admission of Roman Catholics. (Hear, hear.) y Objected ,au then because it was a religion (0 Hear, hear,'" and "No, n you deemed to be false— o, —and a religion you con- sidered to be false, and that you considered to be worse than no religion at all. On the same ground you objected for many years to. the claim of the Jewe. I think the House may be ealled upon to (Hear,. hear.) consider that the hon. member for Northampton for many months hits sat in this goose; there has been no member of the HoneeW h has cenducted himself with greater propriety. (Hear, hear.) 21 He has brought to our discussions at least average, and perhaps more than average, ability, and there is no single word that he has said, me act that he has committed, which in the slightest degree ought to debar him from taking bis seat in this assembry. (Question.) I would ask hon. gentl‘ men to Alb* for a moment--whether it is in accordance With that Christianity • which they presume to defend after years, almost centuries, of discussion, to raise up a welw barrier against that civil freedom which our conwituencesi believe

div.head: ,THE
div.p: ,THE

that they enjoy, and to proYeAtAn lon. member who )tas been duly elected' froto-- LiktAk briWoframongst us. One of our poets has said soinethiegaleiut bigotry of this kind. (Oh, oh.) I hope hoe. gentleman Will, forgive ins for using!the word "bigotry,"-but I think that to debar the hon. meinber from taking-the oath prescribed by law is an act°, bigotry. . Bigotry may swell the sail be sets for heaven With blasts from hell. (Oh, oh, and cheers.) °I hold that there can be sothing consonant with Christianity in its highest principles, and nothing consonant with that religious freedom for which our fathers have striven, in determining still to I obstruct the hon. member for Northampton when he comes to the table to take the oath. I hope no gentleman in the House who has any regard for religious freedom, for civil, and constitutional freedom, will give a vote that shall debar the ctrnatitturncy of Northampton from their due and lawful" representation in this House. (Cheere.)— Mr. BRADLALKIII was heard from the bar. He said that in the few words he would address to the House in favour of his claim to do that which the law required him todo he would be as brief as possible. He had stated to the commit- tee that the essential part -of the oath was in the fullest degree binding upon bit honour sad his vonscience ; and he now said that he would not go through atiy,form, munch as he valued the right to sit in that Roue% much as he hoped to win and use it, unless it were freely and completely binding upon him. He trusted the House would pardon him if In , the course of what he said anything seemed to costa from i him dictated by feelings which one n his poeitionaught not to manifest. His had been no easy 'position. He had been elected by the free votes of a free 'constituency. His return was untainted. There was no.charge of bribery, no charge of corruption, no charge of inducing men to go to the poll. He Carne there with a pure, untainted return. For 13 long years had he fought for the right to sit in the House, and through five -contested elections. The- Howse had the forces in their hands. On his side was the law. (Hear, hear.) He lad, paid the penalty for not taking the oath. Litigation; fostered by men who had not the courage them- selves to appear in court—(Liberal cheers)—had been forced on him, and 'he, a penniless man, would have been ruined had it not been that people in workshop, pit.. and factory had enabled him to fight. Would they inquire into his con- duct as well as his opinions? If his opinions were to be inquired into why not his conduct? He trusted that as to any obnoxious views supposed to be held by WI, there was So'duty on him of saying one word there. There was no legal disqualification. If there was, why not take it before the °election judges? They had no right to know his opinions; no right to deal with them; no right to-examine into them save as the law gave them power. An -attempt had been made to put on the Government compli- '. his-views, or complicity in his return. The Liberal party had never aided him in his way to that House. ("Oh.") He had fought for his own hand. (" Oh, oh," and Order, order.") He had been hindered in every case that it was possible, and it was only by the same help from the 'people who had enabled him to fight 4his fight, that he was there that day after those five struggles, right through those twelve years. If the House had the right of standing be- tween him and the table, it was the right of force, not of law. He appealed to the generosity of the House, as well as to its strength—its traditions of liberty on both sides. He did not complain that members on the Conservative benches. did their best to keep him out. They acted according to their rights. Perhaps his poor services might affect them. No.: Thea let him in. (Liberal cheers.) Either ',twee the politician to whom they objected, and Abet they bad no right to do, or it was that they suspected Wino's:tele opinions which they did not hold, and which barredbis entrance into this House, for one or other of these infrkes'they must have. If they refused to allow him te take his ,seat the law gave him no remedy. If they 'i(ret him outside the law, then they only left him lawless.— Mr. GLADSTONE, who was warmly cheered, said—Mr. Brad- laugh is upon his trial before this House, but this House alto, permit me to say, is upon its trial. (Cheers.) Ic would be unpardonable in me, sir, though it is perfectly pardon- able and perfectly natural in the honourable gentleman the member elected for Northampton, if I were to speak on this occasion with the slightest tinge of warmth, or were to devi- ate from the dryest lines of argument, and I shall, endeavour °entirely to avoid everything of the sort, following—l must way only following—in that respect the speech in which the motion that is now before us was submitted to the House. (Cheers.) The House is upon its trial before the constitu- ency which hat returned the hon. member for Northamp- ton, who justly says that, apart from the authority our constituencies, give ps, we are nothing and we are nobody. It is upon its trial before the general public. It is upon its trial upon an issue which will possibly come before future Parliaments, as the Parliament that proceeded against Mr. Wilkes was tried by a subsequent Parliament, and was, em- phatically, formally, and ignominonsly condemned (Cheers.) It requires, sir, I admit, great selt-denial to look closely and calmly at. this question. Let us consider what is and what is not the question that is before us. Let us con- sider what are the judgments of those whom we may regard as authorities. Ido not understand that the highest author- ity in this House—namely, the Speaker of this House—has declared any legal objection to the taking of the oath by Mr. Bradlaugh. Ido not intend to charge on the hon. members opposite what they would disclaim—namely, that they are adopting principles whose obvious consequences would be religious inquisition. lam going to charge upon them this —that, without any Such', intention, I am afraid they are recommending us to take a step which, if it be taken or systematically followed, can- not but lead to those consequences. (Cheers.)— Sir S. Northcote's resolution was carried en a division by a majority of 33-208 to 175. After the cheers with which the announcement of the numbers was received had subsided, Mr. Bradlaugh again presented himself at the table, but was directed by the Speaker to withdraw. This he declined to do, alleging that the order was illegal, and the SPEAKER asked the House for directions. There were loud cries from the Opposition for Mr. Gladstone, met by counter-cries of -"No, no from the Ministerialists; and, after a pause, Sir S. Noa'ritcont, rose amid lend cheers, and asked the Prime Minister whether he intended to take any steps as leader of the House to carry out the resolution ,jnst agreed to. Mr. Granerossreplied that having voted with the minority, he should leave it to the majority to carry out its resolution. Sir S. NosTacoxis at once. moved that Mr. Bradlaugh be -ordered' to withdraw ; and this was carried without a division, though Mr. Labouchere offered some opposition, and warned the majority that, to carry out their resolution„ it would be necessary to keep Mr. Bradlaugh in prison daring the remainder of the Parliament. On the advice of Mr. Bright, he did not press his opposition to a division, and the motion was agreed to.—The SPEAKER: I have now to call upon you, Mr. Bradlaugh, to withdraw. Mr. BRADLATME: I am here in accordance with my legal right and duty. and I respectfully refuse to obey the order of the House, which is absolutely illegal.—The SPEAKER: I-have to call the Sergeant-at-Arms to remcve Mr. Brad- laugh.—Mr. Bradlaugh (amid some confusion): I request that the Hobse will not resort simply to force—(order, order) —because lam here in pursuance of my legal right. (Order, order.) I shall only return when I get to the bar.—The Sergeant-at-Arms having placed himself beside Mr. Brad- laugh now walked with him to the bar, where, however, the hop. member turned round and returned towards the table, the , Sergeant-at-Anns , pulling backwards upon his arm. This incident aroused some laughter.— Mr. BRA.DLALIGH (pausing in the middle of the floor) : I am ' here to take the oath according to.law, and I refuse to sub- mit to physical force. (Hear, hear, and Order, order.)—Two of the messengers had, while Mr. Bradleugh was speaking, I seized his arms and drew him backwards towards the bar, confused exclamations arising among the members present. —Captain PRICE moved that the House should adjourn, but ..he proposition was unnoticed.—Mr. BRADLAUGH (walking again towards the table and drawing the messengers with him): I refuse to submit to physical force. Lam ready to submit to a legal order. (Hear.)—A fcrce of five officials now surrounded the bon, member„ who stood apparently waiting foran arunier,-'while the crowded House watched the scene with the deepest interest —Mr. ______Ttnaneenets (after a pause): I ask the House not to put me to the indignity of a physical struggle. ,(Hear, hear, and Order, order.) The House has an authority to which I will submit. (Hear, hear.)—The SPEAKER: I must again throw myself upon the Honse—(" No, no," and "Order ")—for instructions. (Cries of " Northcote," followed by Gladstone, Glad- stone.")—Sir S. NORTHCOTE said he would not shrink from the responsibility of moving to commit Mr. Bradlaugh to custody, but for the evident fact that the proceedings were countenanced by Her Majesty's Ministers.—This Mr. Glad- stone warmly denied, but repeated that he would not take any step until he thought it could be done with advantage. —Ultimately, after this line of recrimination had been pur- sued for some time, the scene was brought to a close by Mr. COWEN moving that the House do now adjourn, in order, as he said, to give time for cool reflection.—The motion was agreed, to with only a few dissentients, and the House accordingly Adjourned at a quarter-past two o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNEsnay. The Speaker took the chair at 12-15. Lona'. Prrrnow.—A petition praying the House to pro- hibit the Government traffic in opium between India and China was presented by Mr. McMinnies from Wycliffe Con- gregational Church, Warrington. Mn. Bsematicor's Bradlaugh walked up the floor of the Matte, and, standing at the table, stated that .he was there to take the oath according to law.—The SPEAKER pointed out that, the House having already ordered. Mn-Bradlaugh to withdraw, it was his duty to see 'that the order of the House was carried out, and he must call upon the hon. member to withdraw below the bar, otherwise he should be compelled to call for' the exercise of forca.—Mr. BitersAtrus said the House had a right to vacate his seat and expel him, but it had no right to inter-' fere with him in the performance of • his duty. He refused to withdraw, except compelled by physical force.—The SPEAKER thereupon called upon the Sergeant-at-Arms to remove Mr. Bradlaugh below the bar, and the Sergeant-at- Arms then touched Mr. Bradlaugh on the shoulder,' and the hon. member, bowing to the Chair, withdrew, and stood at the bar.—Mr. LABOUCHERE said he was very undesirous to see the scenes of Tuesday night renewed, and he would ask the Prime Minister whether the Government would give him facilities to introduce a Bill, printed last year, and which had been blocked by hon. gentlemen opposite, on, the understanding that, if the vote of the House could be taken speedily upon it, Mr. Brad- laugh would not interfere in any way.—Mr. GLessross replied that he could not unless the House was prepared to vote a state of urgency of public business, and he was na prepared to ask for that. The giving of facilities meant the postponement of the Irish Land Bill, and the Government could not assent to that. If the proposed Bill were to be unopposed the question might assume a different aspect. The Government would be prepared to waive every secondary difficulty or objection for the purpose of coming

He objected to any proposal in the -nature of tri bargain, but was prepare 4 to consider any proposal hurl' the Government or a private Member in' the direction, of a solution of ,the case.—Mr )Burcrirr suggested that the reasonable course to.talte 410.0e1loattinik* aahort Act that would give,the Optio of oath or atormation. Mr. NZWDZOATE announced hlsz di- 'sees to move that Mr. Bradlaugb be; committed,,and MaclvEn having intimated his intention to move thatope . member should be taken from Northampton and given to Birkenhead, the subj.lct was dropped. I MR GLADSTOKR AND THE StLVER ORTY.—Mr. GLAD- aroma announced that be proposed te abandon the intention, ' stated in his budget speech, of asking for the removal of the silver duty. He was induced to take this couree,owipg to the disturbance, he was assured, would be occasioned to trade by persisting with hia proposal at the present time. - CHURCH BOARDS BILL.—Mr. ALBZRT GREY moved the second reading of the Church Boards Bill, which, he urged, would be a measure of great practical utiltiy to the church by the admission of the laittinto a share of the management of their own churches. The bill proposed that at the Easter vestry a board should beolected under the provisior.s of the bill, the churchwardens being es-ojficio members of such board, and the incumbent of the parish its state-appointed chairman. The board would have the power to make changes in the method of conducting the service, and in rc-, gard to ornaments and decorations, but they would not be empowered to do anything contrary ta the spirit of the law. 'Or the plain directions of the Prayer Book.—Mr. G. BTJSRZLL 'ttioved the rejection of the bill, which he characterised as a measure thAt would, if passed, effect a revolution in the church such as had no parallel in its previous history. The ponourable gentleman was speaking at a quarter to six o'clock, when the debate, according to the standing orders stood adjourned. - -
TAB ACCOMMODATION.-011 the motion of Mr. SHAW- LETWIRB, a select committee was appointed to consider the proposals for the increased accommodation of the louse.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THIIRSDAY.

PETVATE BILL.—The Lancashire County Justices Bill was, read a third time and passed. REPRESENTATION OF BIRKENHEAD.—MI, DAVID MAC- IVER gave notice that, on Thursday, May 5, he would ask Mr. Gladstone whether he is prepared to re-consider .1-lie decision of last session, and will introduce a short measure, with urgency, for the partial disfranchisement of North- ampton,and giving an additional member to Birkenhead. THE CONSERVATIVES AND THE LAND BlLL.—Lorcl JOHN MANNERS gave notice that he will move an amendment to the Irish Land Bill, declaring that the House, while anxious to maintain and secure the full efficiency of the customs of Ulster, and other analogous customs in Ireland, to remedy the proved defects in the Land Act of 1870, is disposed to seek the social and material improvement of the country by measures for the development of the industrial resources of the country, rather than by a measure which confuses with- out settling on a just and permanent basis the relations between landlord and tenant. THE WOOLLEN AND WORSTED TRADES.—Mr. CELLHHER. LAIN explained for the benefit of Mr. Maclver the Board of Trade statistics for the past eight ycars in reference to the worsted and woollen trades. RUSSIA AND CENTRAL ASlA.—Replying to Mr. Joseph Cowen, Sir CHARLES DILKE said the statement he had made on a former occasion in the House on the subject of the re- call of General Schobeleff was correct. General Schobeleff had been recalled, and military operations bad ceased. Eight battalions of General Schobeleff's troops were now on their return march. Lord Dufferin was his authority for the statement. THE FRENCH TREATY.—Respecting a commercial treaty with France, the PREMIER gave an assurance that the Go- vernment would avail themselves in every way possible of the assistance of the commercial community, and stated that the general bearings of all the proceedings would be fully made known before any final action was taken. The action of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce on the subject was mentioned by Mr. HERMON, and the hon. member for Preston elicited from Mr. Gladstone a promise that any communica- tions of the nature referred to should receive the most care- ful consideration. The Government, added the right hon. gentleman, bad no intention of forcing any measures unless they were in accordance with the general feeling of the com- munity of this country.. TUNIS.—In answer to Baron de Worms, Sir CHARLES DILKE stated that communications had been exchanged with the Italian Government on the subject of sending vessels of war for the protection of British and Italian interests and life and property at Tunis, but nothing further had taken place on the general question. As to mediation, there was a proposal to have international mediation, but they bad not received any communication on the subject. Britain would only mediate alone if asked by both parties. THIS IRISH LAND BILL..—Lord &cm resumed the debate on the Land Law (Ireland) Bill, and moved the amen Iment of which he had given notice, which declared that the bill was in its main provisions economically unsound, unjust, and impolitic. He charged the Premier with bringing for- ward a bill giving effect to the communistic principle of ex- propriating the property of the few for the benefit of the many, and contended that the bill was a concession drawn fremehe Government by the lawlessness which had prevailed and was still prevailing in Ireland.—Mr. CHARLES RUSSELL followed in a speech warmly supporting the Government measure, which he said would afford better protectioa to the tenant, and better security to the landlord. He urged the House to deal with the bill in a fair and liberal spirit.—A prolonged and uneventful discussion followed, and the de- bate was again adjourned.

div.head: LORD BEACONSFIELD'S FUNERAL.
div.p: LORD BEACONSFIELD'S FUNERAL.

The Earl of Beaconsfield's funeral took place on Tuesday at Hughenden, in the presence of several Royal personages, many Cabinet and ex-Cabinet Ministers, representatives of the Queen and foreign sdovernments, members of both Houses of the Legislature, and an immense concourse of spectators. From an early hour in the morning trains left Paddington station, conveying to High Wycombe those who were to take part in the ceremony and large numbers who desired to witness it. The Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaught, and Prince Leopold proceeded by ordinary train at 12-45. At Hughenden the route of the procession was kept and order maintained by 100 metropolitan con- stables and 400 Buckinghamshire Volunteers. During the day there were several heavy showers of rain and hail. The funeral procession, which left Hughenden Manor at 3-30, was arranged strictly according to the programme of the execu- tors. Appropriate selections of sacred music were played as the remains were borne into the church. The altar and surroundings were adorned with camelias and other choice flowers. Beautiful wreaths entirely covered the bier, before which was carried the late Earl's coronet. Immediatcly following the coffin were the Royal Princes, the executors, and other chief mourners, the Duke of Richmond, Lord Derby, Cabinet Ministors, and members of the late Ciovern- rnent. A large body of the tenantry and most of the deceased's servants also took part in the procession. When the hedge which flanks a part of the gaiden had been passed, I the way was bordered by the Buckinghamshire Volunteers, in dark green uniform. Behind them stood, on the sloping sides of the path, several rows of spectators, all bareheaded, as those who walked in the procession also were. Men and boys had clambered into the trees on each side to see over the rest of the people. The procession passed in silence into the churchyard, where many residents in the neighbourhood, political personages, and others were collected. Out of the sunlight the mourners passed into thecomparative obscurity of the church. On the north side of the chancel, where the late Earl, by right as the lord of the manor, used to sit, the chief mourners sat, but leaving his place vacant. Nearest the congregation were Mr. Disraeli, grayheaded, but in other respects resembling his brother, and Mr. Coningsby Disraeli; opposite were the Princes of the Royal House. On the •vacant seat of the late Earl was laid a wreath of gardenias and maidenhair fern, and a cross, formed of the eucharis, leant against the back of the seat. The chancel was in gloom, but the sun threw, coloured lights upon the seats of the Ambassadors through the stained glass of the first south window. In the midst of the gloom of the chancel the coffin, covered with its snow-white blooms, was rested on its bier. The organist softly played Beethoven's Funeral March of a Hero as the coffin was borne up the centre of thechurch. The Rev. H. Blagden, the vicar, read the order for the burial of the dead, and when he ended the first part with the solemn words, "Our labour is not in vain in the Lord," the Music of "0 rest in the Lord!" rose slowly in sounds of gradually augmenting volume while the bearers raised the body and bore it into the open air. It was wheeled to the east end of the church, to the tomb beneath the window of the Montfort Chapel. The turf above the vault was here entirely covered with white wreaths and crosses, at the head one sent by the Junior Carlton Club, with the words, "Respectful memory from the Junior Carlton Club." Another cross had attached to it the motto, "Peace, with henour." The bier being wheeled down the incline plane, Mr. Blagden uttered the final sentences, and the body of Lord Beaconsfield was laid side by side with that of hN wife. The Prince of Wales, the Duke of Connaught, and Prince Leopold had stood by the side of the open grave while the concluding portion of the sad ceremony was being', achieved. They now advanced down the steps to the opening of the vault and stood a little while solemnly gazing into it. After they had turned away, many others took the last view of the remains and of the fragrant flowers which are there walled in to blossom in the dust. The Queen's wreath having been At length brought out the vault was closed, and the slow , process of tilling again with earth the trench which gives access to it was commenced. The guests then returned to the house, where in the saloon where the coffin had been , placed the Prince of Wales and his Royal brothers, the chief , mourners, including the executors, and a few others, assem- bled to hear the will read, .

Lord Beaconsfield, by his last will and testament, read at Hugbenden after the funeral, leaves his estate in Bucking- hamshire and the bulk of his property to his nephew, Coningsby Disraeli, son of Mr. Ralph Disraeli, clerk of the Parliaments. Failing Coningsby and his issue the property descends in strict succession to the other children of the deceased earl's brother. All the letters and nocuments left by his lordship are bequeathed to Lord Rowton, with full discretion to destroy or publish as he shall see fit.
