In concluding his discourse at the Holy Trinity Church, Warrington, on Sunday morning last, the Vicar, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, who preached from Dent. xxxiv., 5, "SO Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there, in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord," said: My rerarks have brought me to IL point where I cannot help referring to an event to which the minds of all of us, I might say of the whole nation, have been directed during the last- few days, the death of one occupying for a long series of years a fore- most place in the public service ot this country. He was an acknowledged leader—one honoured, trusted, and loved by any in the land. Whether we accept the principles of which he was the exponent, and with the advocacy of which his career was identified, or not, it cannot be denied that he did his work well, faithfully, and honourably. No dishonour attaches to his name. No base motives can be chargeable to him, even by those whose lot it was to oppose him. He had difficulties to contend with, opposition to encounter, often of a formidable character, but he had the courage and the patience to meet and conquer them. Always calm and col- lected, he never forgot himself. Rarely have we seen exhibited in public life a temper so serene. There have been those who, feeling the power of his self-command, put it down to a superior astuteness if intellect, an indication of superior genius, of which it was well to be aware. I rather put it down not te his intellect, but to his heart. These are moral qualities, and can only co-exist with a clear con- science, spotless integrity, high and honourable, aims. With regard to the religious side of Lord Beaconsfield's si rparci ntecri,pwe k l esannodw that it was shiswere w onnot none o ethe speak less little,strotnhgo un gn hd sincere. There are passages in his writings and speeches which show that he distinctly held the great doctrines of the Christian faith as they are received and enunciated by the Church. As early as the year 1835 he wrote that "it was a principle with him that the religious discipline and future welfare of our citizens are even of greater impor- tance than their political or present well-being." There are speeches delivered by him at gatherings of Churchmen in his own neighbourhood, ruri-decanal conferences, and meet- ings of diocesan societies, which testify how entirely he had the welfare and progress of the Church at heart, and how entirely he was:at one with her in:spirit and in principle. Churchmen at least have reason to be grateful for the ser- vices he rendered their cause. He is gone; but he has left a noble example of work faithfully done, of patience, and generosity, earning the devotion of his followers, the affec- tion of his friends, and the gratitude of the nation. His work is done; but as God raised up a successor to Moses, dif- ferently qualified, but on that account perchance all the more fitted to the Ames, in the person of Joshua, so we tannot but think that the great leaders and fillers in our land, as they pass from the scene of their labours, will have their suc- cessors in men as well fitted and qualified fcr their own peculiar work as those who preceded them. Though special gifts and qualifications change as the esigencies,of the time required, may it be that faithfulness, rectitude, and honour shall ever remain hereditary amongst English states- men. Special referencee to the death of Lord Beaconsfield were also made on Sunday by the Rev. W. 11. Williams, vicar of Padgate, who preached at St. Anne's Church, and by the Rev. B. B. Prescot, vicar of Christ Church, Latchford; and at St. Thomas's and St. Paul's Churches the organists played the "Dead March in Saul."

div.head: PULPIT REFERENCES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PULPIT REFERENCES AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday morning the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., preached at Trinity Church, Runcorn, and referring to the decease of Lord Beaconsfield, said :—Gloom overspreads the land; grief deep and genuine is felt throughout the country. Mourning prevails around. The grief is poignant, the sorrow is keen, the mourning is sincere that now pervades our land. And well they may be, for a mighty man has fallen in Israel. Sadness my well prevail on all sides considering the deep, irrebarable loss we have sustained in the removal from our midst by the remorseless hand of unfeeling death of that wonderful man, that mighty genius, that fascinating writer, that attractive orator, that brilliant statesman, that noble patriot, Benjamin Earl of Beaconsfield. To his true and , actual worth, as one who restored our little isle to be a lead- ing and foremost power amongst the mighty nations of the world, to bold its head up proudly as the equal of the greatest, who made the name of England to be feared and respected in every corner of the globe; under whose rule the old flag of England never waved more proudly or met with greater reverence, we have testimony corning in from all quarters of the globe, and unanimous testimony. He gave back to England a position she had either lost, ignored, or forfeited. Patriotism was the spirit that moved him, and his country's good and highest welfare were the objects he patriotically endeavoured to secure. The greatness and prosperity of England were his constant aim. As A politician he was gifted with remarkable insight and foresight whereby ' he could readily grasp the mazy problems of the day, and look a long way before him. He had a well-cultured mind, a lofty intellect, and well holds a place with the patriot Palmerston, with Canning, and Bolingbroke. lie has gone! What he did for his country will be more fully realised now. England has lost one of her most gifted, most faithful, most noble-minded, and most loyally-pitriotic sons. Well may she mourn. Well may grief pervade the land. We feel we have lost a friend and. a gifted public servant, who lived to promote the interests of our vast empire, and who whilst he lived faithfully s6ught the public good. Knowing his value we cannot but sorrow, and of him who has gone we cannot but feel proud. The sermon at the Runcorn Parish Church, on Sunday morning, was preached by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, curate of Weston, from I. Sam., xxv.c. Iv. During the discourse the reverend gentleman made the fcllowing remarks appropriate to the death of the ex-Prime-Minister : For the last week at least the bitterness and prejudice arising from party spirit in the country had melted away; and both politicians and the press had united in doing honour to the late statesman. This showed them that under the apparently seething sea of political animosity, there were the calm unruffled waters of generous impulse and cool judgment. The heart of the people could admire and did admire sterling worth and patriotism, even though they might work on different lines and take different views of that which Ministers did to the integrity and interest of the kingdom and its subjects. The Earl of Beaconsfield was dead, one who had guided the destinies of England and exerted an inflnence on his age— whether for good or for evil was a matter which the calmer judgment of posterity would more fairlydecided—.and whose voice had been a living power in the deliberations of the nation. An intellectual giant in an age of giants, an orator among a galaxy of orators, had gone the way of all flesh. No need had he to re.nind them of the shock which they received when the news of his decease was telegraphed through the length and breadth of the land; and of the testi- mony which was borne day by day to the loss which the country had sustained, or of the kindly interest which their good Queen had taken in the comfort and welfare of her dying servant. Theone they had experienced, the others they knew. And although they as Churchmenmight be pardoned if • they expressed their gratitude for the great ability and con- sistency with which he ever supported the Establishment and deplore his loss as bead of the party whose motto was loyalty to the throne and the church, yet there were other thoughts upon which they all might profitably meditate The first of these was the elasticity and the freedom of their Constitution, which admitted of the advancement of sterlink ability to the highest public offices and the greatest distinc- tion. Probably there had been no greater instance of the signal success of genius, industry, and energy than that of the late distinguished earl. A plebeian, a man of the people, descended from a race which yet a little while since was a term of reproach and a byevrord, whose energy was yet in some countries restricted and fettered by enactments; backed by no strong influence or interest and comparatively slender means, by the strength of his own indomitable will and the force of his own intellectual calibre triumphed over all obstacles until having attained to the highest office of state and discharged its functions with consummate ability amid energy he was elevated to the peerage and ranked with the proudest aristocracy, yea, received as the reward of his faith- ful i service the insignia of the most select order n the world.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenall (chairman), and James Manson.

WARNING TO FARMERS.—Joaeph Smith WES charged with unlawfully removing certain animals along the high- way at Appleton, on the 20th inst., without license, contrary to the ruled of the Privy Council. Thomas Jones wan also charged with driving the same.—P.S. Booth said he saw Jones driving a number of pigs from Warrington Market, to Stretton.—Nr. Moore, for the defence, drew the attention of the Bench to the peculiar position of Warrington, one part i being n Lancashire and the other part in Cheshire. The defendant being aware that Lancashire had been declared free from infectious disease thought that that part of , Cheshire where he was taking' the pigs was free also.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 2s. 6d. for each pig and the costs, total 2 ss. George Bulcock was similarly summoned for removing a calf at Appleton on the 21st inst.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, total 12s. Tat SEQUEL TO • " FRIENDLY " GLASS.—Richard D. Fryer, of Antrohus, a: provision dealer, was summoned on a charge of opening his premises for the sale of intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours, and Joseph Brocklehurst with aiding and abetting.—P.S. Dean said, that on Sunday morning, the 27th March, at 10 40. he visited Fryer's house. He found Brocklehurst sitting down in the house, and near him on the oven was a cup half fall of beer. He called the attention of Mrs. Fryer to the beer, and she said that Brocklehurst had called to see Mr. Fry, who was, however, out. Brocklehurst told witness he could have half of the beer if he liked, and then took the pot off the oven, drank up the beer, and fol- lowed the officer out. Brocklehurst asked witness to take no notice of the matter, as did also Mrs. Fryer.—By Inspector Williamson : The reason he visited the house was because he had had complaints as to the manner in which it was con- ducted.—By Mr. P. Davies : Re had threatened to summons defendant on previous occasions for allowing gaming in the house.—Mr. Davies, in defence, said it was a hard case if a man occupying a provision shop, such as defendant's, could not ask a friend into the house on Sunday morning to stop with his mother for a short time, and was considered to have broken the law when that mother asked him to have a drop of "home-brewed ale." He quoted from " Stone "to show that a man occupying a house under the Licensing Act of 1872 could entertain his friends, and supply them with liquor after the hours of closing providing he did so at his own expense. He said that Mr. Fryer on the Sunday morn- ing was on the point of leaving home, accompanied by his sisters, to attend church, when Mr. Brocklehurst came to ask for information with regard to a bankruptcy petition he had received. He had not then time to go into the matter, but invited Mr. Brocklehurst to go in and speak to his mother. Mr. Fryer had lately put up a brewery be- hind his house, and the mother, proud doubtless of her son's "brew,", asked him to have a drink.—Mr. Fryer corroborated his advocate's statement, and remarking as to the evidence of P.S. Booth said he should like his character .thoroughly vindicating. The officer's remarks ought not to have been made.—The Chairman: You will allow me to judge of that.—Mrs, Fryer said she received no money for the beer, and had simply asked Mr. Brocklehurst to have a drink as a friend.—The Chairman said the police had done perfectly right in bringing the case before the Bench, but the magistrates were of opinion that the beer had been supplied bond Me to a friend, and the cases,would be dismissed.—Me. Davies said his client wished him to ask whether it would be considered breaking the law to supply anybody on the premises as a friend.—The Chairman said it would be very questionable.—Mr. Davies said the publicans in Warrington were in the habit of doing so and the police were aware of it, but nothing was ever done to stop it.—The Chairman said I be always considered them very suspicious cases:

EXTENSIVE PILFERING BY A GlRL—Sarah Ann Jackson (14) was charged with stealing .£1 17s. and a quantity of clothing, on the 9th April, the property of John Hallowes, draper, Stockton Heath. Prisoner had been in the service of prosecutor about a month, having been obtained from the Workhouse, where she had a good character. Prosecutor' missing money from the drawer about three weeks after the prisoner was admitted into the family, began to entertain suspicions as to the girl's honesty, and on the 9th inst. he found her with a sovereign in her possession. She at first said her brother had given the money to her, then that she had found it in the road whilst going for the milk, and finally admitted having taken it from the safe whilst her mistress was in another part of the house. A shawl and several other articles were found secreted under the mattress of her bed.—P.S. Booth deposed to apprehending the prisoner at a lodging house in School. brow, Warriturton. He found the scarf produced banging on a line. When charged, she stated she had taken one day, 15s. another, and 2s. on another, and that she had bought several articles and given them to the children at the Workhouse.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for tea days, and then to a reformatory for four years.

We learn from Athens that on Wednesday afternoon the representatives of the Powers had an interview with the Greek Prime Minister, at which they stated that the Powers would interest themselves on behalf of the Epirotes, but gave no guarantees on the subject. The New York Senate has passed a bill exempting Ameri- can shipping from local taxes of every kind. This bill is expected to pass the house and become law. The hope is entertained that it will encourage the establishment of American ocean steam lines from New York. The Viceroy of India reports to the Home Government that the evacuation of the territory around Candabar was completed on Wednesday, and that the march from Cauda- bar was of an entirely uneventful character. All the forts were left in charge of the Ameer's officials.

A clergyman named John F. Morgan, lately of Grantham, and also of Newport, Monmouthshire, pleaded guilty at Worcester assizes to a charge of forging a cheque. It was said on his behalf that he was insane, but he was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. At the meeting of the Baptist Union, in London, on Tliursd ay, the Rev. T. M. Morris moved, and the Rev. W. Balker seconded, a resolution representing the opinion of two thousand Baptist churches, recording satisfaction with the domestic and foreign policy of the Goverment, recognis- ing the numerous and formidable obstacles with which the Governmeut have had to contend, earnestly urging their perseverance in doing righteousness and justice, and express- ing a belief that in pursuing this course they will have the hearty support of the great masses of the people. A copy of the resolution, which was heartily carried, was directed to be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Arthur G. Symonds and Mr. R. C. Richards, of the National Reform Union, addressed a large meeting of Old- ham Liberals on Thursday, on the Irish question, and a resolution was unanimously passed declaring that the Irish Land Bill merits the hearty and vigorous support of every section of the Liberal party, by an ample, generous and statesmanlike measure, well calculated to remedy the evils of land tenure, which have caused so much misery and distress in Ireland. ART FIIRNISRING.—Ever since "design," by persons other than the actual artificers, has been intentionally de- voted to objects of utility with the view of making them beautiful, it appears as if the material of which they were This be composed has been almost universally lost sight of the Rococo and cog- is true not only of work arising out nate styles—nothing better could be predicated from the offshoots of such extravagance—but it also holds good with m Any of the most admired pieces of what are generaLy con- sidered to be the purest,styles. Hidden or disguised con- strut...roil is a common fault even in these. Take for ex- ample many of the fine old chests of drawers and cabinets, whether Dutch or ng tisk], going generally under the name E of Jacobean. It will be often found that the fronts are ap- parently divided into three divisions by upright styles or pilasters, thus suggesting that the drawers or doors are short, and extend only between the uprights. On opening them, however, it is found that they extend the full width of the chest, the apparently dividing style being merelyplanted on he f ront. —From " Cassell's Family Maga zinc' for', April_

TEE SUOONSTED INFECTIOUS DO EASES HOSPITAL. The CHAIRMAN asked if the Clerk had receiCred any answer. from the Widnes, Jxocal Board respecting the Hospital accornmodation:—%e 01.1am:said he bad received the following letter, which he reed: " Widnes, 4-pril 18th, 1881. infectious Diseases Hospital. Dear sir,—Referring to your recent letter on this subject, I am directed by the Health Committee, pending their further consideration of the matter, to inquire whether any, and if so, whatohas been by other places in the Union towards providing accommodation for cases of infectious disease, arising in their respective districts. With every desire to do what is requisite, the Board would remind the Guardians, that Widnes has already one hospital to maintain, besides con- tributing very largely to the support of the Union Hospital, and they desire me to ask, whether in the event of the Board providing an Infectious Diseases Hospital for their district as proposed by the Guardians, tkey (the Guardians) would uevote any portion of the Union funds contributed by Widnes for hospital purposes towards its erection or sup- port. —Yours faithfully, THOMAS BEastnv."—Mr. W. TYRER remarked that if the Guardianscontributed a portion of the Union funds towards the erection or support of a hospital, it would only be like taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another.-The CHAIRMAN: Of course.-Mr. TIBER said the Widnes Local Board rates were very heavy„ and if the Board could get the Guardians to put something on the Union rates to provide a hospital, they would be very glad.—Mr. LONGTON thought the Board had Misunderstood the matter. The Authority wanted a hospital for the recep- tion of infectious diseases only.—The CHAIRMAN observed that in a recent lecture, Dr. Richards recommended the erection of small hospitals for the reception of persons suffering from infections diseases. He (Dr. Richards) ad- vised that a small hospital should be erected in each die- tr i ct, capable of accommodating not more than 2D or 24 persons. The Local Government Board recommended large hospitals, but Dr. Richards said it was a great mistake Mr. Tyarut thought the hospitals ought to be as near as pos- sible to the infected districts, instead of bringing the cases through one or two districts not affected. He thought Mr. Beasley's attention should be called to the fact that is re- quest would not relieve the rates of Widnes.—The CLERN remarked that they had an epidemic of fever at Prescott and the question was—were these people to come into ttie Work- house Hospital? They had been discussing thelikelihood of an epidemic breaking out, but now they had it upen, them. The St. Helens Corporation were providing a hospital for in- fectious cases for themselves.—The CHAIRMAN said the Workhouse Hospital was not intended simply and solely for infectious diseases. The Rev. Mr. CHAMBERS asked if the Widnes Local Beard were aware of what the St. Helens Corporation were doing.—The CLF.RE replied that he did not know, as he had not answered the letter. The Clerk further stated that as a matter of faot one-half the hospital at the workhouse was 'filled with CUM from Widnes. They had warned the Widnes Local Board, and if they would not take the warning they must take the consequences. It was suggested some time ago that that authority and the other local authorities in the neighbour- hood should combine and provide a hospital for the reception and treatmest of infectious cases only.—Mr. LONG- TON asked what accommodation there was in the authoritys' hospital, in case any epidemic broke out in their district.— The Caarnmeas said the medical officer called attention to the deficient hospital accommodation in the workhouse some two or three months ago. It was then suggested that Wid- nes and the other neighbouring local Boards should be asked to combine with that authority in providing an infections diseases hospital.—The Rev. C. CHAMBERS remarked that they had already heard that a fever epidemic had broken out in Prescot, which seemed very likely to spread to the authority's district, and he thought it was desirable that that authority should at once do something towards making pro- vision in case an epidemic did attack any portion of the dis- trict, instead of looking after and legislating for Widnes Local Board. The Board might very properly say "Why legislate for us, and do nothing for yourselves?' He thought as practical and sensible men it was their duty to do some- thing in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN said the question was raised at a former sleeting whether it would be well for the Sanitary Authority to build a hospital for itself or whether it would be more advisable to join with Widnes Prescot, Huyton, and Woolton Local Boards if possible, and erect a hospital to be built and supported by the whole of the authorities. They wrote to Widnes first, and their reply had just been read.—Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Does the Widnes Board positively refuse to join us ?—The CHAIRMAN: Oh, no.—Mr. TYRER: Widnes is an increasing town, and it is desirable they should provide their own hospital the same as St. Helens is doing.—Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Quite so. Let Widnes do for itself, and let us lose no time in amalgama- ting with Woolton, Prescet and Huyton Local Boards and provide a hospital—Mr. TYRER moved that the Clerk com- municate with Woolton, Prescot, and Huyton Local Boards with a view to ascertaining whether they would amalgamate with the Authority into a central district for the purpose of providing a hospital for infectious diseases, and stating that St. Helens and Widnes were large places and must do for themselves.—lt was stated that if action was taken at once it would take twelve months before the hospital would be ready.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS remarked that anyhow they were going a step in the right direction.—The CHAIRMAN explained that the reason for asking the other authorities to join that Autherity in the erection and support of a hospital was that it would be much cheaper for all concerned —The motion was then seconded, and on being put to the meeting it was unanimously carried.

MEDICAL ovric,En's REPORT. Dr. HALL (the medical officer) reported that the health of the district was satisfactory, but that scarlet fever was rife in the vicinity. With present hospital accommodation it would require great vigilance on the part of the Authority's inspector in hunting up any cases that might arise to pre- vent the disease spreading. He also asked the Authority to sanction the prosecution of anyone going into an infected house after a funeral is over, as he was thereby rendering himself liable to a penalty of £5. He had nothing else to report.—The Chairman said it would appear from Dr. Hall's report that scarlet fever was very bad in Prescot at the present time.—The Rev. T. Chambers moved that, in accord- ance with the suggestion of the doctor, persons seen enter- ing infected houses, and then coming out again enter non- affected houses, should be prosecuted, and that posters be printed and circulated in the Authority's district informing the people that if they neglected to observe the warning they rendered themselves liable to a penalty of £5.

div.head: NUISANCE Al' DITTON.
div.p: A NUISANCE Al' DITTON.

The Surveyor called the attention of the Authority to a nuisance at Pitville-terrace, Ditton, caused by the overflow of a cesspool attached to property belonging to Mr. Wareing. —lt was resolved that a notice be served upon Mr. Wareing ordering him to abate the nuisance at once.

div.head: PLANE.
div.p: PLANE.
Plans of two cottages, proposed to be erected at Ditton by Mr. Burrows, were approved; as was also a plan of small shop submitted by Mr. Henry Hunt, Whiston.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

GRAND CONCERT AT WINSFORD.--.A. grand concert was given, on Thursday, by Mre Turner, of Over Hall, in the Town Hall, the proceeds of which were to be in aid of the Winsford company of volunteers, of which Captain Turner is commanding officer. A choice selection of vocal and In- strumental music was given including Hadyn'e and Rom- berg's toy symphonies. In the latter Mrs. Turner, the Misses Turner, Captain Turner, and Mr. J. Turner took part, assisted by the Revs. E. Woodyatf, Mr. Preston, and Mr. Payne, Signor Lingi Camerana acting as conductor. The audience was large and fashionable, the dress circle includ- ing most of the nobility and gentry of the neighbourhood, and all frequently expressed their appreciation of the vocal- ists and instrumentalists. No doubt the volunteer funds will be much improved by the kindness of Mrs. Turner who takes a warm interest in the Corps.

At a crowded meeting of the electors and non-electors of Oldham, on Thursday night, a resolution was 'unanimously passed approving of the Irish Land Bill, which. was declared to be a generous and statesman-like measure, and one well calculated, to remedy existing grievances in Ireland.

- - It is announced that the Mayor of Northampton has convened a Meeting to protest against the infringement of the legal and constitutional rights of the constituency by the hindrance of the duly elected member from taking his seats A committee has been formed in London to agitate for Mr. Bradlangh's admission to Parliament, and a form of petition. has been drawn up praying the Rouse to cause the law to be obeyed. SUDDEN DEATH 07 A GIRL AT BT. 111113.70.—0 n Monday morning Bridget Barrett, aged _lo.years, who re- sided at 8, Bold-street, died suddenly whilst in a fit. De- ceased, who was the daughter of Michael Barrett, a glass- worker, had enjoyed comparative good health) and on Sun- day went to school and chapel as usual. In the evening 'he eomplained of a pain in the ear. She, however, went to the glass works'with her father's supper, and whilst there told her father of the pain. On returning home she went to nett, and was found EOM time after apparently in a St. She lied a few minutes after being found in this state by her nether.

div.p: ten candidates, hundreds of Liberals either only voted for a small portion of the ten Liberal candi- dates or split for one or other of the more prominent of the Tories. Most certainly this is not as it should be. If these elections are to be fought politically—and the Tories determined five or six years ago that they should be —then it is the bounden duty of every member of the Liberal party to sink all minor differences and vote "straight" for those men who have been selected by the general council of the party as the Liberal candidates. Every Liberal should be true to the principles be professes, and should learn a lesson of faithfulness to party from the Tories, who invariably vote straight for their own men—in fact, they "vote as they are told," and if the Liberals would win they must do likewise. It should, however, not be forgotten Cost in the election just passed the Tories have not scru- pled to have recourse to acts of so discreditabb, a character that there is no doubt whatever if a scrutiny had been demanded the electibn would have been upset. The voting papers of several men who are "dead," or have left the town, were sent in duly filled up and signed by somebody. In some cases the d,ad or absent men were well known Liberals, but their papers were filled up in each case for the whole of the ten Tory candidates. Another notable case was that of a person who has not resided in the town for about twelve months, having disposed of his interest in the town, but whose name by some accident shall we say had been left on the rate book. The voting paper in this ease which deseribed the avlostoersaet snenitnit,led to tea votes for each candidate was Therein bore evidence e signed, and filled up for the Tories. the voting papers sent originally filled up for the Liberals, but the initials had been struck out and re-inserted opposite the names of the Tories. More- over upwards of a hundred voting papers were filled up for the Tories in one and the same handwriting, and it is, therefore, questionable whether in cases of this kind the voters themselves had consented to the alterations. We learn that the perpetrators of these malpractices will be sharply looked after in the future, so that further action may be taken in case of such actions being repeated. The re'sult of the election has been to turn out five Liberals who attended most regularly at the Board and remained constantly to transact the greater and more important portion of the business of the Union which has to be done after the reporters have left the room and to replace them by Toriess the majority of whom cannot possibly devote to their duties anything like the same amount of time and attention. In spite, however, of the fact that 2,400 votes were not recorded, and also of the discreditable proceedings of the Tories if the total number of votses recorded for the ten Liberals and for the ten Tories are added up separately and each total divided by 10, the difference bet seen the two results enlyshows a majority of 178 votes for the Tory can- didates. We hope, therefore, that the lesson of the present defeat will be to teach all Liberals the de- sirability and the necessity of united action by means of which the party can easily maintain its position at the head of affairs in the borough.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES,
div.p: LOCAL NOTES,

A rather interesting meeting of Runcorn ratepayers was held, on Thursday evening, in the incommodious room in Allcock-street, in which so many virtuously indignant rate- t ah transaction, hh the eye el interesting yi tet l little f pointedt table ltt ear uaeet, ahyi ce trhf orthkhaaentvoye tt vicaralhelitka oigsnffa gt affecting t. choeDui rrl d. suui ncar ppf ol moul (luso gnamsetl tleaa,anrwmyy oSifucoitttthat the Burial Board, whose accounts the meeting were met to audit, were now paying nearly five per e cent, for eire)rlsaehrdt money which they could easily get at four n s of th state of the money market. Several m were present, and could not very well contest a fact which could be so easily proved from the books; and they looked a little crestfallen that a gentleman, who was not one of their number, should tell them their business. Such a want of shrewdness in driving a bargain, on the part of that long- suffering creature the ratepayer, astonished many of those present, in whose opinion the Burial Board are a body which, as a rule, are not given to any acts of unnecessary extravagance. From what I hear, this matter was not re- ferred to before the time. At the date when Mr. John Hazlehurst applied to the Board, expressing his willingness ta renew a loan for upwards of £2,000 at 41 per cent., it was stated that he had made an offer which, at first eight, ap- peared tempting. This was to renew the loan for ten years at 41 per cent., on condition that it was accepted for that term. The feeling of several members of the Board was to accept this very fair offer. It was quietly hinted that the gentleman in question was a little inclined to relax the usual strictness of a money lender on this occasion, and give the Board a chance if they were only possessed of the good sense to seize the golden opportunity which presented itself, and led on to "fortune." One of the gentlemen present, who must be credited with a little keener intellect than hia brethren round the table, at least in reference to this par- ticular matter, said that if his memory did not fail him, there was in existence a loan, with the gentleman referred to at even as low a figure as four per cent. He was loudly informed that he was mistaken. He, however, stood his ground, and asked for the production of the mortgage book. He also said that it would be rather in- consistent to pay 4i per cent., when several widows who relied upon the interest as their chief means of support, were only getting four for their loans. The book was produced, and it was found that there was a mortgage in existence with my generous friend Mr. Hazle- I burst at even so low a figure as four per cent! Another matter came before the Thursday evening's meeting, upon which I may say a few words. Mr. Fairhurst, who is a Congregationalist, and cannot, therefore, be credited I with too much respect for the somewhat gaudy external trappings of the clergy of the Church of England, pointed out that in the accounts there were three items of as. each, pelt down for washing surplices, and to this charge he I objected on principle. The Vicar, with a quiet touch of I satire, concurred with him in the idea that it was a dreadful thing that the inhabitants of a pretty populous place like Runcorn, should be called upon to pay 9s. in the course of one year for washing the surplices used at the cemetery, though he admitted that it was not a legal charge, according to the Burial's Act. Dr. McDougall, with a dryasdust love of the force of antiquated usage which somewhat surprises me in a gentleman of such a mould of intellect, appealed to what had been the custom from the establishment of the Board. It was stated that it had always been customary to pay for the washing; and he appeared to consider this a conclusive argument, though I very much doubt whether he would have looked upon the matter in the •same light if someone not blessed with so much of this world's goods as the clergy, had applied to the Board of Commissioners to pay Os. per year, to which he had no legal right. The room contained a very fair sprinkling of the Nonconformist element, but Mr. Fairhurst was not supported by a solitary voice in the objection he had taken, as the ratepayers ap- peared to be awed by the bonhomie and tact of the ecclesiat- tical dignitary who presided. They, like obedient children, passed the charge of 95. unanimously, and went home to pay their own .washing bills. Horace says " Iliacoe intra muros peceatur et extra."

Why should Mr. Cliff ba favoured in this respect more than any other person tendering? Here was a subject affecting the entire body of the scavengers, but I suppose that because they mostly, if not entirely, consist of old men, their interests are scarcely worth troubling about. What is to be done with some of these old servants, whose who have been in the employ of the town for years, now that they are thrown out of work by the tender for street cleaning being handed over to Mr. Cliff? Are they to fall into the hands of the Poor Law Guardians and to .be sent to their respec- tive parishes if they cannot claim a settlement in Runcorn ? "Rattle his bones over the stones; He's only a pauper, whom nobody owns !" For a long time there have been great complaints in Widnes as to the wanton destruction of unoccupied and other house property; and those interested in this class of investment have, very wisely, handed together in the form of a society for the purpose of doing what they can to put a stop to the proceedings of the Vandals who infest the dis- trict and appear to think it a good joke to walk off with a doer, like the ancient Samson did with the gates of the city of the Philistines.

Notwithstanding the great amount of grumbling which has been done during the last two years by the mem- bers of the Widnes Owners and Ratepayers' Association and their friends, and despite of the fact of the appear- ance of a deputation from them before the Local Govern- ment Board's auditor, on his last visit, backed by the eloquence of Mr. Pierce, slicitor, the general body -

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 30, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 30, 1881.

of ratepayers appear to give a general approval to the man- ner in which the tewn's affairs are conducted. Some of sour readers may be ready to contest this assertion, but facts are very stubborn things, and it is quite apparent that in the last election the grumbling section of the community were simply "nowhere" when they determined to test their belief in the great dissatisfaction of the ratepayers, by trying to re- turn candidates of their own selection! Their efforts were put forth in vain, and their opponents are jubilant at the comparatively easy victory they have obtained. Certainly the members of the Association may point to the fact that their efforts have resulted in certain surcharges being made upon some of the members of the Local Board, but those who profess to be behind the scenes say that all the talk about the heavy sums which certain gentlemen will be called upon to pay, will end in smoke; and I am inclined to favour this view. Difficulties, apparently insurmount- able, vanish into thin air before the plans of a bold and energetic financier and general man of business like Major Cross, who has again been elected to the post of chairman, which it is generally understood he is to occupy • until the town is in- corporated, when he is to be elevated to the proud position of mayor of the newly-created municipality. The Major says he is quite confident that if the ratepayers will only exercise a little patience, they will find that they have got a splendid investment in their magnificent waterworks; and also in the gasworks. The Local Board barque has of late been sailing throned) very stormy seas, and it is only reason- able to expect summer skies and more peaceful waters under so efficient a captain. If a man is not a total abstainer what qualification ought he to have that would be considered equivalent to being a teetotaler to fit him for taking a responsible situation ? I presume that an answer can be found in the following curious advertisement, which I came across this week "Man—To Bakers.—Wanted a man, a teetotaler preferred; if not a teetotaler he must have three suits of clothes." As this emanates from Penketh, near Warrington, I am led to conclude that the good people who live there, and who are not teetotalers, do not possess " three suits of clothes," or else that bakers generally who are not total abstainers do not do so.
STOPPAGE OF DITTON IRONWORKS.—Within the last few dAys, the men employed at the Ditton Ironworks, who number about 300, have received notice that the works will be stopped, almost immediately.

SLIGHT FIItE AT RUNCORN. —Oa Tuesday night, the window curtains in the house of the Rev. Henry Valentine (Wesleyan), at Runcorn, caught fire. Before the flames were extinguished the venetian blinds and a dressing table were destroyed.

RES= FROM DROWNING .(1' WIDNRS.—On Monday, a youth named William Whalley, was the means of rescuing the child of Mr. Roberts, of Warrington-road, Widnes, from drowning. The little one was playing near a pond close to Mr. Car Ma's timber yard, Lugsdale, when he fell into the water; and restoratives had to be applied before be re- covered.

RUNCORN ELLESMERE STREET IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— On Monday evening, the winter session was brought to a close by a tea, which was well attended. A meeting was afterwards held, at which Mr. John Holford read the report, which showed that during the session the average attend- ance had been 29. and at some of the meetings there had been as many as 70 present. SERMON AT WIDNES ON LORD BEACONSFIELD. On Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar, preached at St. Mary's Church, Widnes, from Numbers, 20th chap., 29th verse., "And when all the congregation saw that Aaron was dead, they mourned for Aaron 30 days, even all.the House of Israel." During his discourse the Vicar referred to the death of Lord Beaconsfield, whom he described as a very successful man, with an indomitable will, and wonderful perseverance.

An ingenious individual possessing a taste for figures and politics has been searching a modern Doomsday Book in order to find out how many acres of land are held by the members of the present Cabinet. The result of his search is that Mr. Gladstone is stated to own 7,000 acres, Mr. Dod-on 30,000, Lord Kimberley 11,000, Lord Northbrook 10,000, Lord Spencer 27,000, and the Marquis of Hartington, although not himself a landowner at present, is heir to 200,000 acres, whilst several other members of the GoYern- ment own less ambitious estates. It certainly says sonic- thing for the unselt,shnesQ of the majority of those great Liberal lan3owners that they have pet their hands to the task of altering the laws so as to make them more favourable to the tenants, and to diminish tbe power of the landocracy of winch they form a part. •

RUNCORN FOOTBALL Cum.—On Tuesday, the members ; of this club, to the number of about 30, assembled at the ! house of Mr. Henry Jackson, the Navigation Inn, Canal- street, to partake of their annual supper. The catering was all that could be desired, and after ample justice had been done and the cloth removed the tembers and their friends commenced the second part of the programme. Mr. F. Bate was voted to the chair, and Mr. William Wright to the vice- chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were heartily given and responded to, amongst them being "The Queen and Royal Family," "Army and Navy," "Presidents and Vice-Presidents," "Captains," "The Town and Trade of Runcorn," "The Visitors," "Host and Hostess," and "Our Next Merry Meeting," The remainder of the evening was spent in singing. The following is a list of the officers for the ensuing year : Mr. J. Brundret, JP., president ; vice- presidents, Messrs. C. W. Hazlehurst, JP., F. A. Lake, E. A. Chorlton, E. S. Hazlehurst, C. Lewin, C. Reynolds, H. Rey- nolds, W. Bate, J. Ashton, J. J. Speakman, J. R. Frith, G. L. VVigg, and S. B. Chadwick, J.P.; Captains Ist team Mr. F. Bate ; 2nd team Mr. J. Shirlock, treasurer, Mr. C. Pownall ; auditors, Mr. W. Riley and Mr. T. E. Booth; secretary, Mr. W. Wright. Besides these, tbere are about 16 others who form a committee to regulate the teams for the matches to be played.

Drunken people are guilty of doing some very funny , things occasionally. I am told of one young gentleman who, when he gets over the mark—and this be it said to his discredit is not an uncommon occurrence—persuades him- self that he is one of the cutest fellows in the world. This thirsty soul has a wife who, whenever she finds her lord in an unusually happy condition, resorts to every stratagem to ' obtain possession of all the loose cash in his pockets. The young gentleman appears to be aware of this weakness on , her part, and latterly he has tried to checkmate his better- half by adopting the tactics of the magpie, and hiding the ' wreckage of his cash in some part of the house before his wife has time to swoop down upon it. The other day this ' young gentleman returned home in an obfuscated state with a more than ordinarily large sum of money in his pocket, . when he resorted to his accustomed ruse. Unfortunately, however, he succeeded only too well in hiding the coin. When he awoke the next morning, and had collected his confused senses, he bethought himself of his money, and not having a particularly clear , 1 recollection as to where he had deposited it, searched every spot in the house—likely and unlikely. It appears that his search was unsuccessful, for he has not found it yet. Probably, it may prove to be a "profitable loss," after all, for it may be a warning to him not to get ' into such a state as to necessitate this game of hide and seek. As a rule, those who in the stern struggle for existence, fall behind, and are trampled upon in the contest about "the survival of the fittest," so that they have to apply for help to the relief authorities of the district in which they live, are by pretty general consent spoken very little about. They are "played out," and for the future are considered of no moment, as a rule, on the stage of life. But there are circumstances in which even a pauper may rise into impor- tance in the eyes of an honorary Canon of Chester Cathe- dral, and these have lately come to the front in the town of 1 Runcorn. When the soul has passed the ivory gates one would imagine that it was a matter of small moment whether the body was consigned to the dark house and the long sleep in consecrated or unconsecrated ground ; but the Rev. Canon Barclay views this question from a different stand-point—the stand-point of fees. He inaintains that Mr. Wright, the Runcorn relieving officer, is acting in strict ac- cordance with the letter of the law when he declined to grant burial fees to the parent of a child who was in receipt of parochial. relief, because the relatives refused to bury in consecrated ground! "It is so nomi- nated in the bond ;" and owing to the matter of fees coming into dispute, the poor person who before death was scarcely considerdd of the slightest importance in the community, emerges from obscurity, and is .heard of in the important discussions raised at the meetings of Guardians and Burial Boards In the talk which arose on the question at the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, the Chairman certainly made a concession of the greatest importanca to the community, for "he gave it as his opinion that there was no necessity for burials to take place in consecrated groand." He, however, added a remark, showing that, though apparently quite willing to let his poor Dissenting ministerial brethren do the work of burying the paupers on a wet day, whilst he was, possibly, pouring over the pages of Plato, Sophocles, or Canon Liddon's latest volume, he should claim the fees!, No doubt our clerical friend feels bound to do this as a follower of the Good Shepherd, a per- fect Abdiel where the interests of Christ's Church, Oxford, are concerned, and a minister of the church as by law established. The humble follower of the despised Nazarene is as keen as the most commercial of men on a question in- volving the current coin of the realm. Nevertheless, the ' sentence still stands in the grand old Book, " Ye cannot 'serve God and mammon." FLACCUS.

HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. , —Oa Monday, the usual tea party and entertainment, in connection with the above society, was held in Trinity School, Runcorn. A goodly number sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by Mrs. Sefton, Mrs. S. H. Daw- son, and Miss Goodwell. After tea, the secretary, Mr. S. H. Dawson, read the yearly report, which, on the whole, was highly satisfactory. °During the year the essay and debating class have held 24 meetings, of which four were devoted to lectures, 14 to essays, one to debate, four to impromptu speaking, two to reading, &re., the average attendance being 18. Fifty-two cottage lectures have been held at Brickkiln Houses, the average attendance at each beirg 13. Fifty-two cottage lectures have also been held at Mill Brow, with an average attendance of 13. The Ragged School mission service has been held on 52 Sunday evenings, and conducted by members of the Association, with au average attendance of 74, and at the close of each service a player meeting has bees held, to which there was an average attendance of 22. The work of the Association is divided into two parts; one for essays, debates, kc., and the other for mission work, both of which branches have been most satisfactorily worked during the past year, the mission work especially having shown most encouraging results, much good having been done by this means in the neglected neighbourhoods of the parish, which, but for these services, would never have the privilege of joining in Divine worship. The Rev, W. Preston, M.A., president, spoke of the various good works carried on by the members, and said the Association rendered him most invaluable aid in carryfhg on his work in the parish. The Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, spoke upon the advantages of such a society and the good it could effect, and hoped all the young men of the parish would become members; after which, the Rev. W. Rebinson said a few words. During the evening the choir rendered the glees "Belts of Eve, " Farewell, ' and "Sweet and Low," and Mr. Keohler gave a recitation and a reading, as did also Mr. Rogerson, a Lancashire reading.—Com.

A HARBINGER OF SPRING.—The notes of the cuckoo were heard on Monday morning at Wallasey for the first time this year, though the "harbinger of spring" has taken up his abc.de at West Kirby since the 14th inst.

WARRINGTON STARR-BOWERIT SOCIETT.—This building society, which was inaugurated in February last, under circumstances that seemed to portend a prosperous career, has corae to a premature termination. We understand, that as the number of members has fallen short of the number necessary for the successful working of the society, the managers have decided to close it, and the subscriptions which have been paid, are being returned. W. Carlile in the chair. All the speakers bore testimony to the serious amount of damage done to empty property at Widnes, and the following resolution was passed: "That a society be formed among the property owners of Widnes for the pro- tection of property in that town under the name of The Widnes Protection of Property Association.'" TEE BANKRUPTCY OF A WIDNES Summon. —Friday week, at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Perronet Thompson, was the day appointed for the public examination of Mr. T. Beasley, solicitor, of Widnes. He did not appear; but the trustee, Mr. Bolland, stated the bankrupt had attended at his office for examination by the creditors, at a meeting to which they were all called, and had undergone an examination by Mr. Henry Gregory, which resulted in an adjournment for the bankrupt to furnish detailed accounts, which would require time for their preparation, and, therefore, an ad- journment of the present sitting was neces- sary. Mr. Segar said he appeared on behalf of creditors to examine the hatkrupt ; and as lie had not been informed of the proposed adjournment, he considered the costs of the creditors ought to be paid. Mr. Bolland said that it was a well-established rule that, as all creditors i.ere assumed to be represented by the trust, no individual creditor could be allowed his costs for appearing to oppose unless the opposi- tion resulted in the discovery of estate which would not have been discovered by the trustee. Here the trustee's investiga- tions were incomplete, and, for aught that appearFcl, the proposed ex imination on the part of the creditors might. be objectiess. His Hohour, after hearing Mr. Seger, said be thought, as ho had been brought to the court to examine a bankrupt no,o Was not present, he ought to be allowed his costs. An ournment on those terms was then taken to the 20th is: Messrs. W. Morris and J. Howard Jones represented the trustee.

FRUIT BANCILTT.—A very interesting meeting was held on Tuesday. evening, in Golborne-street Baptist Chapel Schoolroom, on the occasion of a fruit banquet being given by the Walter Bonehill Lodge of Good Templars. Bro. W. Roberts, P.D.G.W.T. presided, and opened the proceedings in a very appropriate address, in the course of which he pointed out the advantages of total abstinence from all intoxicating liquors and the evils arising from the drink traffic. A very entertaining and instructive programme of songs, recitations, tko., was then gone through, in a manner which reflected credit on all who took part therein.

THE MUSEUM COMMITTEE AND THN LATH Mn. JOHN SHARP.—In the minutes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, which will be submitted to the Council for con- firmation, on Tuesday next, is the following resolution:— " That the members of this committee, having heard of the sudden death of Mr. John Sharp, who has rendered most valuable service to the town by cataloguing and arranging the seals and coins in the Museum, desire to express their regret at his loss, and to record their appreciition of the ser- vices so kindly rendered by him. And that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to Mrs. Sharp with an expression of the sincere condolence of this committee with her in her loss."

COOKERY LECTURES AT WARBINGTOIC—MIS. Thwaitea (of Liverpool) completed her course of cookery lectures in the National School, Church-street, on Wednesday evening. The lecture on Saturday afternoon was a practical demon- stration of high class cookery, and on Monday and Wednes- day evenings the lectures gave practical illustrations of economical culinary preparations. Mrs. Thwaites carefully expounded her recipes for making the various dishes she prepared, and was listened to with much interest by the audiences who had assembled with the object of increasing their knowledge of the CU' illarV art.

A 'WIDNES Pers2a.—A patent has been applied for by Messrs. John Hargreaves, chemist, and Thomas Robinson, ironfounier, both of Widnes, for "Improvements in treating ores and substances containing antimony, and in apparatus employed therein." SUDDEN DEATH AT RIINCORN.—On Monday, the wife of Mr. Peter Hindley, shopkeeper, Ashridge-street, Run; corn, who died very suddenly on the previous Thursday, was interred at Warrington. Deceased, who appeared to be in very good health, went into the town to transact some business, and when opposite the Fleetwood Arms, in Church- street, she complained of a pain in her head and fell down. She was taken home in a cab, and medical assistance called in, but she died very shortly afterwards from apoplexy. MACCABE AT Rus. coax.—On Wednesday evening, Mr. Frederic Maccabe, paid a farewell visit to Runcorn There was a good audience. The sketches given were " Mr. Solemn Sides," " Miss Mary May," " The Lady Killer," " Wandorin Troubldours," " The Excursion Train," "Mr. Tommy Grindle," and " Terry O'Mulligan." Mr. Maccabe' who is very popular in the neighbourhood, was very well received, though his voice was not quite equal to what we remember to have heard in former years.

MERSEY COVER COMPANY, LIMITED: A NEW WIDNES FlRM.—This is the conversion to a company of the leisi- ness of copper smelter carried on by Mr. John Fein ick Allen, of Widnes. It was registered on the 19th inst., with a capital of £15,000, in £lO shares. The purchase includes all property appertaining to such business. The considera- tion is £6,000 in fully paid shares, and £1,500 in cash. The subscribers are : J. F. Allen, Widnes, copper smelter, shares, 1; John Robinson, Whines, manufacturing chemist, 1; T. Shenton, Widnes, copper refiner, 1; Edward Bibby, Widnes, refineryman, 1; John Ellis, Widnes, smith 1 ; William Hughes, Widnes, furnace builder, 1; Hugh Hughes, id- nes, furnaceman, 1. Mr. J. F. Allen is appointed manager, at a salary of £450 per annum. Most of the regulations of table A of the Companies Act, 1862, are adopted.

CHANCELLOR ESPIN ON THE Circncrt.—Speaking at the Ormskirk Parish Church on Monday, at the first of a series of visitations, the Rev. Chancellor Espin referred at some length to the Burials Act, which he suggested should be carried out in a kindly and conciliatory spirit towards Non- conformists. It was, said the Chancellor, the Church, and not a sect, nor yet the dead, that was injured when a lack of generous consideration was shown to those whose hearts were sore in bereavement. Another matter referred to was the Church Boards Bill, which is before the House of Com- mons, and which, the Chancellor said, ought not to pass as it now stood. He condemned the bill as of too sweeping a character, and as likely to hand over the control of churches, services, and decorations to those who were not Churchmen at all. While opposed to this measure, Chancellor Espin thought it would be well for incumbents and churchwardens I to take steps to associate with themselves two or more prac- tical men of business, chosen by the congfegation, so as to form a sort of committee of church finance.

THE DEATH OF Da. PI7NSICON.—The great Wesleyan Methodist orator, whose career has just closed, had several personal friends in the town of Runcorn, and he was not very unfrequently to be seen on the missionary platform at St. Paul's. In the course of his discourse on Sunday even- ing in the same chapel, the Rev. John Nowell (superintend- ent) referred to the great loss which the denomination had sustained by the death of the renowned rhetorician, whose fame was in all the churches. The preacher remarked that he was reminded by the sad event of the fact that they stood side by side when being examined as candidates for the ministry many years ago; and again, three years later, Dr. Punshon stood on his left at the ordination service. A ;bort time ago they met and compared notes, and among ether things they found that though they were of the same minis- terial year, he was his senior by one year. Personally, he felt the removal of Dr. Panshon a loud and solemn call— "Be ye also ready, for in such an hour as ye 11min4 not the Son of Man cometh."

TEA PAETT AT liarrox.—On the evening of the 22nd inst., the members of the Wesleyan Sunday school Bible class, Halton, were entertained at tea by Mr. R. N. Davies, in the schoolroom. About a hundred persons sat down to the substantial repast, which was supplied by Mrs.' Parsons, of Runcorn. The tables were tastefully laid out, being adorned with beautiful plants, covered with blossoms, kindly lent by Mrs. Davies, of the Mount. After all present had refreshed themselves, the room was prepared for a musical entertainment. The various pieces were rendered by the choir, and ladies and gentlemen, hereafter mentioned. Mr. A. E. Davies presided at the piano. The following per- sons gave songs:—Miss Davies, Miss Edwards, Mr. R. N. Davies, and Mr. A. Nowell. Duets were sung by Miss Rigby and Miss R. Edwards, and Miss Davies and Mr. R. Davies. Master A. Davies and Miss Roberts played solos on the pianoforte. Messrs. H. Rowe, J. Dale, S. Saunders, and C. Leathwood also sang a quartette. The vocalists and instrumentalists gave satisfaction to every one. The tea meeting and entertainment passed off very pleasantly.— Coin.

' SUPPOSED CASE OF SLAIN BY DRINK—On Tuesday, Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Bridge- water Arms, Percival-lane, touching the death of Robert Magill, an able seaman on board the Happy-go-Lucky brigantine, and a native of Carrickhill, Belfast. On Monday evening, about six o'clock, the deceased and another seaman named John Clements, left their vessel, which is lying at Weston, to visit Runcorn, for the purpose of buying some clothes. As they were going they called at a public-house whenever "they felt like having a drink." At Runcorn they visited Mr. Collins's outfitters shop in Church-street, and the deceased bought clothes worth upwards of £l, which he left there. In the same street they met the mate of the vessel, and went to a public-house, where they had five or six drinks. About half-past nine o'clock, as deceased declined to go to the vessel, he left him in Runcorn. Clements admitted that be had had "a good lump of drink on board—in fact, as much as he could carry." The deceased had had about as much as he had. On the , following morning, the body of Magill WAS found in the river Mersey, opposite the Big House, by William Brearley, an assistant foreman at the docks. The jury returned an I open verdict.

SOUTHPORT AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANKING COM- PANY, LIISITED.—A private meeting ot the shareholders of 1 this company was held on Saturday afternoon in the Town Hall, Southport. The meeting was convened for the pur- pose of hearing the report of the Directors' and Share- holders' Committee, and to consider the present position and future prospects of the bank. There was a large attendance. —Mr. R. Nicholson, J.P., presided, and pointed out that the great object of the meeting was to try and get the 5,000 shareholders who had not yet transferred their shares from • the old bAnk to the new one to do so at once.—Mr. Alder- man Boothroyd (Southport) proposed that these shareholders be waited upon by a deputation, and that their influence be brought to bear upon them to induce them to transfer their shares.—Mr. Barrow (Coventty) seconded this, and it was carried unanimously.—Mr. Alderman Fisher (Southport), in an acrimonious speech, commented upon the action of those who had not yet transferred their shares. Ile, however, afterwards apologised for the strong language he had used. A large number present at the meeting promised to take up more shares. Some of them said they would have done so before; but from remarks made by Mr. Ni'hinney, the official liquidator, at a previous meeting, they were labour- ing under the impression that they would then be liable for their old shares as well as their new ones. A list of new directors was read over and approved of. It was stated that if the company had had power in their articles of association to create preference stock, the business of the bank would still be going on. It was also announced that they had paid off the mortgage on their handsome building, and had now the deeds deposited safely in the bank. They had over £70,000 in the bank besides. Up to three o'clock on Saturday afternoon there was 31,300 shares taken up. The minimum numbnr required to open the bank is 30,000, but the total number issued by the directors is 38,000. WIDNES SCHOOL Boann.—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Timmis presided, and there were also present the Revs. Fathers Finegan and Clarke, and Messrs. O'Keeffe, Deacon, Davis, and Danby (clerk.)—The report of the District Education Committee was adopted, on the motion of Mr. Deacon, seconded by the Chairman. It stated that during last month the number of cases summoned before the committee had been 527, of whom 124 were for application for payment of fees, and 403 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recom- mended to be paid in 107 cases; id were refused, and one adjourned for feather enquiries. The number of prosecu- tions before the magistrates was 30, the convictions 30, and three children had been sent to industrial schools.—At the last meeting of the Board, a letter was read from the three headmasters, complaining that a statement drawn up by the School Management Committee in regard to the amount earned in the shape of Government grant, was based upon a wrong foundation. The letter was referred to a committee, who held a meeting on the 30th ult. The three head- masters were invited to be present during the discussion of the objections. The report stated that the committee bad unanimously come to the conclusion that there was no rea- sonable ground for complaint about the teaching-staff, and they regretted that so many teachers had signed such a reck- less statement as only two out of every ten teachers made any complaint at all ; and those two had no real foundation for it. They also recommended that the report be adopted and a copy forwarded to each headmaster who signed for all the teachers.—The Chairman said it appeared the committee had been able to give a very good answer to all the charges, and one which was quite satisfactory. The document was adopted, on the proposition of Father Finegan, seconded by the Chairman.—The report of the Sites and Building Com- mittee, which W. 19 adopted, that they had received the half- yearly report of the architects of the Board on the various schools, and they recommended that the repairs should be effected as per the architects' specifications.—The other business before the Board was not of public interest.
THE WIGAN ELECTION.—II is stated that a commission to inquire into the nature and extent of the corrupt practices at the recent election at Wigan will be issued in a few days.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE.OF COMMONS.

EXTENSION OF THE FRANCHISE.—Mr. H. MASON gaVe notice on early day to move the extension of parliamer tary elective franchise to women. . THE Imam Lawn Brer..—Lord Er.cao said he should move his amendment to the second reading of the Trish Laud Bill to the effect that the' leading provision of the bill were in the main unsound, unjust, and impolitic. HIGHWAY ACCOUNTS.—Mr. DODSON, replying to Mr. Stan- hope, said it was intended to medify the inconvenient forms of accounts hitherto filled up by the surveyors of highways in country districts. THE JURY SYSTEM.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL replying to Mr. Broadhurst, said be could uot° promise during the present session to bring in a bill to amend the jury system. Trix OCCUPATION OF LAINGS NEK.—Mr. GRANT DUFF said there was rio Secret understanding between Sir Evelyn Wood and the Boers to the effect that the British troops would not occupy the portion of the Queen's territory in Natal called Laings Nek, but there was a public agreement to that effect. CENTRAL ASIA.—Sir C. DILZE, replying to Mr. Stanhope, said the recall of General Scobeleff was first known on the 22nd of last month, and confirmed by Lord Dufferin, four days afterwards. THE PARLIAMENTARY OATH.--Mr. GLADSTONE stid, notice would be given to-night to ask leave on Monday to introduce a bill to amend the law relating to Parliarneniory oaths, and as the bill would be very short he proposed to take the second reading on Tuesday at two. If that day should not prove agreeable then the bill would be ta kelt on Friday at two.—Lord R. CHURCHILL said he should oppose the bill if leave was asked after 12-30 on Monday night. THE POWER OF COLONIAL REPRESENTATIVES. -- On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. HENRY RICHARD moved that the power claimed and exer- cised by representatives of this country abroad to contract engagements, annex territory, and make war, without the sanction of the Government, was opposed to the con- stitution - and at variance with international law, and injurious to the true interests of the country. He cited instance's, more particularly the Zulu war and actions that had taken place in other parts of the world, in support of his resolution, and said the sooner the power of making war and annexing countries which had ' already cost the country thousands of lives and many mil- lions of money abroad, was limited to the contral govern- ment, the better it would be for this country and for suffer- ' ing humanity. ,—Mr. GLADSTONE said while the aim and purpose of honourable members was good, he was bound to say the resolution was one which could not with safety be accepted, by the House, because if passed, it would become necessary to follow it up with other action. He admitted there had been cases where our agents abroad had acted rashly and im- properly, but looking back there were cases the reverse. He pointed out that in the last Parliament the majority made no attempt to check the war policy of the administration. Ho said the telegraph now gave the central Government in- creased control over its agents abroad, but the great thing to be looked for was an improvement in the central Govern- ment itself, and best results would follow its becoming more modest and less arrogant, and exhibiting greater self-discipline and increased self-control.--Mr. IterunosrE approved of the principles laid down in the resolution.—Mr. RYLANDS thought the authority of our agents abroad ought to be checked before the country was involved in greater 1 loss of life, and further enormous expenditure of monov.— After a few words from Mr. LYULFH STANLEY, the Rouse divided, when there appeared for the resolution, 64; against it, 72. THE OPIUM TRADE.—Mr. PEASE called attention to the present position of the negotiations between Her Majesty's Government and China, in relation to the duties affecting opium, and the position of the Indian revenue, in relation to the monies received from the cultivation of, and the dutiee levied on, the drug. He insisted that the trade now carried on was opposed alike to Christian and international morality, and wati! inetturnental in effecting the moral degradation of thousands of Chinese, *fid. therefore it ought to be abolished, and the revenue surrendered could be made up by increased economy of Indian revenue and expenditure. He thought it was due to the Government of China that the Chefoo Con- vention should be ratified by the British Government with- out demanding from the Government of China a modifica- tion of its original terms.—The House was here counted, but forty members were found to be present.—Sir J. KlinfNae WAY supported the ;views of Mr. Pease. He did not wish. that the finances of India should be suddenly upset, but he thought an intimation ought to'be given that we intended to give up the opium traffic gradually.—Mr. ONSLOW thought no sufficient cause had been shown for discontinuing the present traffic.

COLONEL JOSEPH DE lANTMORENOY, who on the Ist instant, was transferred from the command of the 13th and 14th sub-districts (Liverpool and Warrington) to take over the command of the brigade depot at Galway, Ireland, will, on the let of July next, compulsorily retire from the service under the five years' rule.

PRESCOT UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.— This committee held its first monthly meeting for the ensu- ing year on Thursday, at the Board-room, Whiston Work- ' house. There were prescnt the Rev.'. T. Chambers and J. (Barnacle, Messrs. J. Leatherbarrow, G. J. Paris. T. Dobell, J. T. Hall, P. Longton, and T. Eatock ; with Mr. Hartley, I clerk.—On the motion of the Rev. J. Barnacle, seconded by I Mr. a bell, the Rev. T. Chambers was unanimously re- I elected chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr. Chambers I thought some one else should have the honour of occupying the chair this year. He was of opinion that honours should I be divided.—The other members of the committee, however' I would not hear of it, and Mr. Chambers accordingly took , the chair.—The Chairman returned thanks, and stated that the school attendance officer was not present, he having gone to Cambridgeshire to appear before a Board of Guar- dians respecting the appointment of a relieving officer. He (Mr. Chambers) wished to say that in case Mr. Welch did not get the appointment, he intended to thoroughly impress upon him that he must devote his whole time to his work 1 as school attendance officer, and not get mixed up with the work in the clerk's office.-1-Several members present agreed with the Chairman, complaints having been frequently made 1 to them of children running about the roads instead of being I at school.—lt was resolved that a return be made out of i the number of children in the committee's district who had i not attended school from March up to the Easter holidays. , ' —Several accounts of the local committees were laid before I the committee, and recommended for payment.

LATEST TELEGRAMS. &e.
SAD BOAT ACCIDENT.

r A sad boat accident was reported yesterday, froni the north of Scotland. While a boat containing four men, was making its way from sutherlaudshire to Thurso, it capsized, and the crew of four perished. The boat has been found stranded on one of the Orkney Isles. Two of the occupants were married and leave large families. The other two were young men and unmarried.

MORE ARRESTS IN IRELAND. At four o'clock yesterday, a force of 32 policemen was sent to arrest some persons in Clough, in connection with the disturbances arising out of the serving of the writs on the Grattan Bellow estate, at Jenkineon, Kilkenny. Four arrests were accomplished—two women and two boys. The seizures were effected. quietly.
