div.p: THE SLOUGH MUSDEE:

I The trial of Alfred Augustus Payne (18), for the wilful murder of Ann Revill, at Slough, on the nth instant, was resumed at Aylesbury to-day, before Mr. Justice Lopes. Mr. J. C. Lawrence proceeded to sum up the case on the part of the Crown, and was followed by Mr. Attenborough address- ing the jury for the defence. He admitted that it was a case of grave suspicion against the prisoner, but argued that nothing could be actually proved against him. The Judge summed up, and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty. ATTEMPT TO WRECK A Tp AIN. • A deliberate attempt was made on Thursday night to wreck a train on the North Staffordshire line at Etteley Heath, near Sandbacla, Cheshire. Some person removed a large coping-stone from Etteley Heath bridge and placed it upon the metals, where, fortunately, it was discovercd by an official beforo a train passed. CABINET COUNCIL, A Cabinet Council was held at three o'clock yesterday afternoon, in Downing-street. All the ministers except Lord Granville and Earl Spencer were present, and Lord Carlingford, the new Lord Privy Seal, attended for the first time. The sitting lasted about an hour and a half, during which time the ministers were chiefly engaged is discussing the Irish Land Bill, and the proposed new affirmation bill. T,he Lord. Chancellor, who came up from Itsackley, to at- tend the meeting of the Cabinet, subsequently returned to , his country residence. Earl Spencer is at present on a visit to Lord Granville at Widmer Castle.

div.head: INCENDIARISM NEAR CORK.
div.p: INCENDIARISM NEAR CORK.

At an early hour on Thursday snorning, an extensive farm house and out offices close to Cork, from which a tenant had been evicted for aon-payment of rent, were burnt down. The place had been taken only a few days since by Thomas Sutton, and his employee, in consequence of having received notices threatening them with death the day ,bcfore, had refused to work on the farm. The gates, piers, and fences were also levelled, and shots were heard in the neighbourhood daring the night. No arrests in connection with the outrage have taken place. ETICTIONS AND INTIMIDATION, Two troops of the 20th Hussars, two compatiee of the 57th Regiment, and 150 police, went to New Pallas, near Limerick, on Thursday, to evict 13 tenants of Mr. Apjohn. About 3,000 people gathered, hooting and groaning, and in consequence, the agent was so much intimated that he refused to point out the farms from which the tenants were to be evicted.

FURTHER ARRESTS UNDER THE COERCION ACT. Two brothers, named John and Cornelius Creedon, and a law-clerk named John O'Sullivan, were arrested under the Coercion Act, at Mill-street, bounty Cork, on Thursday. Two of the prisoners were conveyed to Limerick. MEETING OF THE CONSERVATFirE PARTY..

- - • Nearly every Conservative peer or member of the House of Commons who is in town attended a meeting of the party on Thursday, at the Carlton, to discuss the Land Bill. Sir Stafford Northcote acted as chairman, and a long discussion took place on the land proposals of the Cabinet. It is said that the question of the leadership of the party was only in- cidentally mentioned. After the meeting Lord John Man- ners went down to the House of Commons and gave notice of an amendment to the Irish Land Bill. THE TRANSVAAL.

A Pretoria telegram of the 14th inst. says :—lntenae I anxiety still prevails here, and uncertainty as to what will happen. Serious troubles are anticipated. The loyal Boers ) and the English are leaving the country hurriedly, and flarge numbers of women and children are being sent away. The garrisons at Rustenbirg and Marbastsdt are ordered to I concentrate at Pretoria at once. At a crowded meeting at Pretoria to-day, it was resolved to send home a deputation to lay important facts before the Government. The Boers have refused to acknowledge od interim the administration of the British Government at Middleburg and other places, and keep their flag flying. News has been leceived of another brutal mnrder of an Englishman by the Boers on the Yokesei river. Heliographic communication has been estab- lished with l'retoria.

div.head: LORD GRANVILLE'S HEALTH.
div.p: LORD GRANVILLE'S HEALTH.
Earl Granville has now so far recovered that be has been able during the past week to taken open air exercise. THE NEW AFFIRMATION BILL.

The Central News is enabled to state that the new Bill relating to Parliamentary Oaths which is to be introduced on Monday next, will simply provide that all parties who testifying in a court of law are not required to make oath may affirm. The new Bill, in fact, will limit the right of I those being other than Quakers. MoravianS, Separatists, and others already permitted by enactment to . affirm to the making of affirmations in lieu lof oath. This limitation has been devised .by the Government to avoid any scandal such as was suggested by Lord John Manners that might happen, were an Atheist being permitted either to affirm or take oath to resolve to do ! the latter. It is not expected that there will be any organised opposition to the proposed measure, although it is understood that several members on both sides of the House will oppose its passage. I' THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF EDINBUI3DH. The Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh arrived at Charing I Cross, from Dover, bv special train this evening. The Duke of Cambridge travelled by the same train. I __

CRESUIRE SALT DISTRICTS COMPENSATION BILL.—OR Thursday, the Select Committee of the House of Commons, to which this Bill had been referred, met in committee- room No. 16, to choose the chairman, and consider the course of their proceedings. The following are the names of the members:—Viscount Einlvn, Mr. Hastings, Mr. Lyulph Stanley, Sir Henry Tyler, Mr. Blennerhassett, Colonel St. John Barne and Sir Sydney Waterlow. The three last-named were added by the Committee of Selection. There was only a quorum—namely, three members in attend- ance, and Sir S. Waterlow was called to the chair. It was, however, arranged that the committee should meet on the sth, 6th, 9th, and 10th of next month. The Bill will then be proceeded with, and witnesses examined, and it is ex- pected that the proceedings will be protracted. Several gentlemen connected with the salt trade, ratepayers of the district, representatives of railwAy and canal companies, and the River Weaver Navigation Trustees were present. The two other members of the quorum present, on Thurs- day, in addition to the chairman, were Colonel St. John Barne and Mr. L. Stanley.

ST. HELENS WORtneniatw'S 130 LE CLASS.—On Mon- day evening a vocal and instrumental concert was given in the Volunteer Hall, in aid of the sick club and other ex- penses of the St. Helens Workingmen's Bible Class, of which the Rev. Canon Carr is president, and the Revs. C. F. Mer- margen and W. Chaplin the vice-presidents. This Bible class, which was founded by Messrs. George Webster and W. Cross Eccles, has a membership of 400, and has been carried on since its establishment with mt.ch success by the founders. The class has its subsidiary institutions, which, while benefiting the members materially, tend to cement them ' together, and to give greater facilities for the successful carrying out of the primary object of the society; and it is to these auxiliaries, coupled with the energy and attention of Messrs. Eccles and Webster, that the great success of the class is due. The hall was nicely filled, and amongst those ! present were several prominent gentlemen of the town. The brass and reed band connected with the class under the leadership of Mr. W. Jukes, performed several selections of music, which received tha hearty approbation of the. audience. Miss Sawyer, Miss Parry, Mr. George Barton, Mr. W. C. Eccles, and Mr. A. C. Carr supplied the vocal part ;of the evening's entertainment. Mr. W. Strange executed ; several beautiful airs on the piccolo and flute, and was deservedly encored, and Master Harry Webster's performance I on the violin was carefully accomplished, and secured the admiration of the audience, who demanded a repetition. Mr. ; Barton was successful in his attempts to plea the audience. who received his first song, "The Bay of Biscty," with great applause. Miss Parry was a great fs.vourite, and her songs, "To th,, woods," Strangers vet," and "Old Robin 1: Gray," were well received. Miss Sa•Nyer performed her part well, her contributions being, " W'nen the quiet moon is I beaming" and "Should he upbraid! which she sung in a • nice manner. The band played the National Anthem, and a very pleasant concert was brougl4 to a close...

div.head: gdtto to Ott editor.
div.p: gdtto to Ott editor.

THE TRAMWAY TRAMMELS. Dear Sir,—The St. Helens Corporation, it is evident, are doing their best to prevent the Tramway Company from carrying out that work, the completion of which will be of so much advantage to the ratepayers whom the Council pro- fess to represent, but whom in reality in respect to the tramways, they most decidedly misrepresent. There is hardly an interval of seven days free from some injustice alleged to have been perpetrated by the Corporation, or their servants, upon the Tramway Company or its badly used con- tractor. Sir, I speak as a ratepayer, and not as one in any way interested in the matter beyond that intcrest which a ) liatepayer ought to feel, and a good citizen ,olloos feel in matters affecting the welfare of his ,•rtovrn, whether it be "the town of his choice" as Councillor Swift says, or the town he is in some measure compelled to live in. From the commencement the Town Council have thrown difficulties in the way, but in one thing I am glad to say they were deservedly beaten—in the opposition to the Bill for an extensioe of time. WhY did they abject to that bill? Professedly to compel the com- pany to proceed with the branch lines which they said the company intended to shirk, and thus "cheat," to use the word of valiant David, who raleth over us, the town and ratepayers. But is it likely the company would be se idiotic as to go to the expense of a new bill when the main line from St. Helens to Prescot could be finished long before the 24th July—the time specified in the original Bill? No, certainly not. There has been, the streets; and and there is yet likely to be . mush trouble about the setts for paving there is now correspondence going on about the removal of the rails from the Sides of the streets, as though it were ex- pected that the contractor should carry them on his shoulder when he left for the night, and return again with them in the morning. It now appears that the setts and parapher- nalia indispensable to the carrying out of the work, have net to be allowed in the streets at all. When a rail, a paving sett, or a barrewful of sand is required I suppose the con- tractor will have to despatch a man to some out-of-the-way place for the required material. It is much to be regretted nthe contractor cannot carry on the work without having to bother with a paving sett, or a barrowful of earth. The men engaged in the nightsoil department of the corporation do not depcsit their offensive material in the middle of the street; ef course not. The people we read of in the Old Book, were required to make bricks without straw, and it has been said that weavers have had to make cotton shirts of china clay. Very well thee, why cannot our Tramways con- tractor make trainways without paving setts and rails. Why bless my life, he ought to do that easily enough in these days. Of course, when I was a lad they could not do it, but then people were ignorant in those days. In these days of enlightenment a point or two ought to be shown to AN OLD MAN.
St. Helens, April 21st., 1881.

THE POSITION OF CHESHIRE FARMERS. Sir,—Having read the address of Mr. R. Charmley,of Bla- con Hall, before the Wirral Farmers' Club, Birkenhead, with your kind permission I beg to draw a few conclusions. Re- ferring 'So the population of Wirrall Peninsula, he said "that there were 160,527 inhabitants, and that Wirral had a total agricultural area of 112,569 acres." This would only allow seven-tenths of an acre to each person. Also, referring to the relations between landlord and tenant, he stated "there was poor accommodation at the homestead for cheese making, and many landlords did not care to make them any better. So long as tenants could be found who would pay high rents, heavy rates and taxes, with a six months' notice to quit, and a bad agreement as to the tenants rights to improvements, it matters nought to the landlord." Now this may all sound very well at the," Farmers' Club ;" but is there not another Bide to this vexed question of "rights?" viz.: The inexor- able law of supply and demand? If a Wirrall farmer has any cheese, or other product of the farm to sell, and if a stranger offers him a higher price than a former purchaser will pay, to whom does he sell ? The landlord, in renting to the highest bidder, simply recognises the same law or principle of action. If farmers will sign ironclad and "bad agreements as to tenant right improvements," he only has himself to blame. The trouble is here: there are too many applicants for the farms which may be vacant. A good deal was said about the ghost of foreign competition at the meet- ing. Well, that is bad enough, especially when cheese is carried from America to London (3,000 miles) for 20s. per ton cheaper than it is from Cheshire to London; but if farmers would look at it in its true light, and in the Way our statesmen view it, they would extend their discus- Mon more to this "home competition" for farms. Lord Derby, speaking at Rochdale. made the assertion "We are getting too closely packed in this little island of ours, and you may pass what laws you like to prrduce artificial scar- city so long as these conditions exist; nothing that politicians can do, nor any expedient of yours, will prevent your being badly off, and there is no subject more useful than that of supplying to those who want it here trustworthy and reliable information of that country beyond the Atlantic." New whatever rights the tenant farmers may be denied in England, there are no landlords who have the right to pre- vent them front going to America, where, as the noble lord said on another occasion at Liverpool, "It will be difficult for a farmer to quarrel with his landlord unless be quarrels with himself." The writer, having recently returned from the State of lowa, can conscientiously recommend his fellow countrymen to investi gate the claimsof that State as beingbest adapted to dairy, stock raising, and sheep farming, of any State in the American union. As an indication in support of this position, I refer to page 1 of the appendix of the Royal Agricultural Commissioners' Report: "The finest butter in New York now comes over 1,000 miles—from lowa —though originally New York was the principal butter and cheese producing district." lowa is recognised by the differ- ent States as possessing the most favourable natural condi- tions for the production of butter. Weary of struggling year after year to meet payments of tithes, rents, rates, a number of farmers are preparing to leave about the Ist of May to settle in Buena Vista County, lowa, U.S., under the auspices of a party who has lately returned, and who has received special offers of good land. Purchases of 40, 80, or 160 acres can pay six or eight annual payments without interest, seed furnished for half the number of acres ploughed, for one-fourth of the crop if it succeeds. If the crop fails, there will be nothing to pay for the seed. Bond fide settlers acted justly and liberally with. Three thousand acres can be had in 80 acres lots to good practical farmers free of rent, and 83. 41 an acre will be paid them for ploughing this sod land three inches deep (no stones or-tree stumps). The settlers to retain half the crop, also the, seed furnished them, and half the thrashing bill paid." In 1860 the county had no churches or school houses; now there are 93 for 8,000 population. Railroads everywhere, good mar- kets, free pasture. Allexcept the lazy and shiftless, or that man whose creed is "The world owes me a living," I will gladly send information to.—Yours sincerely, 45, Sunny-road, Southport. J. D. SHUTTLEWORTLI.

div.head: LAND QUESTION.
div.p: THE LAND QUESTION.

Dear Sir,—Kindly allow me again to trouble you for a short space in The Examiner while I allude briefly to the waste land of the United Kingdom. Whatever theories men may entertain with regard to the tenure of land, few will be disposed to question the desirability of applying all the means, skill, and labour at our command for the pur- pose of securing its more efficient cultivation, and particu- larly of reclaiming and making productiv a large portion of that which is denominated waste. The total area of the United Kingdom is about 72,000,000 acres. Out of that there are lying waste between 30,000,000 mid 32,000,000 acres; namely—England, 6,398,537 ; Wales, 1,775,289 ; Scotland, 13,863,403; Ireland, 9,710,389; and to this should be added at least 2,250,000 acres of land used simply for the purpose of turning cattle into occasionally, and no more cultivated than it was a thousand years ago. And of these 30,000,000 acres, at least one-half could be cultivated and made to pay a fair percentage upon capital invested, and thus leave 15,000,000 of acres for picturesque scenery, deer forests, game preserves, rabbit warrens, and similar purposes, and for places of recreation for the great masses of the people. Surely this is enough to satisfy the most ardent lover of field spans and out-door exercise. As a set-off against the high figures here stated, it is a well-known fact that immense tracts of land in the United Kingdom returned as under permanent pasture, are simply preserves for game, deer forests, Ltc. ; for in no sense are they used even for pasturage for cattle; and they are seldom visited, except by the gamekeeper or poacher, who is bred and fed by this wasteful neglect of our own natural advantages. Let us take a glance at what could be done by cultivating thispor- tion of waste land. We have in the United Kingdom 1,256,983 paupers, and a total poor rate of £15,462:312.1 This sum annually spent in the shape of poor rates is so lunch sunk capital; it is lost; gone for ever. Now, 200,000 paupers, at least, are able-bodied, and could do something to earn a living if they had the chance. And in addition to this we have on an average a floating population of nearly 1,000,000 persons, who are out of work, oftentimes verging OA the brink of poverty. These are able to work, but can- I not find employment; and, through distress, drift towards pauperism and crime. Vast numbers of each of these classes could be utilised upon our waste lands, PO that by applying this waste labour to these waste lands we could make both productive to the State's benefit. Under State direction the whole of our surplus labour might be employed to reclaim our wasteland; the land so reclaimed to be let on long leases to the cultivator, so as to give him security of tenure; e rents to be paid into the public exchequer, to reimburse the outlay. After the first cost had been incurred and de- frayed, and the Land bad begun to be reproductive and remunerative, it would then employ, at the most moderate computation of two men to an acre, 1,500,000. This would find employment for the whole of our floating labour popu- lation, even if we take the high estimate of 1,000,000, and also for the whole of our pauper and criminal population— the criminals of course being employed on that which was least productive, and where the labour was the most severe and unpleasant, as a punishment for their crimes. The question of the employment of convict labour is now and has been for some time engrossing public attention; and if we could find something more profitable for !hem to do than eternally grinding air we should attains a grand object. Mat making and brush making have been tried, but the mat makers and brush makers have pro • tested strongly because the convicts work was brought into the market to compete with free labour outside the prison to the disadvantage of the honest poor. What, then, is the remedy for all this? One at least may be offered. Employ the convicts in reclaiming waste land along the banks of the Medway, where the land is most fertile, and along the shores of our island home, and transform these wastes into productive land, which, in the event of a dearth of food from abroad, will give us home produce enough and more than enough for our entire people. We have about 15 millions of acres of waste land capable of being cultivated
e,octnee tbnuelant attle in(

at a reasonable and mod' erate outlay which would give s ployment to 1,500,000 persons, representing with their th. pendents 7,500,000 human beings. This would prodirce enough corn to feed 16,000,000 of people with an abuudant supply of green crops, and permanent pasture for cattle and sheep; besides we should develop that which is essentially the produce a small farms, such 'IS -poultry, eggs, and similar articles of borne consumption, and which pays ex- ceedingly well to the cultivator. All this could be done without in any way interfering with what is called natural scenery, and which are closed to all except the lords of the earth, landholders, and their tenants, and poachers. It is very desirable that picturesque scenery should be preserved for the enjoyment of the whol e people, and not fora privileged few. Ido not write in the interests of one class only, although that class be the poorest and most wretched, as well as the largest in the community, but for the whole of Our people—for I car-not conceive that anything which can benefit the poor classes can by any possibility injure any other class. The ilestruction of class privileges even can- not do this, for privilege is at the best but a doubtful good, when all its surroundings and consequences are considered. As a whole is greater than a part, so a nation is greater than any section or class, and it is the duty of the State to secure( the greatest happiness to the greatest number. However,' some may sneer at this indisputable proposition, I have oOdeavoured to adduce facts in favour of the cultivation of our waste land rather than to propound theories. It has been said that it would take years—many years--to mature and work out a plan for this vast work. Granted, but it would be a small thing in the life of a nation, and already evi- dence has been adduced that the principle could be carried out even by individuals. Another objection is, it would not pay within a reasonable time. This is no doubt true, with regard to a large portion of the fifteen million acres, but the State could afford to wait a much longer time for its profits than individuals. If £20,000,000 sterling was raised and applied for the reclamation of our waste lands—on the same principle that a public company for ,the improvement of workmen's dwellings, for the long term of forty years, prin- cipal and interest being repaid at the rate of £5 is. per cent. per aunum—it would prove the best investment ever made by the State. The taxpayer would be benefited, the poor would find employment, and all industries would be pro- portionately increased. Pauperism—now becoming an in- tolerable burden—would be diminished. Let me hope that the diffusion of wealth will bring with it increased activity in all departments of trade. Commerce will flourish, be- cause all can buy. With greater prosperity in the rural and manufacturing districts will come contentment and happi- ness, the first blessings of a free and industrious people. J. SHUFFLEBOTHAM.

THE READING-ROOM OF THE ST. HELENS LIBRARY. Sir,—lt cannot be said that St. Helens and art are synony- mous terms, though a great deal may be put to the credit of St. Helens in other respects. In the short space at my dis- posal I wish to say something in regard to our library and of art in the furnishing of it; and if these observations meet with the appreciation of the Library Committee I shall feel greatly rewarded for the trouble I have taken. In the first place let it be understood that I have a great reverence for a good library, have spent much of my time in libraries, and am of opinion that free libraries exert great good on the minds of these who are brought directly under their influ- ence. A public library is established for the public; conse- quently the object with which it was started is carried out proportionately to the number of its frequenters, and to the number of those who avail themselves of its privileges. And when I speak of a public library, I, of course, include that important adjunct the reading-room with its valuable books of reference, by means of which the education of the masses is carried on perhaps more effectually than by means of the library proper. The authorities, therefore, should not neg- lect to make • this room as attractive as possible ; and I suggest to the committee of the St. Helens Library, that pictures—no matter whether they are oil paintings, water colours, etchings, Mr. Whistler's nocturnes as severely criticised by Mr. Ruskin, or any other class of pictures, provided they are good—be selected as auxiliaries in the furnishing of the Free Library. The refining influence of pictures is universally acknowledged, and art galleries ' are being established throughout the length and breadth of the land as a means of cultivating the tastes, and developing the finer feelings of the people. The reading room of our St. Helens Library, while not altogether lacking in adorn- ment, presents no great attractions. The maps are useful, but not ornamental, and the only thing placed on the walls te please the eye are the principal engravings from the current numbers of the "Illustrated London News" and "The Graphic," the series hf plates "Types of Beauty," now issued with the latter being placed in a prominent position In the room. No doubt the curator, or librarian, or what- ever his name is, is aware there is something wanting to make the reading room attractive, and hits upon a plan which be thinks will in some degree relieve the monotony of the almost bare walls. But I should not care to see our reading room become famous for its print-belittered walls, or an exhibition of specimens of "Graphic" art, however cleverly theplates may be executed. I see from your report of the committee's proceedings that a gentleman in the town ball kindly promised two oil paintings, if the Council will find a place to hang them in. However well-founded the objection entertained by the Council to the "reservations and conditions" in respect,to the park question might have been, stilll think nothing can be said against this condition unless it be that the pictures are not suitable; but on the authority of Councillor Brook, we are informed that the pictures have considerable merit, and are therefore worthy of a place in the Hall. Good pictures hitherto presented to the Council, have invariably found their .way to some obscure place in the Town Hall, inaccessible to the public, and only seen by our representatives and corporate officials. A very large painting in oils of St. Helens, in the days when nature appeared at her best; when the " chemics" and other disagreeablenesses disturbed but little the buccolic individuals in their "daily walks and conversation," hangs not where the public can see it, and admire it, but in the committee-room, where wrangling town councillors "legis- late for the public," and appropriate all the best things for themselves. Thanks are due to those who kindly offer these gifts, and while eleemosynary contributions are not to be .despised and rejected, but thanlaully received, the Council would do well in giving some little attention to the furnishing of rooms where the people meet; and net rely upon the generosity of townsmen, who, seeing what is ' wanting, meet the requirements from their own accumula- 'n. tion of worldly goods.—l am, yours sc., cree A LIBRARY FREQUENTER. seed

A FIRE ENGINE WANTED FOR FRODSHAM. Sir,—On Saturday last, noticing an unusual commotion in our otherwise quiet town, I, in common with other people, proceeded In the same direction, when we found the cause to be afire in a range of buildings owned by Mrs. Rigson, of Oak- mere, and situated at the extreme end of the town. Hew the fire originated does not appear tube known. It was first seen abqut 11 a.m., and in little over an hour all that re- mained standing of the whole range (which is some 50 or 60 yards in length) was the walls. The damage done is esti- mated at about £6OO. As usual the fire engine was sent for to Runcorn, and arrived in time to find that the fire had completed its work. New had we a fire engine stationed somewhere near the centre of the town, I believe the greater portion of the building and its contents might have been saved, as there is within a very abort distance of the building a, good stream of water. The question now is, cannot we have a fire engine in Frodsham.? It appears to me that if some of the gentlemen who are so energetic about the water question had been half as anxious about a -fire engine we should have had one long ago; or had the money been spent on a pre engine that has been spent in devising plans for supplying the public with water, it would by this time have saved hundreds, if not thousands of pounds worth of property, as there have been several extensive fires of late in the vicinity of Frodsham. I am inclined, however, to think that if there was an office connected with it, from which a salary of £5O or £6O per annum could be drawn from the public, there would soon be a fire engine in the town. Now, Mr. Editor, what I would suggest is, that some of our leading gentle- men would kindly take the matter in hand, form a com- , mates, and open a subscription list, and I have no doubtthat some of the fire offices would give a helping band. Then in a short time we might have an engine static) ,ed in Frod- sham, and not have to gallop off to Runcorn or Preston Brook for one, in case of fire, and find the fire had done its work before the brigade arrived. In conclusion, I may say that were an engine situated about the centre of the town, there could at any time be a sufficient number of re- liable and active young men to form a good brigade—men that would take an interest in the work. Hoping the matter will be taken up in earnest,—l remain, yours, em., Frodshain, April 28th, 1881. A RESIDENT.

- --- - A BATCn OF' GAMBLING CasEs.—James Jackson and I William Henry SaYlge, Liverpool ; Sarah Hillidge, Man- chester; and Mary Nicholson, were brought up in custody charged with having, at Tarbock. on the previous Saturda,:, played at a certain game of chance, called " - play." A fine of 10s. and 64. 6d. costs was.inflicted,or, in default, fourteen days' imprisonment.—Michael Crowley, John Cairns, and John Lewis, Liverpool, were charged for having, at the Tarbock race-course, on Saturday, played at the "three-card-trick." Remanded. Mary Murray, no fixed residence, was charged with playing at " dice," at Tarbock, on the same day. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and said she got her leg hurt while being conveyed in a wag- gonette to the police station. Mr. Evans: How did that happen? Prisoner : The conveyance broke down, and I and the other prisoners were pitched into the road. Fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days.—Thotnas Cunningham, Warrington, was charged with gambling. P.C. Scott said he saw the prisoner playing at "nuts and sticks," at Tarbock, on Satur- day. He saw one man pitch four times and only knock one stick over. Mr. Blackwell (assistant magistrates' clerk): Can both sticks be knocked down? The Constable: Yes; but it is not often they are knocked down. Mr. Evans: It is not a game of chance ; it is more a game of skill. The Prisoner: Or course it is. I knocked them down in the police-office, so did the sergeant. I bad only Is. fiKh when I was taken into custody, and I had already lost three nuts, and I have two now. Mr. Evans (to Superintendent indle): How do you make it into a game of chance? Mr. Brindle It is very seldom that a person wins. The prisoner, himself had to throw several times before he could knock bolh sticks down. Mr. Evans said the offence was a very slight one, mud as the prisoner had been in custody since Saturday, he would dismiss the case.—James Gray, Birmingham, was charged with baying, on the Tarbock race-course, on the pre-

Mr. Evans said that was the worst case he had heard that day. Prisoner was remanded. POCKET PICKING. James Hardman, Manchester, was charged with attempting to steal a watch from the person of Mr. James Welding, on the race-course, at Tarbock. While the prosecutor was watching a race he felt a tug at his watch. chain, and immediately seized hold of the hand and found it belonged to the prisoner, whom he gave into custody. Remanded.—John Gellis, Liverpool, was remanded on a charge of having stolen a silver watch, value £6, from the person of Francis Briggs, of Clive Hall farm, Yorkshire. RonsiNG A GATE COLLECTOR or £2o.—Joseph Carter, Liverpool, was charged on suspicion of being concerned in the theft of the sum of £2O from the person of Thomas Ellsworthy, gardener to Mr. A. R. Gladstone, Doure..h,ay, Roby, at Tarbock.—Prosecutor stated that on Saturday lie was engaged as an assistant collector at the enclosure gate. Owing to a crush the gate gave way, and, leaving it in charge of three officers and another assistant collector,' be went to look for a joiner to repair the gate. He was unsuc- cessful in his search, and on returning was attacked hy a number of men who tried to take the satchel containing the gate money from him. He stuck to the satchel, but several of the men managed to get their hands, in and extract scime of the contents. He could not swear that prisoner was bne of the men who attacked him. About £2O was taken from him.—loseph Plythian, another gardener, said that while he was on the grand-stand at the race-course he witnessed a struggle between some men one of whom he recognised as the prosecutor. He saw the prisoner deliberately put this band into the prosecutor's satchel and take some money but, and then make off with it. Witness got off the stand 'and followed him. After following a short distance prisoner Was met by two men, one of whom said to him "How much, did you get ? " Prisoner made some reply, and then hdrided some of the money to the men. Witness then gave him into the custody of the police.—Remanded. Ttrasney.—Before Messrs. W. D. Holt and W. L. Evans. THE MURDEROUS ASSAULT AT RAINHILL.—Bernard Burns, a young Irishman, was brought up on remand charged with having, at Rainhill, on the night of Saturday, the 6th inst., unlawfully and feloniously wounded Michael Cray- mour, by striking him upon the forehead with a large stone, thereby seriously injuring the skull.—Mr. Superintendent Brindle said the man was so badly wounded that it! was deemed advisable to take his depositions on the nexti day (Sunday). Prosecutor was not yet able to appear, and he asked teat the prisoner might be further remanded for a week.—Prisoner applied for bail, but was refused, the Bench observing that the case was too serious.—The remand was granted. ALLEGED Asseurr AT Curnerox.—William Heap si was charged with assaulting William 11. Almond, at Crontdn, on the 9th April.—Mr. W. Tyrer prosecuted, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. Mt. Tyrif mid that on the sth instant complainant appeared as a witness is a case against the defendant for using a dog for the purpose of taking garbe at Cronton, and defendant was convicted. Before the case was heard at the sessions defendant had used threats of violence against the complainant, and on the 9th inst. the complain- ant was proceeding home from Widnes and called at a public house in Cronton. While he was in the house defendant went up to him, stared him in the face, and then left the house. Immediately afterwards complainant's brother'went telt of the house, and on getting into the road he saw defen- dant standing close by with a large stone in his hand. Suspecting he was about to do some mischief he went !back and warned his brother not to leave the house by the front entrance. In order to avoid meeting defendant, the !com- plainant left by the back door, and while passing a garden belonging to a person named Leather a stone was thrown, which passed over his head and struck the ground close by. Complainant turned round to see who had thrown it, when he was struck on the side of the jaw by another stone, which came from the direction of the garden. He had no witness who actually saw the stone thrown, but the circumstances pointed to the defendant as the real culprit.—Evidence was given in support of Mr. Tyrer's statement, the complainant adding that defendant had, on more than one occasion, threatened to "shorten his days."—Mr. Swift, for the defence, contended that there was no evidence to show that the defendant threw the stone.—The case was dismissed. NEGLECT OF WIFE AND FAMlLY.—Patrick Waldren was brought up under warrant charged with having, on the Ist July, last year, left his wife and family of five children, whereby they had become chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Parkinson, relieving officer for the Prescot district, said the prisoner's family had been re- ceiving relief more or less for the past two years.—Prisoner having been previously convicted for neglect of family, was now committed to gaol for two months with hard labour. GAMBLING AT TARBOCE RACES.—EXEMPLARY PUNlSH- mEtrr.—Michael Crowley and John Lewis, Liverpool, were each sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour for playing at the "three card trick" at Tarbock race ' course, on the previous Saturday.—For a similar offence John Cairns, Liverpool, who had been previously convicted, was committed for three months with hard labour.—Thomas Lea, Widnes, was charged with playing at a game of chance called "prick-the-garter," and the charge being proved he was sent to gaol for a month.—James Gray, Birmingham, was also committed for a month for playing at "red and white horses," at Tarbock, on Saturday. ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH.—John Gellis, Liverpool, was brought up and remanded for eight days, on a charge of having, at Tarbock race-course, stolen a silver watch, value £6, from the person of Francis Briggs, of Clive Hall farm, Yorkshire. KEEPING Docis Wmotrr LICENSES.—For keeping' dogs without previously having taken out licenses, the following were fined ss. and costs, 17s. in all :—James Grace, 'Rain- hill; John Hooton, James Stevenson, and Thomas Speed (three charges), Huyton. BREACHES OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) Acr.—Thomas Hedgcock was charged with causing three cows to be driven on the highway at Roby, on the 15th March, without having a license authorising him so to do ; and Charles W. Swingsley was charged with driving the said cows. P.C. Barnes proved the charges, and the first -- mentioned defendant was fined ss. and costs, and the charge' against the latter was Withdrawn.—Job Hayley and Edward Green were charged with having committed similar offences on the Liverpool-road. Huyton, on the 12th March.— Haylsy was fined ss. and costs, and the charge against Green was withdrawn. , HIGHWAY OFFENCES.—WiIIiam Hollandwas fined 7s. 6d. and costs for being drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Knowsley, on Saturday, the 2nd inst.—William Massey was charged with being asleep in his cart, at Prescot, on the sth inst., and fined ss. and costs.—Thomas Ashton Was fined 2s 6d. and costs for riding on the shaft of his cart without reins to his horse, at Huyton, on the 26th ult. PITCH AND Toss.—Richard Melia, Michael. Melia, and Joseph Woodward, were each charged with playing at pitch and toss on the Prescot fair ground, in the 11th inst.—P.C. Thompson gave evidence in support of the charge, and Richard Melia was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, and Michael Melia and Woodward 10s. and costs each. DAMAGING FENCES AT WHISTON.—HEAPY FINE.—Wm. Welsby, of Dragon-row, was charged witleunlawfully and wilfully damaging a certain fence on the farm of Mr. Henry Fogg, Middleton House, Whiston, on the 20th inst.—P.C. Bell deposed that the defendant resided in the vicinity of the fields which were occupied by Mr. Fogg, at Whiston. Com- plaints had been made to him at various times of consider- able damage haying been done to the fencing on Mr. Fogg's land. About three o'clock on Wednesday aftercoon, the 20th met., he saw a man in one of the fields, and suspecting be was bent on mischief, witness concealed himself behind a hedge, and in a short time after- wards he saw the man, whom he recognised as the defen- dant, take a piece of wood railing from a fence. He moved further down the road, and directly after he saw the defen- dant making towards his home with five pieces of wood railing in his possession. When he saw witness he three/ the wood behind a wall and ran away, but witness caught him and said he should report him to Mr. Fogg.—Mr. Fogg said he had laid the damage at 6d., but there was no doubt the defendant had done damage to the extent of 2s. ed. Such serious damage had been done to the fences in his fi Ads, that he felt bound to prosecute, or all the fences would be carried away. He might engage a person to repair the fences one day, and the next day they would be pulled down again.—Mr. Evans: Yes; I know Mr. Fogg has suffered an immense amount of damage. Is the defeadant a young rnan?—Mr. Fogg: No he is an elderly man, and respectable. I was surprised when the officer told me he had caught him.—The Bench characterised the offence as a very serious one, and fined the defendant 40s. and costs, and ordered him to pay the damage, or go to gaol for one month with hard labour. RATE DEFAULTERS.—James Mercer, Thomas Houghton, and Charles Robinson, were summoned at the instance of the Prescot Local Board for hot having paid their rates, and the defendants not being able to give satisfactory excuses, ai oriler for payment was made in each case.

t 30 E3l --THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 18 a I RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT WHIS. PROTEST AGAINST THE ANNEXATION OF THE TOWNSHIP. It having been decided by the Prescot Board of Guar- dians to apply to the Local Government Board for permis- sion to annex the township of Whiston to those of Huyton and Prescot, so as to form one collecting district, a meeting of the ratepayers of Whiston was held in the National School-room,on Friday, for the purpose of protesting against such annexation. Mr. Ottiwell Ward presided, and there was a large attendance of ratepayers.—The chairman said he did not think there was one present in favour of the township being joined to Prescot and Huyton. Ile called upon Mr. John Leatherbarrow (guardian for the township) to give the meeting an explanation of the intentions of the Guardians. —Mr. Leatherbarrow said that some little time ago there was a bit of unpleasantness with regard to the collection of the poor rates at Widnes, and since that time it had been decided by the ratepayers of that township to ask the Guar- dians to sever Bold, Cronton, and Ditton from the Widnes I collection district, and allow the collector to devote the whole of his time to Widnes alone. Of course, that meant the appointment of a new collector for Bold, Crouton, and Ditton. On going to the Board meeting a fortnight previous he heard that the Finance Committee had recommended the Board that when a new collector was appointed for Bold, Crouton, and Ditton, they should amalgamate Whiston with those townshigs. Mr. Tvrer (guardian for Prescet) said it was far more desirable that Whiston should be joined toi Huyton and Prescot, and that Rainhill should be taken from the Prescot collection district and joined to Bold, Crouton, and Ditton. Mr. Tyrer's suggestion was agreed upon, the recommendation was altered to that effect, and it was decided to apply to the Local Government Board asking for a re-division of the townships accordingly. He (Mr. Leatherbarrow), on behalf of the ratepayers of Whiston, protested against any attempt to join Whiston to other townships, but afterwards he thought he would correct him- self, and ascertain if the ratepayers would rather conduct their own affairs, as they had done for the last thirty-five years, or not. e thought it was not fair or reasonable for the Guardians to make a kind of "bat and ball work" of them, and not allow them to have a voice in their own affairs. (Hear, bear.) The reason he got the overseers to call that meeting was to see whether the ratepayers were in favour of remaining as at present, or of being annexed to the Prescot collection district. Formerly the township was part and parcel of this district, but about 35 years ago, at the earnest request of the ratepayers, it was severed, and it had remained severed ever since. It was for the ratepayers to decide whether they would have their own man to collect the whole of the rates,&c., or be joined to Prescot and Huy- ton, and have the work done by the collector of these town- ships.—Mr. D. Seddon: Perhaps Mr. Leatherbarrow will be I able to tell us whether or not we have the power to protest against the annexation.—The Chairman: We must have.— Mr. Seddon: It's no use saying we must have. The ques- tion is—Have we the power ?—Mr. Leatherbarrow: Most certainly you have. It is entirely in our own hands to do as we wish.—Mr. Seddon: Then it is certainly necessary that every ratepayer should strongly protest against the township being joined to Prescot and Huyton.—Mr. Hewitt (one of the overseers): There is no definite resolution be- fore the meeting at present, I believe. I did not bear Mr. Leatherbarrow propose anything.—Mr. Leatherbarrow: It is not for me to propose any resolution. Mr. Hewitt: Oh, no; it occurs to me now. Well, I beg to propose "That this meeting of ratepayers of the township of Whiston object entirely to the course proposed to be taken by the Guardians of the Prescot Union, to join the township to Prescot and Huyton districts."—Mr. Storey seconded Mr. James Blundell, in supporting the proposition said, if the suggestion of Mr. Tyrer at the Guardians' meeting was carried into effect, it would cause great inconvenience to the people of Whiston generally. He pointed out that Whiston was not in the same position as Prescot. In the latter township the small Tenements Act was in force, but it was not so in Whiston; each householder bad to pay his own rates and taxes. Besides this, the population of Whiston was a moving population, consequently it was highly necessary that a collector should be on the spot to look after the rates. He was of opinion that the appointment of one collector for several townships was altogether wrong; it was a great evil, and such collectors had great tempta- tions thrown in their way.—The Chairman observed that the Guardians had previously tried to get in the thin end of the wedge and they were now trying again, and there was no doubt, they had some object in view. He trusted every- one present would vote "dead against" the proposed annexa- tion.—Mr. W. Travis: Let every township fight and pay for itself.—Mr. Gerrard: If we unanimously protest against the annexation, can Mr. Leatherbartow assure us that it will have its effect P—Mr. Leatherharrow : I am only one of 33.1 It would be very much out of place if I said I could I guarantee for the other 32. I will say this—l will do the I best I can. (Hear, hear.)—The proposition was then put and unanimously carried.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said that in case they were against the proposed annexation, he had pre- pared and brought with him a petition to be signed by the ratepayers.—Mr. Hewitt thought a deputation should be ap- pointed to wait upon and present the petition to the Guardians. Mr. Seddon: Would the Guardians receive a deputation ? Mr. Leatherbarrow: They could not object. If they did I I should leave my seat.—Mr. Rimmer : Then would it not be as well to send the petition to the Local Government Board ' instead of to the Guardians 7—Mr. Leatherbarrow: We all know the recess is on at the present time, and consequently the letter has not yet been sent to the Local Government Board, asking their rermission to the annexation being made, and I thought it more advisable to take steps to stop it's being sent if possible. It is far better, you know to treat " matters "at home than send them up there.—A deputation consisting of Messrs. T. P. Hewitt, H. Smith (overseers), H. R.l,d'A Wills, J.P., E. Fidler Ottiwell Ward, and T.Lea, was appointed to present the following petition :—" That your petitioners herewith regret that it is the intention of your board to annex the township of Whiston to other townships for purposes of poor rate collection. That the proposed an- nexation will not in any way benefit the ratepayers of Whiston. That the township for a number of years has formed a separate poor-rata collection district. That no disadvantages have been experienced. That with the col- lection of a separate sanitary rate and of water rents, almost the whole of the collector's time will be occupied. That the proposed annexation is not favourably received by the other townships concerned. That your petitioners believe that if the township is joined to others the expenses of collection to Whiston will be considerably inVeased ; and your peti- tioners respectfully request you to permit the township of Walston to continue to form a sep irate poor rate collection district."—A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting.—The petition was then signed by about one hun- dred ratepayers.

They were a regular nuisance, and were stopping pie-nice from coming to Frodsham—Defen- dents in chorus: It's a lie.—Sergeant Johnson, on being applied to by the Bench, said it was quite true that the defen dants and others were frequently troublesome, and their practices wanted stopping. Strangers, respectable people, could seldom go to Frodsham witheut being interfered with by these men. They were Five Cross-men. Some of the excursionists came to the police station bleeding. These meq„ followed down from Overton to the Bear's Paw, and actually went after them into the hotel. He (the Sergeant) saw them rushing after the wagonette in which the pic-nic party were going away. They were actually chasing the people out of the town.—Mr. Youd said this pic-nic party had ordered tea at his house, and the defendants actually ordered them out: and they were really so frightened that they went —Beyond a general denial of the allegations in the complainant's case, the only plea set up by any of the defendants was that two men and two women of the pic-nic party challenged them to fight, and so commenced the row. 'the defendants conducted themselves throughout the case with the utmost indifference and levity.—The Bench fined Hillidge, the Astons. and Dids- bury, 10s. and the costs each; Garner in consideration of his having been fined already on a charge of being drunk, aris- ing out of the same affair, would only have to pay the coste, 4s. 6d., and John Mullineux would also have to pay the costs, 45. 6d.

ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. W. Pilkington. A BOY CHARGED WITH A GRAVE ASSAULT ON TRH POLICE. —Lewis Davis (16) was charged with assaulting P.C. Fielding whilst in the execution of his duty.—The officer stated that he was conducting a prisoner to the police office, when the defendant threw a brick (weighing about a pound) at him. The missile caught him on the cheek, eausing a disagreeable cut on the side of the face, and severing the chin strap. He knew the boy by sight, so he did not trouble to run after him—Defendant denied the charge in toto, and said he was not there, but was in bed at half-past nine—the time of the alleged assault. His landlady, with whom he lodged, having recently been confined, could not appear as a witness at present, but would have come forward had she been able.—The Bench said this was a serious case, but they would adjourn it for a month to enable defendant's landlady to appear. THE PITCH AND Toss NUISANCE.—JOhII Brennan Henry Ijrch, and Thomas Clitheroe, residing on Greetffiank, were charged with playing at pitch and toss, on Sunday, in High- street.—P.C. Sheriff proved the case, and added that tossing I was a great nuisance in that locality. He never passed there on a Sunday or on a holiday without seeing 12 or 15 men and boys playing at the game. The yards attached to the houses could be entered from each other by means of gaps in the walls, and it was a very difficult matter to capture the offenders.—Each defendant was fined la. and costs. HER 35TH APPEARANCE.—Bridget Garrity made her 35th appearance, and was fined lOs and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the 13th inst. DARING ROBBERY BY A GlRL.—Mary Ann Lynch (17), of Oxfard-street, was charged with stealing.—Francie Morley, baker, of 63, Cooper-street, said he had a bakehouse in Ox- ford-street. About eight o'clock on Saturday evening, the 26th March, he left his dwelling-house locked up securely, and about eleven o'clock he returned and entered the house by the front door. He found the middle door leading to the back part of the house closed. That was not so when he left. He found the kitchen all upset, the drawers being pulled open. He gave information to the police, and after- wards examined the place more minutely with Inspector Wood. He waissed a small shawl, brush, a scent bottle with filter top, two loaves of bread, some butter, tea, and sugar, a towel, a breast pin, a jar of jam, and a towel. The value of the property taken amounted to about LL—Sarah Lives- ley, 17 years of age, servant for Mr. John Sirncock, Barton- street, said she knew the prisoner. On the 26th March, prisoner came to see her in the morning and remained until seven o'clock at night, when she said she would have to go to the shop for her mother's groceries. In about an hour she came back and witness asked her if those things she had under her apron belonged to her mother. Prisoner said her mother had given them to her for a tea party. The articles were those mentioned above. She left the towel and breast pin with witness.—P.C. Thomas Peebles said he searched the house of John Simcock, 25, Barton-street, and found the towel and breast pin produced in the house. He charged the prisoner with stealing the articles mentioned in the charge, and she replied "I only took one jar of preserves. I took all the other things but no clothes brush."—She was sent to prison for three months.—There was another charge against the prisoner of stealing Is. Wid. and some sweets from a shop at Moss Bank. two small children were alone in the shop the prisoner entered and took the money out of the drawer.—The case was not gone into. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Pilkington and W. L. Evans. ASSAULTING THE POLICE WITH A SHOE.—Elizabeth Lawrenson, a young woman, made her 31st appearance charged with being a common prostitute, and behaving in a riotous manner in the streets. She was further charged with assaulting P.C. Mather whilst in the execution of his duty.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Mather stated that at a quarter-past eleven on Friday night prisoner was creating a disturbance and making use of bad language in the street. He went to her, when she struck him in the face ' with her fist, and, whilst taking her into custody, she pulled off her shoe, and struck him on the head with it. At the police office she again assaulted him with her shoe.— Prisoner: It didn't hurt you; you ought to be ashamed of yourself.—P.C. Addison deposed to seeing the assault at the office.—Mr. Pilkington : Was it a violent blow? Witness: Yes, with the heel of her shoe.—P.S. Jackson corroborated the statement.—Superintendent Johnston said prisoner had been 30 times before the magistrates previously, and had been committed to gaol frequently for periods up to three months. She was one of the worst characters he ever saw. —Mr. Pilkington : You will have to go for two months in each case—one to take effect after the other—Prisoner: Thank you, you couldn't have given me much more. • A GREENBANIC INCIDENT.—Ann Henry, a young woman residing on Greenhank, summoned Margaret Brady, an elderly woman, John Brady and Margaret Gorman, her children, and Luke Gorman, husband of Margaret Gorman, for assaulting her on the 12th April.—Prosecutrix said that Margaret Gorinan threatened her because she had been the means of giving her brother fourteen days' imprisonment. She also pulled her hair in a shameful manner, and while she was doing this the two men came up and kicked her.—Mr. Swift, who appeared for defendants, said the prosecutrix had told falsehoods; and he called wit- nesses to prove that in theffit st instance she spat in Mar- garet Gorman's face, which resulted in a fight of 20 minutes' duration, during which time the women were engaged chiefly in pulling one another's hair, with an occasional variation in the shape of fisticuffing., It was stated that prosecutrix . .

ILLuarnaxan HOUSEHOLD JOURNAL (London: Ward, Lock and Co).—This excellent magazine for April is profusely illustrated with all the newest fashions and costumes, needlework, etc., and contains well written tales, essays, and articles on etiquette; a large coloured plate of fashions also accompanies this number. MYRA'S MID-MONTHLY JOURNAL contains coloured fashion plate, diagram sheet of fashions, cut out paper pat- tern of dress for young children, notes on novelties, latest news from Paris, designs for embroidery, Jrc., and is evi- dently much appreciated by young ladies, whose wants are well catered for.

CAMDEN VICTORIA (RUNCORN) V. PENAP.TII JUNIORS (PEN- KETII).—A. match was played between these two clubs on Saturday last. on the ground of the former, and resulted in an easy victory for the home team by 51 runs. Appended are the scores: Camden Victoria, 62 ; Peniceth Juniors. 11. J. Gatiey played a very good innings of 33 for the home team, and J. Woods deserves a word of praise for his excellent bowling and falling five wickets for the home team.

Sr. HELENS CONDERVA.TIVES AND. LORD BBA.CONSFIELD. _ —During the past week an announcement was posted in the Conservative Club to the effect that a meeting of the -mein- hers would be held on Thursday evening to pass a vote of condolence respecting the death of Lord Beaconsfield, to be forwarded to the private secretary to the deceased statesman. Reporters were not admitted.

div.p: St. Helens about five years. Barker was a widower with two children. Ryan had never been charged with any offence before, and was a married man. They had been en- gaged at Peasley Cross, and while passing through the fair ground on their way home they found, as he had been in- structed, a quantity of toffee scattered about on the ground. —They were remanded until Friday, bail being accepted. A SUSPICIOUS CASE.—Elizabeth Yorke, about 14 years of age, was charged with wilfully and maliciously damag- ing a door, the property of Catherine Mulvaney, doing damage to the amount of 59.—1 t appeared that the occupier of the house Ann Hurst, on Monday went to Liverpool, and arranged with a neighbour to keep the fire in. Whilst the neighbour, Mary Ann Wilson, was engaged in the house during the afternoon she heard a noise at the door, and to her surprise found that a hole had already been cut in the door close to the bolt, and another one under the latch. She looked through the holes and saw the defendant on the other side. She asked her what she wanted, and the defen- dant replied that she wanted to get in as she had lost some- thing. Subsequently she said that she thought the house was empty. She had then in 11.3 r hand the sharp instrument with which she had made the holes in the door.—Mr. Pil- kington said this was a very extraordinary proceeding, and the girl must either be very naughty or short of serse. She would be fined ss. and costs, and would have to pay damages, altogether 16s. 6d., which was paid by the father of the girl.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.

MONDAY.—Pefore His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pick- mere), Coancillors Crosfield and Ziba Armitage. Va.:maxim—Robert Best was charged with being a vagrant. He was found asleep on the premises of Mr. Ash- ton the Bridge Inn, Wilderspool Causeway, about three o'clock that morning.—In reply to the Mayor, prisoner said he had lately come from Massachussetts, and:was searching for work at Warrington as a labourer.—He was committed for seven days with hard labour. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Wm. Moran was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Bridge- street on thel 16th inst.—The officer said the defendant's head and breast were covered withlbloo d.—He was bound over to keep the peace for six months. DEFRAUDING THE CHESHIRE LINES RAILWAY COMPANY.

—Wm. Bradbury was charged with riding from Manchester to Warrington on the Cheshire Lines Railway, on Saturday night, without a ticket, and with intent to defraud the Corn- pany.—Prisoner was seen to alight from the S-15 train whilst in motion, and endeavour to evade the collectors. When asked for his ticket he was very insolent, and stated that a friend in the train had his ticket. He was taken to the inspector and asked to point the man out, but the one he pointed out denied all knowledge of him. Prisoner was then given into custody.—He was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. USING THE COVET TO EXTORT MONEL—James Wilkin- son an old man, was charged with unlawfully assaulting and beating Margaret Clare on the 16th inst.—Complainant said defendant had paid all the costs, and as he was a rela- tion she did not want to give evidence.—Mr. White: You
must not make the court" a means of extorting money for this sort of thing.—Defendant was bound over to keep the

peace for six mo-nths. TUESDAY.—Before Council lor Broadbent (in the chair) and Alderman Webster. A SPORTING FORGEMAN cx TROTJELE.—John Bennett, a forgeman employed at Bevisey ironworks, was charged with having assaulted John Daley, the landlord of the Vulcan beerhouse, Dallam-lane. on Saturday.—lt appeared that the prisoner, who was of a sporting turn of mind, went into the beerhouse, and the landlord, knowing he had a tendency to gamble, watched him. Prisoner offered to bet with another man, and Mrs. Daley endeavoured to prevent him gambling by trying to separate the men. Bennett then struck the landlady, and on Mr. Daley coming to her aid prisoner "struck him twice and afterwards tore his jacket off his back." Although the landlord had had trouble with him twice before, Mrs. Daley said she was disposed to forgive the prisoner, as she had had " his wife, father, and nearly all the men out of the works " pleading on his behalf.—The Bench said they were glad Mr. Daley had endeavoured to maintain the good character of his house, and as he did not wish to press the case, fined the prisoner 205, including costs. A PROSECUTOR FAILS TO APPEAR.—John Corcoran, also a forgeman, was charged with stealing from the person of William Morgan, whilst at the Royal Arms public-house, Bank-street, on Monday, the stun of 3s. 6d. As, however, the prosecutor failed to put in an appearance, the prisoner was discharged. WEDNESDAT.—Before Alderman Chandley and Co uncillor Pairclough. A TATOOED MILITIAMAN.—George Cahill, a tall, well- made young man, was charged with fraudulently enlisting into the 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia, at the Brigade Depot, Warrington, on the 22nd inst.—Prisoner pleaded not gull ty.—Sergeant-Major B ryne said he remembered the prisoner offering himself for enlistment in 1877 or 1878, when the regiment was stationed at Liverpool. He was taken before the doctor, who, on making an examination, discovered that prisoner was marked with a military D on the left breast, and he was at once ordered out of the bar- racks. Witness did not again see prisoner until Monday, he having in the meantime enlisted in the Wexford Militia, and from which he wished to be transferred. Witness imme- diately recognised the man, and told the doctor that he would find a military D stamped on the left breast. The doctcr made an examination, but it was with great difficulty that he discovered the mark, as a basket of flowers had been beautifully tatooed over R.—Mr. White said the Behch bad no jurisdiction in the matter, as the fraudulent enlistment had occurred at Wexford.—Sergeant-Major Bryne therefore asked that prisoner be remanded until he had communicated with the Wexford authorities, and this was done. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and John White, Esq. CLAIM AGAINST A VOLUNTEER.—Arthur Burgess was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to pay £1 10s., undertaken to be paid by him to the funds 6f the United Lancashire Rifle Corps.—Defend int admitted his liability, and promised to pay ss. per week.— The Bench made an order accordingly. A SCENB IN COURT.— Nancy Lee, a married woman, was summoned for stealing a cart, value £7, on the 26th inst., the property of George Kirkham. She was also charged with doing damage to a lock, by forcing and breaking the same.—Complainant applied for the case to be adjourned, but defendant would not agree to this, and as complainant was not ready to go on with the case, it was dismissed —A woman then came into court, and advancing excitedly up to Mr. Hunt, handed him what appeared to be a "badge" book, and charged complainant with defrauding her of £4 10s., by selling her cart and never giving her the money.—Mr. White with some difficulty succeeded in convincing the woman that the Bench could do nothing for her, and that she must sue the man in the County Court—She thanked the Bench, and, glancing " daggers " at Kirkham, left the court. THE MARKETS COMMIT-TOE AND THE STALLHOLDERS.— David Plinston was charged with having on the 6th April, unlawfully obstructed a certain passage in the Market Shed, by alto wing a crate of fowls to stand there contrary to the bye-laws of the borough. Mr. Whittle, deputy town clerk, said the defendant would not have been summoned had he not previously offended. The stallkeepers were gettieg in the habit of encroaching on the passages by placing their crates beyond the land allowed to them. Defendant said there were three stalls which encroached on the passage.,to the same extent as his, but they were not summoned. He had been too long in the market to be disgraced in this kind of a manner. Mr. Whittle: You have brought it upon your- self. Captain Reynolds: Yes, Mr. Whittle, but there should be the same law for each, and no man should be allowed to do that which is not allowed to another. Mr. Whittle said such was the case. As Mr. Whittle did not press the casetit was dismissed with costs, on defendant promising it should not occur again.—Rebecca Locker was charged with a similar offence, having obstructed the footpath with four barrels of apples. Defendant complained that there was not sufficient accommodation allowed for the unloading of lurries, but Mr. Place, the market inspector, said she received too many goods for the space she occupied. In answer to defen- dant, Mr. Place said he simply carried out the orders of the Markets Committee. Defendant : You have too many masters. I wouldn't have your place for a thousand pounds a year. (Laughter.) I have been working for the Markets Committee forty years and I want pensioning off. (Laughter.) Captain Reynolds: Then you say the Markets Com- mittee make more by you than you by them? Defendant: Yes, 1 should think so. (Laughter.) She was ordered to pay costs, ss. 6d.—Thomas Holland was charged with obstructing the footpath in Market-street with two boxes of oranges. Defendant said he did not know anything about it as his wife was at the stall. Mr. Place said that was so. He ha el ten times more treuble with the women than the men. (Laughter.) Captain Reynolds: It won't mend matters if you say that. Defendant remarked that they ought to have been summoned before the Markets Committee instead of at the Police Court. He went on to say that members of the Markets Committee went to stalls and ordered them to remove things, and lie thought, they ought to put the matter into the hands of Mr. Place. It was not very nice. They did not in many cases know the par- ties, and he had come out with language that was not VCI pleasant to them.—Defendant was ordered to pay costs. THEFT OF.
