div.head: RUNCORN MADRIGAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MADRIGAL SOCIETY.

The third concert of the season was given on Monday evening, in the National school-room, Runcorn, but the I attendance was not se large as on previous occasions when the members of this society hare appeared before the public. Mr. W. I. Argent acted as conductor, and Miss Fisher presided at the pianoforte. The programme was as follows :

PART I. Overture ........................ .' Talleredi " Rossini Chorus •. " Oh, the flowery month of June," Jackson Song '• II Bacio," Arditi Miss L Haworth. Duett 'Onto the field of glory," Messrs. Morrison and Batty. c Gavotte " Mignon." Thomas 1 Serenade " Liebesliedchen," Taubert Part Song "Come Dorothy," Swabian Bong "Mignonette." Champion Mr. Morrison. Cantata "Fair Ellen," Max Broth Fair Ellen Miss L. Haworth Lord Edward Mr. Batty. Part 11.
Bonita
Toy Symphony Romberg Toy Orchestra by Ladies of the R.M.O. ttoo Serenade "When lovers say good night," ...... Mr. Morrison.

Violin Obligato .Mr. Thorpe. Bong "Bid me discourse," . Miss L 'Haworth. Chorus Bong '' The Vikings," ... . ................... leaning "Let me love thee," ..................... Arditi Mr. Batty. Trio " Zitti, Zitti. Rossini Miss Haworth. Mr. MorriwT, and Mr. Batty, Chorus ............................ Tramp. . Bishop March ........................... " Cornelius,' Mendelssonn The cantata by Max Bruch, the able conductor of the Liverpool Philharmonic Society, proved a capital selection. Miss Haworth took the part of the " Fair Ellen," admirably, being quite equal to what was required of her in point of naturalness. Mr. Batty proved a very good "Lord Edward," and his fine baritone voice told to advantage. We regret to have to state that during the proceedings the conductor bad to apologize to the audience for the fact that the piano was out of tune. Romberg's "Toy symphony," which was so well received at the last performance of the members of the society, was well given, though if we desired to be at all hypercritical, we might say that there was a slight unsteadiness manifest in the rendering. The singing of the choruses was remarkably good. Miss Haworth was encored in "Ii Bacio," and Bishop's well-known "Bid me discourse," but in the trio " Zitti, Zitti," in which the same lady took part with Mr. Morrison and Mr. Batty, there was a complete break down, owing to the ludicrousness of one of the passages proving too much for the singers, who had to leave the platform, which, we may say, in passing, is not very well suited for the presence of such a large number of people. Mr. Morrison, of Widnes, sang in a delightful style Champion's " Mignonette " and "When lovers say good night." This gentleman displays great taste in the rendering of his songs, and he was deservedly en- cored. It is scarcely necessary for us to say that Mr. Argent was all that could he desired as a conductor. We will con- clude our notice by expressing a hope that the next concert given by the members may prove a somewhat better pecu- niary success. -oso

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TuESDAV.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Judge. ACTION AGAINST A. RUNCORN WIDOW LADY.—Mons. B. Meunier French Master at the Runcorn Collegiate School, applied 'for, a commitment, under a judgment summons, against Mm. Annie M. Labone, residing at what is known as Runcorn High School, for non-payment of £.3 Bs., the cost of tuition given at Rock Ferry.—An order was issued for the defendant to pay tbe amount within four months, or be committed for 40 days. MARRYING WlTilonT COIRITING Tits COST. Williai Telford, Scotch draper, Manchester, sued William Johnson, labourer, of Spring Gardens, for £1 7s. 11d., being the price Of a suit of clothes supplied to him, and £2 16s. for a pair Of blankets, pair of sheets, counterpane, and table cover.— Mr. Beasley appeared for the plaintiff, awl called the plain- tiff's agent, Adam Thompson. He stated that the order for the snit was given by the defendant and his mother; and he supplied the goods to defendant on the 27th September, 1879. Sometimes the money was left with the mother, and at others sent up to Mr. Lee's Temperance Hotel.—De- fendant said he never ordered the things from the agent, and never paid him one halfpenny upon them. His mother gave the order, and agreed to pay is. 111. per week.—Mrs. Lawton, defendant's mother-in-law, was called in support of the case, and said that when defendant was about to get married, she asked him what he was going to do about fur- nishing the bedroom in his 'lapse; and he told her to get the necessary things from the plaintiff. She, defendant, and his intended wife, went for them. Defendant, upon seeing the goods on the sofa, said they would do very well and he would see they were paid for. *Johnson left his wife on last Christmas Day, and she was now living as a set- Taut, at the house of Mr. Molyneux, the Wesleyan Metho- dist chapel-keeper. Witness bad made payments on account of the articles for the house, with money given to her by defendant. She could say nothing about the suit.—His Honour said he had no douit, eve e from defendant's own statement, that he had had the goods; and there would be judgment against him for the full amount claimed, at the rate of Sc. per month. Before Mr. H. B. White, (acting as registrar). THE CASE OF TUE WESTON EMIGRANT AND His WILL. —This case, in which Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, sued the executrix of Mr. William Hibbert, (who some time ago went to the United States, where he died,) for the sum of .£6 7s. Pd. being the cost of maintaining the deceased's wife and Child, again came on for hearing. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the plaintiff, and defendant was represented by Mr. Husband, of Widnes. The facts have already been fully reported in The Examiner. The hearing had been adjourned, in order that Mrs. Hannah Hibbert, the executrix, and defendant in the case, might be examined. She stated that deceased lived with her previous to leaving for America. She was accustomed to work in the fields, and take in washing. In the previous April deceased and his wife began to have dif- ferences. She spoke to her son about it, and he referred to the £BO in the Lands of the Building Society, saying " never mind, mother. When the club is broken up, I will put the money in your name." Witness had worked for part of the £BO. When he transferred the money, be gave her the scrip, and told her it was hers. Deceased drew £2O out of the Building Society when be was married, and another £2O when he went away. The wife paid nothing towards the £3O. She could not say how much of the sum named was her son's solely; but the money was put away for witnese, so that she might have something to rely upon when she was old. A verdict was given for the executrix.—Mr. Charles Houghton, shoe- maker, of Churel-street, also sued Mrs. Hibbert, the execu- trix, for 58 11d, being the value of goods supplied to I her. Plaintiff conducted his own case, and, by consent of Mr. Husband, cal'ed the deceased's wife, and Mr. Joseph Griffiths, of Manchester, son-in-law of defendant, who ap- pears,to have had the management of the estate. Mr. Houghton caused some amusement at the commencement of the proceedings by his orieinal remarks, and it appeared to the general public as if he was going to utterly fail in estab- lishing his claim. However, after insisting on several ques- tions being answered by Mr. Griffiths as to how the money bad been expended by Shim, he obtained the acknowledg- ment that the expenses incident to bringing the case of assault against the plaintiff before the magistrates had been put down amongst the sums spent, in addition to one or two other matters, amounting to about £2 133., which the Registrar ruled could not properly be charged. During the course of the cross-examination, Mr. Griffiths was asked by plaintiff what he had done with the money placed in his I hands, on which witness became a little irritated, and re- plied, amidst some laughter, " I wasted a lot of it in law expenses over the likes of you." The Registrar gave a verdict for the full amount claimed in this case, and allowed Me. Houghton the coets of two days' attendance at court.

THE SUSPENSION OF THE SOUTHPORT - AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANK. THE PROPOSED RECONSTRUCTION. Another circular was issued on Thursday to the share- holders of the suspended Southport and West Lancashire Bank. It says" The following scheme for the reconstruction of the Southport and West Lancashire Banking Company, limited (incorporated on the 21st day ef May, 1875), has been decided upon, viz :—A new company to be incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862 to 1880, in the same name as the old company. The new company to take over the business, goodwill, dm., and the spacious and convenient premises of the old company, with its assets and liabilities, including the costs of winding.up. Out of the capita of the company it is proposed to allot as nearly as may be 38,000 ordinary shares of £5 each to the shareholders in the present bank, according to their respective holdings, and to make a call of £1 per share thereon, payable in instalments at a short notice; and that the remaining £4 per share shall be called up before any further calls are made on the pre- erence shares—a contingency which is not expected to arise. Twenty-five thousand out of the 50,000 preference shares to be subscribed for are to be entitled to a cumulative dividend at the rate of £5 per cent per annum on the amount paid up. After payment of such dividend, any surplus profits to be equallg divided between the ordinary and preference shareholders, according to the , amount paid up on their respective shares. To provide for the estimated losses of the shareholders in the old company the £5 per share paid on the old shares will be written off, but:anythim, realised of the amount se written off shall be ratably divided among the holders of ordinary shares for thd - than being, in accordance with the provisions contained in clause 9 in the agreement. . About 30,000 ordinary shares have up to the present time been applied for, and it is re- quested that applications for the preference shares be made on or before Wednesday, the 4th day of May next, after which slay it is proposed to register the company and to allot the shares. Before the opening of the bank it will be neces- sary that en arrangemebt be made with the creditors of till old bank for the payment of their flebts, and there is little doubt an arrangement can be made by which the creditors will be paid by instalments at three, six twelve, and eighteen months, boring interest at the rate of sit per cent. per annum."

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst. WIFE ASSAM.T.—John Bailey, a boatman, was charged with assaulting his wife Mary, on the 22nd inst.—The com- plainant was passing up Bridge-street when he was seen, by Inspector Hollingworth, to strike his wife several times. The officer took him into custody and lodged him in the lockups.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs, Bs. Mom:wt.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and Mr. Wm. Reynolds. CLAIM AGAINST THE OWNERS OF A VESSEL.—Mr. Robinson Smith and Mr. Samuel James Goldsworthy, owners of the Brigantine Topaz," were charged with neglecting and refusing to pay certain seamen's wages, amounting to £23 3s. 4d.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, appeared for the men, and Mr. Lake for the defence.—Mr. Burton said the defen- dants were two of the five owners of the vessel, and they ' lived in Swansea. The brigantine arrived at the port of Runcorn at the commencement of March, and unloaded her cargo. On the 16th of the same month the mate was dis- charged from the vessel, and received his account of wages, showing that £l2 is. sd. was due to him. From that day to this the man had not been able to obtain payment either from the masters or the owners, and the vessel had been seized under an order from the Court of Admiralty. Com- plainant was quite friendless, and was placed in a very un- fortunate predicament. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1880, said that seamen's wages were to be paid within two clear days, and unless the delay was caused by the act of seamen, the wages were to continue to run and be payable until the time of the final settlement.—Thomas Griffiths, the mate, and who made the claim, was called to prove that the original amount of the wages was £l2 is. Bd., and £ll Is. Bd. had accumulated since, according to the allowance provided by the Act, since kis discharge.—Mr. Lake raised several legal objections, but they were over-ruled by the magistrates, who made an order for the immediate payment of the amount claimed, and £2 costs, which included 10s. towards the advocate's fee.—Mr. Burton said he wished to take out five other summonses against the same owners.--The magistrates said that they would be issued, as the position in which the seamen were placed by the conduct of the owners was a very bard one. NON-PAYMENT OF WATER RATES.—Mr. William Wright, collector to the Ytuncorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Co ,summoned 32 people for not paying their water rates.— Orders were made for payment in each case. Smoot. Beam) CASES.—The following people were summoned by the Runcorn School Board, for not sending their children to school : John Sutton, Nelson-street ; John Molyneux, Ross-street; James Marshall, Gilbert-street ; Edwin Lewis, Spring- gardens; Joseph Mannering, Rutland-street ; Ann Row- bottom, Porter-street; Joseph Nelson, Mill-brow; John Edward Leberett, Nelson-street ; James Riley, Cooper-street; O'Neil, Mersey-street ;Felix McConn, Nelson-street; Patrick Doud, Loch-street ;Patrick Baxter, Cooper-street; Charlottte Done, Mill-brow. The cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, and an order made for payment of 6d. fine and 4s. 6d. costs in each case. PROSECUTIONS BY THE RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. —Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, summoned James Percival for leaving his mother, Esther Percival, chargeable to the common fund of the union. Defendant did not appear.—Mr. Houghton said the man's mother had been chargeable to the union for some years, at the rate of 3s. 6d. per week. She lived in a cottage in Halton-lane, and defendant, who was a labouring man, seldom came home except at night time. The Bench made an order upon the defendant to pay 3s. 6d. weekly towards I the support of his mother, and lls. 6d. costs.—John Spencer a labourer, was similiarly charged in the case of his father, Wm. Spencer. Mr. Houghton said that the. weekly was paid to the old man and his wife. Defendant lived with the couple in a cottage at Acton Grange; and application had been made to him to contribute 25. 6d. per -seek towards the 55.,1 but he had done nothing. In cross-examination by defen- dant, who appeared to be a very obstinate man, the collector said it was quite correct that the couple had another son who lived at Bank Quay, but be had a wife and two children to I keep, two of whom were unwell. Defendant said his parents I had paid rates and taxes 56 years, during which time the father had worked for Mr. Baxter. Defendant had an order made upon him to pay 21. 6d. weekly and costs lie. 6d. He, with a very bold front, said he might give his mother the 2s. 6d. weekly, but he would not pay a penny to the Guardians. YESTERDA.Y.—Before Mr. John Brundrit, and Mr. Charles W. Hazlehurst. CHARGE OF FELONY AGAINST A BUTCHER.—Harry Harrison, a butcher, was charged with stealing Sibs. of suet, 3lbs. of beef, four iron weights, and a number of looks and skewers, the property or Mr. George Booth, butcher, Run- corn. Robert Spafford, brother-in-law to the prosecutor, identified the things, and said that prisoner had been in Mr. Booth's employ for about eight months. Prosecutor had a shop in Regent-street, and a slaughter-house in Halton-road. The two pieces of suet produced were safe in the ship at about seven o'clock on Thursday morning. Owing to having suspicion of the prisoner, he inserted about half-a-dozen small pieces of paper, with Booth's name upon them in the I suet. He identified several of the things produced in court as beieg the prosecutor's.—Sergeant Handford proved going to the prisoner's house on Thursday morning and finding the suet in one of the rooms upstairs, and the other property in various parts of the house.—Sergeant McMichael said he apprehen led the prisoner, who admitted being guilty of te sling the 911.1.1 het deni,l having stolen the other things. —He was remanded until Monday.

div.head: LATE MISS ANN JOHNSON, OF
div.p: THE LATE MISS ANN JOHNSON, OF

RUNCORN. With reference to the recent death of this much respected lady, who was a constant worshipper •at Holy Trinity Church, and a friend of all charitable movements connected with the parish, the Rev. William Preston, incumbent, on Sunday night last preached a sermon from Acts ix. 39, and remarked The lote)s which the Christian Church at Joppa sustained in the death of Dorcas was but temporary. But at Holy Trinity they bad sustained a permanent loss, by the hand of death, of an old, faithful, and attached member, concerning whom it would in truth be most unbecoming of him got to say something from that pulpit. Miss Ann John- son was no Imre. Death had taken her away, and she sweetly slept in Jesus; but their loss was her gain. Of her they could say— I know thou art gone t ) the home of that rest, Then why should my soul be so sad? I know thou bast gone where the weary are blest. And the mourner looks uo and is glad. She was in truth a very Dorcas. Her faith in Christ was exhibited in works of charity, in good deeds, and in alms- giving. It showed itself in loving and anxious solicitude for the welfare of others and for the salvation of souls. She was an ardent supporter of the Church Missionary Society, of the Bible Society, of the Jews' Society, and kindred socie. ties. She threw herself energetically into the work of the parish, and like the Dorcas of old, and the Master whom she served, she went about doing good. She was diligent as a Sunday school teacher, and active as a district visitor; in fact, she was useful in every department of the Church, and helped both by purse and by counsel. The last enterprise in which she was actively engaged was the bazaar which was held to clear off the heavy debt upon Trinity Church Day Schools. Yes, in that very church they had something to remind them most per- petually of her; for those comfortable pews resulted from her suggestion and from her initial enterprise. She gave the work the initial impulse by suggestion, and by offering to raise a certain substantial sum, in order that the work might be carried out; and this she did. With a clear conscience he could ray—and would to God be could say it of everyone—she was a Christian in thought, a Christian in life, a Christian in walk, in conduct, in con- versation, and in consistency. But now all was over, and she was reaping the reward of well doing. The widows of old showdl Peter the coats and garments which Dorcas made while she was with them, and of their Dorcas they could. point out the things she did while among them, and further, they could say in truth, " Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord; even so saith the Spirit for they rest from their labours and their works." Oh how much better was it to spend a life for Christ and His serv,ce lather than to live a cold unsympathetic listless life; living for themselves alone and doing little or nothing for Christ's service. Which would bring the highest reward? Which kind of life would cause their name after they were departed to be held in most lasting remembrance? The brief sentence, "Well done, good and faithful servant," would amply atone for a life of self-denial and hard work in the Lord's vineyard. They would sadly miss her who was gone. They could not but sorrow and sympathize with those who more immediately sorrowed for her, but should they not rather rejoice, for she was now at rest. She had entered the home above, and joined with the redeemed whose robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb; and with them united in extolling the Lamb who redeemed them by His own precious blood. There was a large congregation. Mr. John Itavenscroft, organist, played, as the opening voluntary, "Blessed are the Departed," aid at the close, "The Dead March in Saul."

COMMEMORATION DINNER. On Wednesday, the 21st anniversary of the formation of "A" Company was commemorated by a dinner given at the Fleece Hotel. Colour-Sergeant Dunn occupied the chair, wko was supported by Lieut.-Col. Gamble, Captain Bramwell, Major Willcocks, Captains Windus, Johnson, and White. Fifty members were present, out of the total num- ber of 64. The dinner was served in Mrs. Taylor's usual good style. The menu consisted of ox tail soup and spring soup. Removes: Roast beef, roast pork, boiled fowls, roast turkey and sausages, ham, tongue, boiled leg of mutton. Sweets: Pastry, blanc mange, cheese, salad. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts had been given, Captain BRAMWELL proposed the toast of the officer commanding the 21st L.R.V., Lieut.-Col. Gamble. He might say be came there very innocently that evening, and had no expectation whatever that he should be called upon to pro- pose what they would all look upon as the toast of the evening. (Cheers.) He thought it was about, as near as he could remember, 21 years and 6 months since that very same room, which had that evening sounded to the clatter of knives and forks resounded to the tramp, tramp, tramp of No. 1 company of what was then the 47th Lanca- shire Rifle Volunteers. (Cheers.) He, among a few others —he should like to know how many othemprobably not more than a dosen—(a voice: four)—present joined No. 1 com- pany ; and they bad at that time a very important duty to perform, a duty which they performed ably, and that was the appointment of a gentleman as their leader, a gentleman who had the ability and stability to preside over them, com- mand them, and who had led them on to what they now were, a large, strong, and able regiment—that gentleman was Lieutenant -Colonel Gamble. ( Cheers.) Colonel Gamble was the first captain of No. 1 Regiment, and he (the speaker) rememsered with what feeling of responsibility Colonel Gamble took upon himself the duties of his office, and he had no doubt that the feeling of responsibility still lay at his door. They had progressed up to the present time, and he was quite sure that it was to Colonel Gamble— much more than many of them thought—they owed the present status of their regiment, not only in its finance and drill, but in many other important points which they had not time to go into that evening. (Cheers.) He thought, therefore, they could not do less than propose the health of Colonel Gamble. The health of the colonel was enthusiastically drunk with musical honours. • Colonel GAMBLE, in responding, said he had unfortunately been away from duty a good deal last year, and if the reporters were not present, he should be inclined to make a confessmn. Though he bad not been at drill, he would not say that he had not been on regimental duty. He could not resist the pleasure of accept- ing the invitation of which they had been good enough to give him to be present. At the cummemoration of the formation of the "A" Company should he say—no he would propose to call it the formation of the 47th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers. (Cheers.) It consisted at the time of only one I company, and that company made several drills in that very room. A great many changes had taken place since its formation, and he need not tell them of the increase in numbers; and he need not repeat what he was very fond of repeating, namely, what they had done in the way of shoot- ing, and the credit .they had got for their drill sometimes. He need not tell them they had risen from a single com- pany to ten companies. (Cheers.) He was glad to notice their friends in scarlet that evening as off-shoots of the 47th doing credit to the dress they wore. He did not know whether a great many of them would remember the kind of ' drill they began with. He had been trying to find the first I drill book, but unfortunately the housemaid had been re- arranging his library, and he could only find the 6th edition. The book was written by a distinguished soldier, Colonel LiSSODS, and be put into it all he I considered necessary for a volunteer to know. The writer had taken the advice of Sir Charles Napier that la volunteer should learn to march, wheel company, form ' squares, and rallying squares, and quoted the words of Sir Charles—" Don't let anybody persuade you to learn more." (Laughter.) lie (Colonel Gamble) knew nothing about soldiering when the movement commenced; he had lived in peace. He did not believe in going to war for glory, but had a desire in those days to prevent the Frenchmen meddling with his wife antifamily, and either to shoot them or be shot, if necessary. (Cheers.) Knowing nothing of soldiering he took the best guide he could, and if they re- membered their early drill in that room as conducted by two sergeants from the Warrington militia, they would know they had great difficulty in keeping the sergeants to what he might call the three R's of the duty of a soldier or volunteer. The sergeants liked going into more elaborate manoeuvres, which did not belong to regular drill. He (Colonel Gamble) therefore did not find himself master of the situa- tion, but when they got Sergeant Hudsor, whom those who were seven years in the regiment knew, they commenced to learn under his tuition the formation of battalion squares, as far as it could be done in that room; and he remembered quite well following Sergeant Hudson into the next room and seriously pointing out to him that they would have none of that in future. (Laughter.) However, before they had been live years in the service they were ordered to take the red book and go through the duties of a soldier, and most of those present had joined the force under those rules. They had tried to do their duty in learning that drill book. lie could not say that it had been done very effectually by him- self. Captain Windus was said to be the best drill in the regiment, and knew the drill book from beginning to end. (Cheers.) They had, however, done their duty in such a way as not to disgrace themselves. It was always con- sidered that a volunteer should be a good shot, and the greater part of that little book which he would pass round for their perusal was devoted to musket instruction; and they expected to be so efficient as to be able to stand behind a hedge to be shot at. They had produced a great many good shots, and the volanteers genetally throughout The country had learnt to use their rifles as to he able to in- troduce considerable improvements in the rifle shooting of the army. It was said that they had got something to learn yet, and no doubt their division would have to adopt plans by which the g 'eat bulk of the volunteers would become like Sergeants West, Junor, and Taylor whom they were all so proud of, and be able to hit the mark at three or four hundred yards without spending ten rounds of ammunition in the attempt. (Laughter.) He did not know how many men they could consider first rate shots in their regiment, but it was quite clear that three-fourths, or five-sixtbs,or six- sevenths of their regiment could not shoot nearly so well as they ought to do, and it would be well if they could adopt some means by which they could he induced to take some pride in their shooting. He did not know how it was to be done, but it was quite clear that it would have to be done. , As for himself he had done what he could for the regiment, and he was sorry that he had, throw;li unfortunate circum- stances, been obliged to neglect a great deal of his work which he ought to have done. But he had not neglected the regi- ment, and as soon as he was able, he would try to make up 'fel- it in better superintendence than he had (lane. Talking about old drills be had found a much older book than the other without date, but he had reason to believe it was printed before thebegiuning of this centary.ll contained some details of the drills and regulations of the volunteers in force at the beginning of the century. There were some little pictures in the first and last pages illustrative of manual, tiring, and platoon exercises in those days. It was given to him bye person who said he wane volunteer in the olden days. St. Helens must have had a pretty considerable volunteer force from 1804, to 1812 and from the accounts he had heard they used to assemble; on Moor Flat always on a Sunday. (Laughter.) The farmers' carts, with the best horses in the neighbourhood. attended, everyone being there belonging to the regiment, both men and women—(laughter)—and it was said their principal duty was getting out of the carts. (Laughter.) The women were regularly. there as nurses, enrolled as volunteers, and were expected to march with the regiment when it did march. This was go ng a little further into military completeness than the Liverpool volunteers ven- tured at the lest review at Aintree when they brought their ambulance waggons with them. It was a very necessary part of the volunteer movement, and one which the 47th had not yet commenced. He congratulated them upon the happy idea of commemorating the formation of the corps, and resumed his seat amid applause. The CHAIRMAN proposed the health of the officers of "A" Company. Having known the several officers of "A" dur- ing a period of 21 years, it was with a strong feeling of pleasure that he proposed their health. He had always known them to respect them, and he was only re-echoing the sentiments of "A" Company when he said that as a body they esteemed their officers as no other company in Lancashire did. They took very great pains in trying to make them as efficient as possible. They summoned the men to drill by circular time after time, and if any member of the company was behind in his drill he got a pleasant reminder that the: e was to be a drill at the hall on a certain night. He had , heard it expressed that Captain Windus had no equal amongst the volunteers. (Cheers.) He thought it would Ibe hard to find his equal amongst the volunteers. At the reviews he had heard individuals, who were qualified to pass an unbiassed opinion, say that Captain Windus was par excellence as a soldier. lie coupled with the toast the names of Captains Windus and Johnson. The toast having been drunk, Captain VVirmus responded, and in the course of his re- marks said he had not been at every drill on account of his business arrangements, but he could say that he had been present at every review since the first one in July, 1860. (Cheers.) He had been present at every inspection of the corps, and it gave him very great pleasure to be able to esti; that. He was a ppsdnted ensign on the 29th February, 1866; lieutenant on the sth April, 1862; and captain on the 20,1 i September, 1865. On the 3rd March, 1860, the regiment was sworn in before the magistrates in the Town Hall, and 54 men attended. The company had kept well together, and although they had never reached the maximum of 100, they had numbered over 90. He bad never asked a person to jog' the corps, but it had been purely the spontaneous offering; of the men so far as he was concerned. He thought it was the duty Al every young man who had the opportunity to be- come a volunteer, because the discipline, although not severe, was calculated to improve them morally and physically, and gave them an object in life. He did not think the Government encouraged the Volunteers as much as they ought to do and he did not know why 500,000 should not be the limit instead of 200000. the great centres of the Volunteer movement were in Lantashite, Yorkshire, Middlesex, and Lanarkshire in Scotland; and he did not see why it should not be developed in other places,

as he believed it would be if the Government would offer greater encouragement. Some little difficulty was ex- perienced in finding suitable officers, but they could get over that difficulty by appointing officers of the line who retired on half pay. Having spoken of shooting and urged the necessity of greater attention to this branch of the ser- vice, he said that his father-in-law was a sergeant of the Volunteers in 1803 and went through the drill of mounting carts—(laughter)--and on one occasion marched to Chester with the garrison. They had now better travelling facilities, and did not need carts to take them from one end of the

kingdom to the other. Captain Joniesox also responded. The CHAIRMAN gave the toast of the non-commissioned officers, and coupled with it the names of Colour-sergeant Ashton and Corporal S Wolfenden. The toast was drunk, and Colour-sergeant ASHTON responding, said the first drill I took place OR the 30th January, 1860, and he put in, from that time to the 3rd March following, when the corps was sworn in, 43 drills. The first rifle contest was on the 30th October. Corporal S. WOLFIINDEN also responded, and said that the duties of non-commissioned officers were not sufficiently known, and those who took their places were sometimes placed in an awkward position. He suggested that an am- bulance department be formed in connection with the corps, as he had known some of the members to require medical assistance when out in the field. Private F. Honnsow proposed the health of "Our shoot- ing members" in a few well chosen remarks; and at this juncture Col. Gamble referred to a member of the corps— Sergeant West—who, on account of his energy, perseverance, and success had done much to uphold the character of the corps. He wished to ask if something could not be done in the way of subscription to provide him with a left sleeve. (Laughter.) His present one was covered with badges of all kinds, and there was really no place for any more; and it would be a great trial to him to have to give up. They could buy him a new sleeve to receive fresh badges, and the other one could hang behind. (Applause.) The toast having been drunk, Sergeant WEST responding humorously, said they should also provide him with a glass case with a silver plate in front. He enumerated some of the principal prizes won by the members of the corps, and remarked that soon after the formation of the corps the first county Lancashire rifle meeting was held at Altcar, from which place the 47th (now 21st) took away £326 whilst £421 was left for the remainder of the county. Private J. J. TICKLE also suitably responded. Captain WHITE proposed the health of "The Staff," and coupled with the toast the name of Adjutant Major Will- cock., of whom the proposer said his instructions were plain and simple' and drill efficiency could be obtained by atten- tion under his instructions. Major WILLCOCKS, in responding, said that was a proud moment for him, as he was the first appointed adjutant of that corps. "The past members of 'A' company" was proposed by Captain WINDUS, and responded to by ex-Serjeant WooD. The " Ladies " was suitably proposed and responded to by Private E. A. ROBINSON and Corporal J. L. WOLFENDEN respectively. Lieutenant-Colonel GAMBLE proposed "The Chairman," and said that Colour-Serjeaut Dunn was one of the early members of the corps. He was number 12 on the regi- mental roll, which numbered 5,600. The CHAIRMAN responded, and the proceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem. At intervals during the evening, songs were rendered by Private Pentland and Mr. J. Taylor.

THE LATE REV. J. WILKINSON. OF LATCHFORD. A very impressive service was held on Sunday afternoon, in Bethel Baptist Chapel, Latchford, on the occasion of the delivery of the funeral sermon of the late Rev. Joseph Wil- kinson, pastor of the chapel. It will be remembered that the rev. gentleman's death took place on the 10th inst., and as he was deservedly esteemed and highly respected by a very large circle of friends, the announcement that his funeral sermon would be preached by the Rev. Jos. Harvey, of Bury, on Sunday last, drew togethSr a vast concourse of people. Some time previous to the time fixed for the com- mencement of the service the chapel wad filled, and the aisles and vestries were also crowded to overflowing, many having come a long distance to be present, and the affection shown for the deceased pastor was manifest by the fact that at times during the service there was scarcely a dry eye in the chapel. Mr. HARVEY took for his text the 12th verse of 14th chap- ter of Matthew's gospel—" And his (John Baptist's) disciples came and took up the body and buried it, area went and told Jesus," He said : Death is very busy in our midst. Since we commenced this service there have been according to calculations made with some degree of precision, 30 of our fellow creatures gone into eternity, and before the close of the service there will be 60 added to the number, so that during the l hours, comprising the length of our present service, some 90 persons will have left this earth for the eternal world. Solemn thought! for both preacher and hearer! Death lately has had some high marks; the wearers of crowns have had preached in their ears a solemn warning in that sudden and lamentable death of the Emperor of Russia. They seem to me to be thus addressed—" Seek ye the crown that will never fade in the kiagdoin from which you can never be dispossessed." Men in high office in our own country have had an admonition front on high that statesmen, however and whatever might be their poli- tical opinions, have to prepare for that event that is com- mon to all. It seems to say to all alike, rulers and ruled, "Be ye also ready." The ranks of our ministerial body have been visited, and the Spurgeon of the Wesleyans, Dr. Punshon, has been called away when we might have sup- posed there were still years of work in him ; and to-day we are summoned together (and I feel the task to be no easy one) to improve the removal of one from amongst us, who was much and deservedly loved by all. I hold that these men—Dr. Punshon and Joseph Wilkinson —as representatives of the ministerial body, occupied a position greater than the emperors who wear the purple or the statesmen who hold the destinies of nations, for if we are faithful preachers we are God's ambassadors, receiving from His lips the message we have to deliver to our fellow men. Among the fallen noble . and mighty, I reckon the man brought before us in connection with our text, John Bap- tist—the Dreadnought of his day—a man who feared not the face of men nor courted thei smile of the king. He died a violent death. He became the victim of foolish dancing. He did not dance himself, but a giddy girl danced before King Herod and his court, and the monarch, when excited bY wine and bad company, was so pleased that a giddy girl could skip so pleasantly, that he said to her "I will give thee whatever thou askest, even to the half of my kingdom." The girl knew not what to ask, so she went to ask her mother, who proved to be an unwise counsellor, for in answer to the girl's enquiry, "What shall I ask for ?" she said, "Go back and ask for the head of John Baptist, who told me I did wrong to live with another man. I'll silence that accuser ; I'll shut that month that dared to charge me with adultery. Go back and ask for his head, and tell them to put it on a dish and give it you." And she went and asked for it, and she got it; but Herod might have kept his vow, and John's head might have remained on his shoulders, for that head was worth more than the whole of Herod's kingdom, but he understood it not. If there are any here who see no harm in the dance, let them look at the court of Herod, look at the girl dancing betore them, look at the head still quiver- ing, and bloodying the dish all over. All the doing of the dancing. I knew a young lady in Liverpool 'who attended a ball held in St. George's Hall. She dressed for it, or rather partially dressed for it, and in the evening when heated and flushed with the dancing she passed to her carriage. It was but a short die- tance, but the cold wind assailed her, and her death fol- lowed. Another victim to the folly of dancing; and how many have lost their virtue there. But, say some, " Yon are going to stamp out our pleasure." Not so : no greater mistake could be made. We want to give lasting pleasure and a hope of Heaven, and that will make your hearts dance with joy and gladness, aid you will praise and bless the Lord. There is one thought I should like to enforce before we come to the purpose of our meeting, and that is the in- ' tense suffering to which the early Christians were subjected. Besides the ordinary ailments of life they had some extra- ordinary trials, seine of which we find in connection tvith 1 John the forerunner's history. Here, in the Bible, is the record of another successor in the work,—Stephen stoned to death at the bands of the persecutor. Here also is the re- cord of the doings of Paul before his conversion when he was busy from morning to night hailing to prison all that he found calling upon the name of the Lord Jesus. In our day it is easy to make a profession of religion ; then it was dangerous. Were it not for taxing your patience I should like to give some additional proof of this. Where Paul is writing to the Corinthians, and giving them a short account of his suffering after his conversion, we find an example of what you farmers know something about, that " Whatsover a man eoweth that shall he also reap." Paul once sowed sorrow, now he was reaping it. In the 11th chapter of his 2nd Epistle to the Corinthians, he says, " In stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft. Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one. Thrice was I beaten aith rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered ship- wreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; in journeyings often, in perils of water, in perils of robber's, in ; perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the sea, in perils among I false brethren; in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fasting.; often, in cold and nakedness. Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily the care of all the chinches. And why is this P God loves His people, loves them with an everlasting love. Why then does He permit them to suffer. Ills here. He does two things by it. In the first place He shows the wickedness of man in doing these evil deeds, and in the second place He shows the power of His grace to eustain them under it. Man is so wicked as to do them. God is so good as to sustain under them. John lost his head, a young man of 30, in the prime of life. Strange providence this! But this is not all. It was the beginning of the Gospel of 'Christ, and men I were to have proof of its divine origin. To do this the gold was put into the fine and subjected to trill 'rho doctrines of Christ which have thus stood the test are those ; on which we rest our immortal interests, thus less-inc not only the wickedness of man ; to be revealed but the grace of God in sustaining under the 'sufferings inflicted. The disciples of .John had lost their

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

These returns show that the total population of Runcorn I is 14,757, being an increase of 2,693 during the decade. Of this number 7,456 are males, and 7,273 females. There will Also be a floating population of about 300 to be added to this. In Weston and Weston Point the population is 1.674, being an increase of 214. This number is made up of 911 males, and 763 females. During the last ten years there has been a decrease in the population of Halton of 181. The popu- lation of that township is returned as 1,439, made up of 707 males, and 732 females. The total population within the Runcorn Urban Sanitary District, or within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, is 15,066.

ST. HELENS, PRESCOT, AND FARNWORTH. The census returns for the Prescot union have not yet ken completed, but they probably will be in a few days. The returns sent in are as follow :—St. Helens district.— Eccleston, 13,436 inhabitants; Sutton, 12,696 (including the inmates of the asylum); Parr, 11,272; Windle, 19,469; total, 56,873. Of this number 29,510 were males, and 27,363 females. Prescot district,—Eccleston, 4,599; Prescot, 5,546; Rainhill, 2.219; Whiston (including the inmates of the workhouse), 2,705; total, 15,069. 7,605 were males, and 7,464 females. Farnworth district,—Bold 880; Cronton, 468; Ditton, 1.412; Widnes, 24,871: total, 27,631, including 14,831 males, and 12,750 females. These figures are subject to alterations when the books are received at the central office, London.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION.

The returns of the census of the Warrington Union, as supplied to us by the superintendent registrar, Mr. J. C. Sutton, show an increase in the populations of all the town- ships, except Southworth-with-Croft and Houghton, during the last ten years. In the township of Warrington there are 7,802 families, who inhabit 7,381 houses. With regard to dwelling-houses the census shows that Alderman Kean was not far from the mark when he stated a short time ago that there were in Warrington 500 empty houses, as the official statement gives the number of uninhabited houses at 477. The population within the municipal boundary has in- creased during the last decade from 29,174 to 37,482, and that within the extra municipal boundary from 723 to 3,478, the total population being 40,960, which gives an increase of 11,063 in comparison with 1871, when the total population was 29,897. In the ecclesiastical parishes the census reveals the following results :.—St. Elphin's, 16,400; St. Paul's, 13,492; St. Anne's. 5,689 ; and Holy Trinity, 5,379; but we are unable to institute a comparison with the last census as to the growth of the population in these districts. Middleton, arid Arbury Newton and Haydock 3,017 2,928 8,747 7,696 16,443 13,530 Burtonwood 224 1,288 1,112 Cuerdley 221 185 Penk,th Sankeyllo 633 630 On the whole the schedules had been intelligently filled up, although the orthography on some of the papers would have delighted Artemas Ward. The schedules from the lower quarters of the town had for the most part been filled by the younger members of the families, and the schoolboy handwriting upon the papers gave unmistakeable evidence that the enforcement of the Elementary Education Act is having the desired effect. There were, of course, many amusing instances met with in making up the returns. In many cases children of tender years had been seriously described as " unmarried "; and one man who, whilst not going so far as to describe his wife as his "better half," evidently regarded her as his equal, both being entered as "head of the house." The enumerators, too, witnessed several humourous incidents which tended to relieve the monotony of the work in which they were engaged. One enumerator called at a house in the kitchen of which he found a man and three children. Accosting the man he told him the object of his visit, when the householder, whose condition showed that he had spent a considerable portion of his week's earnings in the "dear cratur," peremptorily said "Take ish 'way. I won't hav'sli yer papersh." The enumerator endeavoured to explain what he was leaving. but was again cut short by the man who hiccapped " Go. awaysh—hic—and take—hic—yer papersh—hio yoush." Although the man was angry, the enumerator began to reason with him and by and by the inebriate softened down, when it transpired that the cause of his anger arose from the fact that he had mistaken the census paper for a summons which he was expecting for neglecting to send his children to school. At another house the only oct,upant was an old lady of the Mrs. Gamp type, who, after the enumerator had explained the object of his visit, quickly asked " how much he would pay her for her trouble in filling up the paper ?" The old lady was apparently not in the habit of rendering gratuitous services to any one, as it was a long time before he could convince her that there " was no pay about it" on his part, but that there would be on hers if she failed to give the rewired Information. On collecting the papers an enumerator called at a house ef which the only occupant was an elderly Irishwoman, clean and respectable, who in- formed him in the richest brogue that she "hadn't a frind to help her laid the papher." The enumerator expressed his readiness to act the part of the "friend in need," on which she eyclaimed "God save ye, sorr, ye're a koind hearted gintleman," and after he had filled up the schedule she called Upon all the saints in the calendar to bless him.

The census reveals the startling fact that a decrease in the population of rural parishes in the West of England is going on with a rapidity which threatens almost entire de- population. Towns are becoming villages and villages hamlets, while hamlets are passing out of existence, tiers are some figures :

teacher and master, and they came and toek up the body and went and buried it. The occasion of our services to- day is something like this; and I want to point out one thing, and that is the resemblance between John the Baptist and Joseph Wilkinson. Both were children of Godly parents, and both had received Godly training. Zacharias and Elizabeth were the parents of our Lord's forerunner, and we have their characters given to us with clearness and and brevity. They were both righteous before God—walk- ing in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. It was John's position to be trained under their roof and subject to their teaching; and my brother Wilkin- son, although ascribing his conversion in the first instance to God, owed much to a praying and God-fearing mother and the teaching in the Sunday school at Hill Cliffe. God be praised for Sunday schools and for the success with which He blesses them I There was another point of resemblance. They were both sound Baptists. If I have any Methodist friends here, pray bear with me whilst I mention this. Don't be afraid of a little cold water. I say they were both sound Baptists. There was no mistake about my brother; but although he held firmly to Baptist principles, yet he could hold out his hand to all who loved the Lord in sincerity, and say to such, "Grace, truth, and mercy be multiplied." It was his to preach fearlessly the whole commission, "Go ye, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost." The preaching first, baptising after, mark you. Do not change the order; if you have done so, re-change it at once. This was John's teaching; this was the teaching of Jesus Christ; and thisis the teaching of the New Testament, so I believe. John cried to those who came to be baptised of him, "Bring forth fruits meet for repentance," and not till he saw the fruits did he baptize them; and this was my brother Joseph Wilkinson's teaching. I find that during the course of his udnistry he administered the ordinance to some 106 professed believers, showing that it was to him not a matter of theory only, but an every day practice. Lien there is another point of resemblance, and that is they were both successful preachers. We cannot tell much about John's early ministry, but I have some information respecting my brother Wilkinson's work. The first time his voice was heard in public was at a little prayer meeting at Hill Cliff, where a few of the mem- bers were met together one week evening. Here he lifted rip his voice in prayer to God with such an effect upon those present that impulsively they sang, " Praise God from whom all blessings flow." As for his first attempt at speaking, it was at Little Leigh, during the course of some pro- tracted revival services that were being held there. Here someone called on him to speak (I think I had something to do with it) and I was much rejoiced to hear his voice raised in addressing his fellow sinners and speaking of the Divine Redeemer. That is now 40 years since. His last sermon was preached in this place four months ago, when the address of Anna, the prophetess, on our Lord's presentation to the Temple, was his theme. To illustrate more fully the character of our brother, I would say that within three weeks of his removal he desired that one of his children might take down from his lips the out- line of a sermon he intended to preach if he recovered and could occupy the pulpit again. The text was the 28th verse of the Bth chapter of St. Paul's Epistle to Romans, " We know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them that are the called according to his pur- pose." Instead of preachiog the sermon here he is experi- encing its blessedness yonder. As regards his work in con- nection with this church, I would say that for 18 months in his own hired house at Stockton Heath he was telling the tale of a Saviour's love. Afterwards the Old Barn Chapel was vacated by some of the Wesleyan brethren, and the Baptists took it aad worshipped there for 13 years until becom- ing too small it was thought desirable to build a larger place, and 21 years ago the foundation of the building in which we are now assembled was laid, and it was opened for divine worship 20 years ago last Good Friday. Three years since the spacious schoolroom in the rear of this building was built, and our brother was able to see it free trona debt. With regard to spiritual results, I find that some 33 met together for worship at first, and between 60 and 70 are left, so that not a few of the 106 who were bap- tised by him have welcomed your pastor to the better world. Just a few words now on the funeral. John's disciples came and took up the headless body of their master and buried it; and just such a solemn and impressive service I wit- nessed on the day before Good Friday.. Whilst the proces- sion wended its way to the old burial ground at Hill Cliff there were two or three little incidents that I shall here notice. I saw that amongst the school children there was not one but what here some mark to denote that they were mourning for their pastor. It might be only a black hat or a black ribbon that was worn, but still the feeling was plainly manifest. This was particularly noticeable amongst the girls. The body also was borne upon the shoulders of men who- had benefited by my brother's labours. They took up the body, just as John's disciples did, and when the last act ef kindness had been done, and the body committed to its last resting place, they went and told Jesus. We sometimes go and pour the tale of our sorrow into the ears of our fellow creatures, and though they may have a heart to feel, yet they have not a band to help. It is not so with Jesus. r. His hands bear the print of the nails, showing how much he suffered that he ight help and save. Go and tell Jesus; tell him all—what you dare not tell to the nearest and dearest friend you have. The Lord Jesus sometimes removes our loved ones that there may be nothing to come between us and Him. Jesus was to follow John. Jesus was greater than John, and John must give place to Jesus. "He must increase," .said John, but I must decrease :" as if he had said, "I must stand aside now that you may get at Jesus." For this purpose, this closer union to Himself He sometimes empties the cradle, leaving little shoes, and silences the little prattling voice that was once the joy of the home, 'and all this that we may come closer to Himself. Such are his methods. Our brother is gene, but is the partiog a final one? Am I never to see his smiling happy face again, or hear his kind, sincere words again. I have to see him again. I have to meet him again. I have to hear him again. His singing was joyful here, but not what it is up yonder. I • know he has sung at times with a tearful eye and quivering voice, but now That poor, lisping, stammering tongue Lies silent In the grave, In a far nobler, sweeter song, He sings His power to save. Have you the same grace as our brother? Have you the same hope? I know that he has wept and prayed for you often, and he has spoken to you often • for I find that he must have delivered, during his minis- terial life, no fewer than 1,600 sermons ; and those who are in the habit of speaking !mow what an am ount of labour and anxiety is here entailed. Now that he has gone you may say that you have lost a friend, yea, one of your best friends; but if you trust in the Lord Jesus Christ you'll meet again, and part never. I want to meet him again and to stay with him. I want you to do it too, but only believers in Christ can ever hope for it. God prepare you for it; and if our brother's life has not had an effect upon you, may his death impress you. May the Lord bless the sorrowing bereaved ones, and to one and all I would say, "Go and tell Jesus." In the evening a very affecting prayer meeting was held in the school-room at which the Rev. J. Harvey and other friends delivered Crief addresses.

----....,..—_-------- the Investigation Committee were the most perplexing coin mittees connected with the Council. It had been suggested that more children be sent to the industrial school, and they hardly knew what to do. At the last Investigation Committee 182 were before them; 39 were ordered to be . summoned, and 31 had been fined.—Alderman Johnson re- marked that it would be a very good thing for some of them if their children were taken away from them.—Mr. Craik , mentioned a case of a boy who had only attended 16 timer out of 35. That lad went down upon his knees is the office and promised him (Mr. Craik) that he would never be Absent again, yet he was as bad as ever. This was all the business.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, Councillor Cook presiding. There were also present--Aldermen Cook and Johnson; Councillors Bishop and Wilcock.

div.head: OFFICERS' REPORTS.
div.p: OFFICERS' REPORTS.

- Mr.TßogAs DUTTON reported that since the date of las' meeting the names of 918 absent and irregular scholars had been sent in by the teachers of the schools in his district. Notices to appear before the Investigation Committee were served on 69 parents representing 138 irregular scholars, and 14 summonses were ordered to be taken out against parents who did not give a reasonable excuse for their children's irregular attendance; and on the 25th inst. 12 were fined in the usual penalty of 55., including costs, the other two cases- being dismissed. During the month he had filled up and signed 215 children's school books. To recover tines inflicted by the magistrates in former cases he had obtained eight commitments and one distress warrant. Five parents had since paid OR the commitments, on had been sent to prison, and two commitments were not yet executed. In the case of the distress warrant the defendant had since paid both fine and costs. Mr. BAMFORD reported that 848 absent and irregular scholars had been reported by the teachers in ' his district. The parents of 130 of the most irregular had been notified to appear before the Investigation Committee. Twenty-five parents not being able to give reasonable ex- cuses ler their children's absence, were ordered to be sum- moned, and the following were the results :-19 fined 6d. and costs; 3 attendance orders granted with a view of send- ing the boys to the truant school; 2 dismissed (in one case the mother produced a doctor's certificate stating the child had been sick ; and in another case the father stated he had been in the hospital for some time, and promised that the boy should attendlregularly for the future); 1 case adjourned for a month in order that investigation might he made; 1 boy, Patrick Gallagher was ordered to be sent to the indus- trial school.—The committee decided to take steps for the admission of two boys to the truant school. REMARKS ON THE ATTBNDANCE OF CHILDREN. Alderman Johnson asked how often the officers visited, or I should visit the schools. Mr. Bamford replied that it de- I pended on the extent of the connection they had with school.—Alderman Johnson: But for the purpose of ascer-. taming how the scholars attend Bamford : The teachers send in a list every fortnight; but when we want to get a special return of the attendance we don't wait. 1 very often call in when I have no business in hand.---Alder- man Johnson: I ask this because they say there are a good many children not attending.--Mr. Bamford :It is their own fault. When the teachers send us a report we attend to it. Alderman Johnson: How often do they ,report ?—Mr. Bain- ford : Usually every fortnight; but we have only received about two reports from the Holy Cross School this year, and then I had to fetch one of the lists.—In answer to Alderur Johnson, Mr. Biinford said the school in question was the " nuns' " school.—A conversation ensued, in which e Chairman said the children were attending very badly, and no doubt poverty had thaoufte ailt deal to do with h.—Alderman Joth nsto n was soynething worse than poverty, and that in certain cases school they could not be too severe. The mei Committee did not take action as often as they ought to do.—Councildo Bishop smilingly suggested that Alderman Johnson shotikl attend the committee a little better.—Alderrnart Johns ii n promised to do so.—The Chairman acid this committee r

TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST CHESHIRE. CIENTLEMEN,—I hasten to return to you my sincere " thanks for the votes ,and support with which you have honoured me in the late contested election; the result of which, although not an actual viotory for the Liberal cause, nevertheless shows so marked a progress in Liberal prin- ciples throughout the constituency, as to be an earnest of future 1111CCEISs. lam satisfied that with future organization, and a stricter attention to the registration of voters, a victory may be en- sured on the neat occasion, when I shall be ready, should you do me the honour of again accepting me as your candidate, to contest the seat In the Liberal interest. I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant, JAMES TOMKINSON. Willington Hall, Tarporley, April 23rd, 1881.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE WEST DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF CHESTER. GENTLEMEN,-1 beg to return you my hearty thank for the honour which you have done me, in returning me as your representative to the House of Commons. lam extremely gratified to believe that the Election has been conducted throughout with an entire absence of that 111 feeling which so often embitters a political contest. I wish most gratefully to acknowledge the support which I have received from the majorlty of the Electors of this Divi- sion, and more especially to thank those kind friends who have exerted themselves so generously on vny behalf. To those who gave their support to my opponent I would say that, although I may be unable to represent their political opinions, still I shall always use my best endeavours to study their wishes and to support their interests. Again thanking you, Gentlemen, for the honour which you have done me, I remain, Your faithful Servant, HENRY J. TOLLEMACHE. Dorfold Hall, Nantwich, April 23rd, 1881.

THOMAS SUTTON, at the BLUE BELL INN, HOBSEMARKET-STREET, WARRINGTON, on WEDNEST>AIr, the 11th day of MAY, 1881, at 5 for 6 o'clock, in the Afternoon, Subject to certain conditions then and there to be produced. All that LEASEHOLD DWELLING-HOUSE, situate in Arpley-street, in Warrington, lately the property of Mr. Frederick Wall, veterinary surgeon. Also all that VETERINARY SURGERY, and the Hay Lofts above, the same, and five stables with accommodation for 12 horses, and the yard shed and other outbuildings adjoining the said Dwelling-house and Stables. The Dwelling-house is entirely ner and is well and substan- tially built by Messrs. Collin and Son, and contains on the ground floor, entrance hall; drawing-room, 18 feet by 16 feet; dining•room, 16 feet by 14 feet; large and small kitchens, pan- tries, lavatory, and the usual domestic offices ; on the first floor four good bedrooms, lavatory, bathroom, and vr.c., and the house has also good cellaring. The surgery, hay lofts, stables, and outbuildings were recently built by Messrs. Gibson. and are very substantial and well built. The stables comprise six loose boxes and stalls for six horses, and afford every accommodation for a veterinary sur- geon. The dwelling-house, stables, yard, and outbuildings are built upon 534 and square yards of land or thereabouts. Also all that valuable piece of BUILD NG LAND adjoining the above-named premises, and situate on the south side of Sankey-street and west side of Arpley-street, in Warrington aforesaid, measuring in front to Sankey. street aforesaid 45 feet or thereabouts, and measuring in front to Arpley-street a'ore- said 59 feet 6 inches or thereabouts, and containing in the whole 390 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts. This is a valuable piece of building land by reason of its frontages to Arplerstreet and Sankey-street. It is situate opposite Bank Park, and would prove a valuable investment for a builder. The whole of the above premises, including the site of the dwelling-house, surgery. stables, yard, and outbuildings, are held under a lease for 990 years, from the Ist day of January, 1877, at the yearly rent of £27 195.3 d., and contain in the whole by a recent admeasurement 924 and I square yards of land or thereabeuts. Theabove property would prove of great value to a Veterinary Surgeon starting business in Warrington, as it is perfect in accommodation and situate only a few yards from one of the busiest thoroughfares in the town. If a purchaser desired it could lje arranged that a considerable portion of the purchase money might remain on mortgage. The exceedingly Choke COLLECTION of PICTURES of the late Mr. Miller has been widely known as containing many very valuable and beautiful productions by the most celebrated painters of the present time. The more important are of that class which have proved strong attractions wherever they have been exhibited over the country; indeed every picture has recommended itself to the taste of its late possessor by its merit alone, and bears evidence of the judgment and great discrimi- nation which do honour ti his love and knowledge of art as a collector. The most remarkable Oil Pictures which may be considered In the highest degree of excellence, include J. M. W. Turner, R.A..'s grand work " Saltash, Devon' (engraved in the Royal Gallery of British Art) ; "A fine English Landscape," of gallery size, by Thomas Gainsborough, R.A.; " Oranmore, Gal- way Bay," a noble example of J. W. Oakes, A.R.A.; "A Vene- tian Water Girl," by Val Prinsep, A.R.A.; "The Surgeon's Daughter," one of the best specimens of W. L. Windus, besides several other equally important works by the same artist ; a remarkable portrait by Greuse ; The Outcast," W. Muller ; "The Forge," by Paul Boyer; " The Mother," a pleasing cabi- net work, by Ford Maddox Brown; a very fine portrait by Sir Joshua Reynolds, P.R.A.• "The Bowlers." by Sir George Har- vey, P.S.R.A..
